lou proposes a dialogical framework, but it is only vaguely drawn and mixes
wildly divergent ideas. By way of example, she (Fotopoulou 2012a) invokes Gadamer’s her-
meneutic notion of “horizons of understanding ” (the situated and contextual nature of all
understanding), acknowledges the “epistemological gulf” that exists between psychoana-
lysis and neuroscience, but then calls for “establishment of a clear and adequate concep-
tual framework that can be shared across different disciplines.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_129
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
ent of a clear and adequate concep-
tual framework that can be shared across different disciplines. Once such a framework is in
place, alternative explanations can be translated into a common language and can be
evaluated on empirical grounds” (p. 5). This is like Opatow ’s( 1999) aspirational, empirically
grounded bridging discourse, of course. One feels the slippage, unexplained, from the
notion of dialogue without any need for agreement, into “translation,”“ a common
language,” and “empirical evaluation.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_130
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
without any need for agreement, into “translation,”“ a common
language,” and “empirical evaluation. ”
It certainly seems as if epistemologically divergent knowledge is being collapsed into
an empirically validated, unimodal kind of knowledge, despite the fact that Fotopoulou ’s
framing description insinuates something quite different. She seems to endorse the dialo-
gical character of an anti-reductionist hermeneutic (Gadamer 1960, 1981), and proceeds
under the pretense that dialogue needn ’t risk alterations of epistemic commitments.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_131
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
, and proceeds
under the pretense that dialogue needn ’t risk alterations of epistemic commitments.
However, if difference is maintained, can real dialogue of this sort actually avoid epistemo-
logical violence of some kind? Can the objectivism of neuroscience “dialogue” with the
subjectively grounded interpretive epistemics of psychoanalysis without it resulting in
either incoherence or important epistemological accommodation? Because the knowl-
edge she is talking about is not all the same; the psychoanalytic mind, as I ’ve argued, is
a very particular elephant.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_132
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
about is not all the same; the psychoanalytic mind, as I ’ve argued, is
a very particular elephant.
In the end, neuropsychoanalytic integrationists do not regard the difference between
mind (which is grounded in subjective experience) and brain (which is an objectively
described neurobiological entity) to include difference at the level of fundamental ontology.
However, this disregards the idea that, because each exists as a different category of being, a
18Pulver (2003) also argues that partnership with neuroscience will not affect psychoanalytic technique or how we talk per-

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_133
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
ues that partnership with neuroscience will not affect psychoanalytic technique or how we talk per-
sonally with patients.
19Mayes’ (2005) neuropsychoanalytic description of the dialogue between the “two epistemologies ” of developmental
science and psychoanalysis is another influential example of this problem, where a methodological difference is misre-
presented as a meaningful epistemological distinction.
438 B. H. CLARKE
different kind of entity, each can be known and talked about only in certain ways, which
means they cannot be known or talked about in other ways.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_134
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
talked about only in certain ways, which
means they cannot be known or talked about in other ways. To this point, Mills ( 2012)
remarks specifically on the “mereological fallacy,” also discussed in Bennett and Hacker
(2003, 2007), operating in the neuroscientific position. He describes this as “a fundamental
attribution error where one ascribes the acts or characteristics of a whole to its parts, ” thus
reducing the human subject to “material-efficient reductive forces” (fn, p.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_135
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
le to its parts, ” thus
reducing the human subject to “material-efficient reductive forces” (fn, p. 53) or, in the case
of neuroscience as applied to psychoanalysis, reducing the mind to the brain.
There is indeed a material substructure and physical laws underlying every moment of
psychoanalytic experience. Also, there are physical patterns in the brain that correlate
(however complexly) with these “internal” subjective experiences.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_136
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
terns in the brain that correlate
(however complexly) with these “internal” subjective experiences. However, our experi-
ence is not of neurobiological patterns; it is rather of the mental events that accompany
these patterns, the feelings and thoughts, the rhythms and meanings.
When a feeling of existential dread washes over a patient, they might feel for a moment
that they can ’t breathe, but then they breathe, and then they talk, and perhaps the dread
subsides. However, without a language of dread, the language of receptors has no referent,
tells no story worth hearing.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_137
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
thout a language of dread, the language of receptors has no referent,
tells no story worth hearing. “It is worth remembering,” Dominique Scarfone (2012)r e m a r k s ,
“that there are no ‘words’ in Broca’sa r e aa n dn o‘fear’ in the amygdala, although these brain
structures are vital for speech and for feeling fear, respectively ” (p. 1288). Languages rep-
resent different ways of ordering reality, and sometimes different ways of determining
what “reality” is exactly, and then of coming to knowledge about that reality.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_138
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
ways of determining
what “reality” is exactly, and then of coming to knowledge about that reality. While neuro-
science is the realm within which research into neurological disorders is possible, it is gen-
erally not helpful in our talking about the meaning of anything, not even the meaning of
neuroscience (whether in a personal, cultural, historical, or psychological sense), without
resorting to a separate discourse designed to capture cultural or personal meanings.
The discourses of mind and brain: a semantic dualism

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_139
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
gned to capture cultural or personal meanings.
The discourses of mind and brain: a semantic dualism
The languages of mental and physical experience offer very different ways of looking at
oneself and the world. In saying this, we make an important shift. Although the brain is
a “thing,” a definable physical system, the only way we can know about it and talk
about it is by way of a kind of discourse, a brain discourse.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_140
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
nly way we can know about it and talk
about it is by way of a kind of discourse, a brain discourse. So we have mind discourses,
and we have brain discourses (Brothers 2002), and we use these different languages to
talk about perception, thought, memory, affect, or about our sense of self, meaning,
and value, all the ways in which we experience ourselves in the world. Ricoeur (Changeux
and Ricoeur 2003) expresses the difference very clearly:
These discourses represent heterogeneous perspectives, which is to say that they cannot be
reduced to each other or derived from each other.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_141
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
perspectives, which is to say that they cannot be
reduced to each other or derived from each other. In the one case it is a question of neurons
and their connection in a system; in the other, one speaks of knowledge, action, feeling —acts
or states characterized by intentions, motivations, and values. I shall, therefore, combat the
sort of semantic amalgamation that one finds summarized in the oxymoronic formula, “The
brain thinks.” (p.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_142
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
semantic amalgamation that one finds summarized in the oxymoronic formula, “The
brain thinks.” (p. 14)
Yet such amalgamation is endemic not just to neuropsychoanalytic writing, but to con-
temporary psychoanalytic discussion more broadly, a consequence of the widespread
assumption that brain language is applicable to any realm of psychoanalytic knowledge
—it should be permitted, that is, to go wherever it pleases.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_143
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
any realm of psychoanalytic knowledge
—it should be permitted, that is, to go wherever it pleases. When Damasio ( 2010) suggests
INT J PSYCHOANAL 439
that the principal objection to assuming equivalences between brain processes and
mental events is that “to date science has not been able to determine the physical attri-
butes of mental states ” (pp. 335 –336), he intends that the solution is at hand, which
assumes the reducibility of subjective mental experience to brain language or some
hybrid discourse.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_144
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
ssumes the reducibility of subjective mental experience to brain language or some
hybrid discourse. In this, I would suggest (adopting a phrase from Nagel ’s[ 1995a] critique
of Dennett), he “misses the real problem from the start ” (p. 86).
As Blass and Carmeli ( 2015, 2007) suggest, seeing mind and brain discourses not just as
different ways of looking, but as concerned with different objects (or subjects) of study,
appropriately complicates the causal linkages between them.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_145
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
fferent objects (or subjects) of study,
appropriately complicates the causal linkages between them. Just as there is no apparent
solution to the problem of consciousness (what is it, and how do we describe not just its
nature, but the simple fact of its existence?), there is no reductionist answer to the irredu-
cible “ontological density ” (Ricoeur 1973, 75) of mental experience.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_146
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
tionist answer to the irredu-
cible “ontological density ” (Ricoeur 1973, 75) of mental experience. As Nagel ( 1986) says,
“The subjectivity of consciousness is an irreducible feature of reality —without which we
couldn’t do physics or anything else —and it must occupy as fundamental a place in
any credible world view as matter, energy, space, time, and numbers” (pp. 7–8). Neurobiol-
ogy cannot answer the philosophical problem posed by consciousness, nor can it solve the
philosophical riddle posed by the mind/body relation.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_147
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
posed by consciousness, nor can it solve the
philosophical riddle posed by the mind/body relation. In the end, neither question is a
neurobiological question.
I do not oppose objective methodology in the service of explanation, but specific
important qualifiers should be considered. First, it is understood that systematic research,
most especially in the social or human sciences, emerges from prior contexts of meaning,
some entirely hidden or outside of awareness, some simply by necessity excluded for the
purposes of thinking in a certain way.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_148
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
side of awareness, some simply by necessity excluded for the
purposes of thinking in a certain way. Second, in coming to interpret and understand the
findings of systematic research, any number of possible perspectives might be brought to
bear, and the findings will be interpreted in any number of different ways. This is a process
of critical reasoning, not of objective, empirical study.
20 So, prior to systematic research, in
its organization and delimitation, and at its conclusion, in the variegated interpretations of
its findings, objective study is framed by interpretive activity.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_149
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
the variegated interpretations of
its findings, objective study is framed by interpretive activity. And psychoanalytic interpre-
tive activity, psychoanalytic thinking, is especially rooted in individual, affectively colored,
unconsciously influenced subjective experience. This is where psychoanalytic thinking
begins and where psychoanalytic thinking ends, wherever else it might travel in between.
Ms.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_150
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
inking
begins and where psychoanalytic thinking ends, wherever else it might travel in between.
Ms. B begins her session elaborating on her struggle to break free from entanglements with
her mother and siblings, an incremental and painful process made worse by the incestuous
and sadomasochistic bonds that held the family together and insinuated themselves into
Ms. B’ s sense of self. She spontaneously shares a memory. She is quite young, perhaps five
or six or seven, and it is winter.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_151
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
spontaneously shares a memory. She is quite young, perhaps five
or six or seven, and it is winter. She has decided, for reasons she can’t recall, to venture
outside, and (in her recollection at least) she dresses herself in snowsuit and boots, gloves
and hat, determined to be outside in the white expanse of yards and houses. The snow is
very fine, swirling fiercely, biting her cheeks, with drifts past her knees. She manages to slog
to her neighbor ’s back yard. She looks up only to see white and gray, the houses down the
street vanishing into shadows behind the blur of snow.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_152
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
y to see white and gray, the houses down the
street vanishing into shadows behind the blur of snow. She looks inside a snow fort but it
is empty except for a single half-buried rubber boot. She remembers her feeling of utter
20Sometimes advocates for objectivism in a normal psychoanalytic process want to refer to such clinical reasoning as part of
a scientific activity, thus eliding any difference between a complicated lived engagement which includes practical reason-
ing, and a scientific process of hypothesis formulation and testing.
440 B. H.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_153
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
es practical reason-
ing, and a scientific process of hypothesis formulation and testing.
440 B. H. CLARKE
aloneness, how desolate this familiar landscape suddenly seemed to her, not a single other
moving human form anywhere. Shivering and exhausted, she surrenders and goes back
inside. She feels damp and unhappy, and her toes are numb, and this scares her. When her
mother finds her on the floor of the mudroom she says, “What is wrong with you! ” and
sends her to her room.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_154
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
nds her on the floor of the mudroom she says, “What is wrong with you! ” and
sends her to her room. Now everything is damp, her hair, her underwear, so she takes every-
thing off and crawls into bed with a towel wrapped carefully around her head so as not to get
the pillowcase wet. She thinks she will never feel her toes again, and she decides right then
that she will never tell anyone about it, not even the doctor.
As any reader of Proust or student of contemporary neurocognitive science knows,
memories are reconstructions shaped by the moment in which they are made or
remade.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_155
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
science knows,
memories are reconstructions shaped by the moment in which they are made or
remade. Our memories are notoriously unreliable narrators. According to Gadamer ’s
(1960) notion that experienced meaning can only be prejudicial, can only occur within par-
ticular contexts of meaning and value, our minds and memories are necessarily unreliable
in the sense of incomplete, framed, idiosyncratically focused, pre-organized.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_156
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
ecessarily unreliable
in the sense of incomplete, framed, idiosyncratically focused, pre-organized. Without the
prejudices afforded by a particular horizon of experience, a point of view, we could not
make sense of anything, and knowledge of the sort that interests us psychoanalytically
would not be possible. Hence, learning about the neural correlates of our identifying pro-
jections, our capacity to feel the light or the wind, to experience desire or aloneness, adds
nothing of psychoanalytic interest in deepening our understanding of the feelings and
meanings of Ms. B ’s memory.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_157
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
hoanalytic interest in deepening our understanding of the feelings and
meanings of Ms. B ’s memory. Seeing which regions of her brain light up on a PET scan
when she experiences an ache of beauty is, in the context of our clinical encounter, of
limited interest to her. This brings to mind Ricoeur ’s (Changeux and Ricoeur 2003)
remark: “when I am told that I have a brain, no actual experience corresponds to this; I
learn about it in books ” (p.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_158
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
told that I have a brain, no actual experience corresponds to this; I
learn about it in books ” (p. 16).
Assuming the absence of significant organic pathology, the recollections, silences,
defensive shifts, changes in mood or sensation, daily recountings of ordinary events, for-
mulations of meaning or value, graspings after what exceeds articulation, are listened to in
a psychoanalytic context much as one might hear this described memory.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_159
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
culation, are listened to in
a psychoanalytic context much as one might hear this described memory. We are each
drawn idiosyncratically into our own or our patients ’ subjectively colored recollections,
and yet the meanings and evocations for each listener will change and rearrange as the
moment of vantage point shifts, much as the speaker would tell the memory differently
depending on where she is situated, or would feel moved just once or rarely to think it
at all.
As Karlsson ( 2010) points out, “the subject, in terms of a meaning-bestowing, inten-
tional subject, disappears.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_160
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
2010) points out, “the subject, in terms of a meaning-bestowing, inten-
tional subject, disappears. … in neuropsychoanalysis. And, in consequence, the world is
also missing, with all that goes with it —other human beings, history, future projects,
and a relation to oneself ” (pp. 55– 56). This is not intended critically, except to the
extent that neuropsychoanalytic writers are inattentive to what is missing and why, and
to the complications of bringing neurobiology into relation with the “world” as understood
psychoanalytically.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_161
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
lications of bringing neurobiology into relation with the “world” as understood
psychoanalytically.
The neuropsychoanalyst will often use the word “world” and assume they are engaged
in dialogue using a shared language. Fotopoulou ( 2012a) does this when she invokes
Gadamer’s idea of “horizons” without at all meaning what Gadamer means. Ricoeur
makes this point to Changeux in this way:
INT J PSYCHOANAL 441
You employ the term world too freely. The world is not only the immediate environment; it is
the horizon of a total experience.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_162
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
o freely. The world is not only the immediate environment; it is
the horizon of a total experience. This notion of horizon is perhaps exactly what is eliminated
in the construction of the mental object in order for this object to furnish an equivalent to
what you have constructed in the neuronal field (Changeux and Ricoeur 2003, 92).
Ricoeur remarks on the fact that neuroscience relies illegitimately on “metaphysical
anthropomorphisms” (Changeux and Ricoeur, 2003. p. 89) and semantic amalgamations
as bridging terms.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_163
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
nthropomorphisms” (Changeux and Ricoeur, 2003. p. 89) and semantic amalgamations
as bridging terms. The neuroscientist wants to traverse from a neuronal assembly to an
attribution of meaning, and create the sense that the one follows from the other, by
mixing languages without acknowledgement of the fundamental distinction between
objective and subjective experience. Ricoeur says bluntly that, if the term “mental
object” is intended to link the physical and the mental, “Then it ’s an illegitimate term ”
(p.101).

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_164
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
bject” is intended to link the physical and the mental, “Then it ’s an illegitimate term ”
(p.101). It is illegitimate because it presumes to synthesize what are semantically divergent
discourses and to circumvent the gap, the semantic dualism separating brain and mind
discourses, merely by constructing a hybrid term. Of course, “neuropsychoanalysis”
might serve as another example.
I understand this to mean that, while it is true that the “dual-aspect” of a neuropsychoa-
nalytic epistemology should not be misconstrued as an ontological dualism (we can of

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_165
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
neuropsychoa-
nalytic epistemology should not be misconstrued as an ontological dualism (we can of
course look at the same thing from different perspectives), neither should a monistic
ontology (the proposition that mind and brain are a single entity) be used to legitimize
the merging of different “aspects” or epistemological systems. Ricoeur encapsulates his
approach in this way:
I proceed, then, from a semantic dualism that expresses a duality of perspectives.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_166
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
ach in this way:
I proceed, then, from a semantic dualism that expresses a duality of perspectives. … Mental
experience implies the corporeal, but in a sense that is irreducible to the objective bodies
studied by the natural sciences. Semantically opposed to the body-as-object of these sciences
is the experienced body, one’ s own body. … I do not see a way of passing from one order of
discourse to the other: either I speak of neurons and so forth, in which case I find myself in a
certain language, or I speak of thoughts, actions, and feelings that I connect with my body, to

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_167
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
n a
certain language, or I speak of thoughts, actions, and feelings that I connect with my body, to
which I stand in a relation of possession, of belonging. (pp. 14– 15)
Ricoeur’s point is simple, but full of implications. Ordinary experience, protean and dynamic,
always outstrips any scienti ﬁc effort to capture it; and the phenomenology of subjective
experience, once understood, carries with it obligations that must be honored in the formu-
lation of psychoanalytic ideas about subjectivity and psychoanalytic knowledge.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_168
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
nored in the formu-
lation of psychoanalytic ideas about subjectivity and psychoanalytic knowledge. Only when
the distinction between basic referents is maintained, and the pull toward sameness (in the
registers of knowledge and of Being) is unyieldingly refused, should psychoanalysis under-
take an assessment of the relative value of neuroscienti ﬁc information.
Somewhat unexpectedly, perhaps, philosophical hermeneutics and phenomenology
return us to the Freud of the Project, but from a perspective quite opposite that of
Solms and neuropsychoanalysis.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_169
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
Freud of the Project, but from a perspective quite opposite that of
Solms and neuropsychoanalysis. From this vantage point, Freud ’sn e u r o b i o l o g i c a l
speculations, to the extent that these created initial maps for his theories of the
mind, turn out to be proto-psychoanalytic narratives whose true value rests in their
(broadly speaking) metaphoric and concep tual effort to capture and understand the
mental as corporeally lived experience, as embodied subjectivity in the context of a
lifeworld.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_170
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
the
mental as corporeally lived experience, as embodied subjectivity in the context of a
lifeworld. The emphasis here is not on drive as a mere expression of biology, but on
drive as a mental event grounded in biology. The neur obiological particulars of the
organic substrate are, in my view, relevant primarily as guardrails that help direct a
442 B. H. CLARKE
larger process of psychoanalytic explorati on; what matters psychoanalytically are
simply the various ways in which we experience ourselves as embodied, desiring sub-
jects, not the neurobiology of that experience.

chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
we experience ourselves as embodied, desiring sub-
jects, not the neurobiology of that experience. 21
Conclusion
The preferred position among neuropsychoanalysts is some form of epistemological plur-
alism or dual-aspect monism, although the shadow of an unavowed biological reduction-
ism often lurks beneath the surface. One sees evidence of this in the slippage common in
neuropsychoanalytic writing, where epistemological differences are divested of epis-
temological obligation.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_172
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
hoanalytic writing, where epistemological differences are divested of epis-
temological obligation. As I have tried to show, this has potentially devitalizing impli-
cations for how psychoanalysis regards itself as a discourse, how it understands the
nature of psychoanalytic knowledge, and how it conceives of the psychoanalytic
person or subject.
In my view, this position carries us to the threshold of granting privilege to scientific or
objectivist explanation.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_173
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
osition carries us to the threshold of granting privilege to scientific or
objectivist explanation. This is readily evident in neuropsychoanalysis ’ cardinal assump-
tions: the sense of urgency in needing to correct psychoanalysis ’ isolation from main-
stream science; an epistemological bias towards explanations grounded in biology; and
a conviction that neurobiological science, before any other discipline, should be employed
to rescue psychoanalysis from the body of flabby guesswork known as psychoanalytic
theory.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_174
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
employed
to rescue psychoanalysis from the body of flabby guesswork known as psychoanalytic
theory. By acceding to these assumptions, psychoanalysis opens itself to unwarranted,
yet radical, revision, based on neuroscientific theories and findings.
22
My response to urgent calls to interdisciplinary pluralism and charges of negligence is
simple. Psychoanalysis is not a comprehensive mental health treatment or general psy-
chology. It is not a branch of psychiatry or biology.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_175
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
nsive mental health treatment or general psy-
chology. It is not a branch of psychiatry or biology. It is not required, by reasons of
science or practical economics or cultural preference, to reconstruct itself according to
the rules of other disciplines organized according to theoretical, methodological, or epis-
temological principles and assumptions different from those of psychoanalysis.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_176
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
odological, or epis-
temological principles and assumptions different from those of psychoanalysis. While not
opposed to interface or dialogue with related disciplines, psychoanalysis should insist on
privilege within its domain, should be “epistemologically careful” (Scarfone 2012) and una-
pologetically protective of its right to interpret critically whatever comes to light in its
interactions with neuroscience, to decide what matters and what has no interest.
23 The
relationship of one to the other is a discussion, offering a spectrum of opinion, and cer-

chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
.
23 The
relationship of one to the other is a discussion, offering a spectrum of opinion, and cer-
tainly not necessary to the practice of psychoanalysis.
21I borrow the notion of a “guardrail” from Westphal ( 2011) in his discussion of Ricoeur ’s use of objectification.
22Thompson (2012/2001) reminds us of Heidegger’s conviction that modern culture is dominated by an “ontic,” objectifying
form of thinking which often only alienates us further from the reality we intend to know —in the case of psychoanalysis,

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_178
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
often only alienates us further from the reality we intend to know —in the case of psychoanalysis,
from the unconscious beliefs and fantasies undergirding and informing our experience. Heidegger asserts an “ontological
difference” between the “ontological” (the fundamental forms by which the world is disclosed to us) and the “ontic” (the
empirical “objects” themselves which populate the world).

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_179
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
is disclosed to us) and the “ontic” (the
empirical “objects” themselves which populate the world). Psychoanalysis is fundamentally concerned with the ontologi-
cal aspects of human being—temporality, care, the ongoing tensions between loss and possibility, anxiety and the avoid-
ance of suffering, being-towards-death and its avoidance —as constitutive of our humanness. Science is concerned with
the ontic, with worlds of objectively observable things.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_180
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
f our humanness. Science is concerned with
the ontic, with worlds of objectively observable things. As Sass ( 2015) remarks, one consequence of forgetting the onto-
logical difference … is the tendency to conceptualize even consciousness or subjectivity itself as what Husserl called a
“tag end ” of the world —namely, as something that, whatever its specialness, nevertheless has the status of another
entity within the world rather than as the condition for the world, as the grounding for “worldhood” itself. (p. 424)
23By this I mean psychoanalysis as a discourse.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_181
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
, as the grounding for “worldhood” itself. (p. 424)
23By this I mean psychoanalysis as a discourse. As Brothers (2002) points out, analysts in practice might function as psychia-
trists, or might refer an analytic patient to a psychiatrist, neurologist, or other specialist. However, when functioning as
analysts, they are operating in a specific realm and in a particular way.
INT J PSYCHOANAL 443
Psychoanalysis tells a psychoanalytic story about the progress of desire through the fila-
ments of ordinary human experience and in a language of its own, organized by theoretical

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_182
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
the fila-
ments of ordinary human experience and in a language of its own, organized by theoretical
concepts that are to a significant extent uniquely psychoanalytic. For Ricoeur (1970) psycho-
analysis includes a “semantics of desire,” which brings with it a notion of a complexly con-
structed desiring subject with a “vocation” for meaning and for language. 24 This is at the
heart of psychoanalysis, and what neuroscience has to say about it is often going to be
either inherently reductive (the terms of psychoanalysis being reduced to, or re-transcribed

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_183
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
to be
either inherently reductive (the terms of psychoanalysis being reduced to, or re-transcribed
to fit with, the terms of neuroscience), or simply beside the point. This is true in part because,
from within the frame of neurobiology, one has only a mediated, indirect recourse to psy-
choanalytic ideas and language. Although astonishing, even revolutionary, neuroscience is
something else altogether, a different epistemological animal, one peculiarly unequipped to
grasp the “ontological density”—the meanings, affective coloring’s, and unconscious fantasy

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_184
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
pped to
grasp the “ontological density”—the meanings, affective coloring’s, and unconscious fantasy
constructions—of our subjectively experienced “lived biology. ” Neuroscience cannot go
where psychoanalysis lives, cannot speak to its most salient parts, and this fact alone
argues for the necessity of a respectful, sensibly cautious relationship. Any interrelation
between neuroscience and psychoanalysis warrants care and suspicion.

chunks.id: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf_185
chunks.source: A cat is not a battleship  thoughts on the meaning of  neuropsychoanalysis .pdf
chunks.text:
elationship. Any interrelation
between neuroscience and psychoanalysis warrants care and suspicion. There are far-reach-
ing, potentially grave dangers for psychoanalysis when neuroscience is misrecognized in its
fundamental differences, and is injudiciously employed to answer questions that properly
belong to the language and conceptual architecture of psychoanalysis.

Alternation in functional connectivity 
within default mode network 
after psychodynamic psychotherapy 
in borderline personality disorder
Saba Amiri1†, Fatemeh Sadat Mirfazeli2†, Jordan Grafman3, Homa Mohammadsadeghi2*, Mehrdad Eftekhar2,

ba Amiri1†, Fatemeh Sadat Mirfazeli2†, Jordan Grafman3, Homa Mohammadsadeghi2*, Mehrdad Eftekhar2,

Abstract 
Background Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is characterized by impairments in emotion regulation, impulse 
control, and interpersonal and social functioning along with a deficit in emotional awareness and empathy.

study, we investigated whether functional connectivity (FC) within the default mode network (DMN) is affected by 
1-year psychodynamic psychotherapy in patients with BPD.
Methods Nine BPD patients filled out the demography, Interpersonal Reactive Index (IRI), Toronto Alexithymia Scale 
20 (TAS 20), the Alcohol, Smoking, and Substance Involvement Screening Test (ASSIST), and the Borderline Evalua-
tion Severity over Time (BEST) questionnaire.

psychodynamic psychotherapy and then every 4 months for a year after initiating psychotherapy.

Results The results indicated that patients with BPD present with aberrant DMN connectivity compared to healthy 
controls. Over a year of psychotherapy, the patients with BPD showed both FC changes (decreasing nodal degree in 
the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex and increasing in other cingulate cortex regions) and behavioral improvement 
in their symptoms and substance use.

degree in regions of the dorsal cingulate cortex and a decrease in the score of the TAS-20 indicating difficulty in iden-

Conclusion In BPD, there is altered FC within the DMN and disruption in self-processing and emotion regulation.

Conclusion
In BPD, there is altered connectivity within DMN and 
disruption in self-processing and emotion regulation. 
Psychotherapy may not only alleviate behavioral dys -
function but also normalizes connectivity within the 
DMN.

chotherapy. Evaluating DMN before and after psycho -
therapy might help to determine the potential target for 
treatment and to better identify neuroimaging results

Recent advances in the field of neuroscience have dramatically changed our understanding of brain–
behavior relationships. In this article, we illustrate how neuroscience can provide a conceptual and
methodological framework to understand our clients within a transdiagnostic developmental perspective.
We provide directions for integrating neuroscience into future process and outcome research.

Integrating Neuroscience Into Contextual
Counseling Interventions
Neuroscience researchers have identified several psychosocial
mechanisms that promote neuroplasticity by impacting neurogen-
esis and synaptogenesis in different neural systems. Four of those
mechanisms that we believe warrant investigation by counseling
psychology researchers are nurturing and caring, healthy behavior,
and environmental enrichment.

and environmental enrichment. Animal research has consistently
shown that nurturing and caring behaviors have a strong, long-
lasting effect on the neurodevelopment of the offspring. For ex-
ample, research on maternal behavior among rats indicated pups
from mothers showing high levels of licking and grooming during
the first week after birth show less vulnerability to stress, with a
decreased corticosterone response (
Bagot et al., 2012 ).

research is now being conducted with humans, showing that caring
and nurturing attitudes have a significant impact in children’s brain
development. For example,
Milgrom et al. (2010), trained pregnant
women in the use of specific strategies to reduce stressful experi-
ences and influence infants’ brain development.

attitude (e.g., facial expressions, movement and massage, skin
contact, and multisensory stimulation). Results from this study
showed that white matter connectivity and maturation was signif-
icantly impacted in the trained group, which suggests that this type
of parenting training could positively influence neurodevelopment
of children.

The practice of healthy behaviors, particularly those associated
with nutrition and exercise, have also been linked to positive brain
plasticity. For example, Griffin et al. (2011) found that short
periods of intense physical exercise increased the levels of brain-
derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and improved performance in
a memory task (i.e., face–name matching).

fatty acids and control) had significant effects in terms of memory
as well as in biological markers underlying processes of synaptic
plasticity such as improved insulin sensitivity and reduced inflam-

psychology researchers should seek to examine the natural and
intentional manipulation of these contextual factors, such as pa-

behaviors, and environmental enrichment, as a way of enhancing

modulating the emotion regulation network and influencing tasks
across developmental domains (cognitive, emotional, vocational,
social, and identity development), (b) the mechanisms by which
aerobic exercise promotes cognitive development and enhances
attention networks, and (c) the influence of exposure to different
patterns of culture diversity on social cognitive networks and the

fluence of exposure to different

Concluding Remarks
It is our hope that this article will serve as a call to action for
counseling psychologists to pursue research that integrates neuro-
science with traditional counseling psychology paradigms. We
argue for a transdiagnostic developmental perspective for under-
standing our clients and have provided directions for integrating
neuroscience into future process and outcome research as well as

rovided directions for integrating
neuroscience into future process and outcome research as well as
future research directions regarding the effects of contextual coun-
seling interventions. We suggest future research is needed to
explore the interaction of interpersonal and environmental factors,
psychological processes, brain networks, and development, includ-
ing cognitive, social, emotional, identity, and vocational develop-
ment.

Attachment Model of Depression
An Attachment Model of Depression: Integrating 
Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory 
Jeremy Holmes
This paper is written from a psychodynamic clinician’s perspective, juxtaposing 
a psychoanalytic-attachment model of depression with recent developments in 
neuroscience.

aposing 
a psychoanalytic-attachment model of depression with recent developments in 
neuroscience. Three main components of the attachment approach are described: 
the role of loss, of childhood trauma predisposing to depression in later life, and 
failure of co-regulation of role of primitive emotions, such as fear, despair, and 
helplessness. Blatt’s distinction between anaclitic and introjective depression is 
delineated and related to hyper- and de-activation of the attachment dynamic.

delineated and related to hyper- and de-activation of the attachment dynamic. 
Recent advances in evolutionary, sociological, epigenetic, biochemical, and neu-
ro-imaging studies of depression are reviewed. A dynamic model of depression 
is proposed, linking interpersonal and intra-psychic perspectives with neuro-an-
atomical models. The final section of the paper considers the specific role of psy-
chodynamic approaches to the treatment of refractory depression.

Therapist: “Unwanted by whom?” I

Patient: “Oh, my boyfriend at the time

Th: “And you…?”

A PSYCHODYNAMIC-
ATTACHMENT MODEL  
OF DEPRESSION 
In the section that follows, I shall pres-
ent an attachment-derived theory of depres-
sion which builds on, revises, and extends 
aspects of the psychoanalytic viewpoint first 
put forward by Freud in Mourning and Mel-
ancholia (1917). 
The attachment account of depression 
picks up on three principal themes.
1. The Centrality of Loss
True to his title, Freud starts from par-
allels between the phenomenology of mourn-

2. The Role of Childhood Trauma
One of the most painful features of 
depression, both for the sufferers and those 
close to them, is the way that the self turns 
against itself. This was the crucial issue that 
Mourning and Melancholia tried to unravel.

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_30
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
turns 
against itself. This was the crucial issue that 
Mourning and Melancholia tried to unravel. 
In a famous passage, Freud argues:
Thus the shadow of the object fell upon 
the ego, so that the latter could hence-
forth be criticized by a special mental 
faculty like an object, like the foresaken 
object. In this way the loss of the object 
became transformed into a loss in the 
ego, and the conflict between the ego 
and the loved person transformed into a 
cleavage between the criticizing faculty 
of the ego and the ego as altered by the 
identification. (Freud, 1917, p.

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_31
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
the criticizing faculty 
of the ego and the ego as altered by the 
identification. (Freud, 1917, p. 248)
Here, Freud links childhood “loss” 
with later depression, and he accounts for 
the phenomenology of self-attack by sug-
gesting that protest rightly belonging to the 
forsaking object is now transposed into the 
inner world. The attack on a part of the self 
is, via the “shadow” identification theory, an 
indirect attack on the abandoning object.
From a contemporary perspective, 
Freud’s theory is outdated for two related 
reasons: first, because it fails to differentiate

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_32
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
ve, 
Freud’s theory is outdated for two related 
reasons: first, because it fails to differentiate 
between the normal developmental process 
in which all children have to cope with the 
loss of exclusive possession of the mother, as 
opposed to specific pre-depressive childhood 
trauma; and second, because Freud’s account 
ignores the actual behavior of a caregiver, 
seeing trauma and loss merely in terms of a 
putative narcissistic investment with which 
the child imbues the object, which in depres-
sion is withdrawn back into the self.
Nevertheless, implicit in the “shadow

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_33
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
ject, which in depres-
sion is withdrawn back into the self.
Nevertheless, implicit in the “shadow 
of the object” theory is the idea that child-
hood trauma can be the developmental pre-
cursor of adult depression. For Freud, the 
Oedipal situation is inherently “traumatic.” 
We now see childhood trauma as resulting 
from actual events—neglect, abandonment, 
or physical and/or sexual abuse. Brown and 
Harris (1978), Paykel and Herbert (1989), 
and more recently, for example, Artero and

Parker (1979) showed that, as compared

Bowlby (1980) built his theory of de-

(Bibring, 1953; Seligman, 1975) characteris-

terms of an unresponsive environment in 
which the infant feels that whatever they do 
to try to elicit care makes little difference. 
This model encompasses the low self-esteem 
characteristic of depression in that self-es-
teem depends on feeling that we can make 
a difference, first to significant others in our

a sense of efficacy more generally.
For Bowlby, loss is experienced as ir -

For Bowlby, loss is experienced as ir -
reversible separation. Separation from a 
secure base exposes the individual to risk; 
risk evokes fear. Anger at separation can be 
seen as a negative reinforcement schedule de-

secure base—whether it is the baby crying 
for her mother or the parent reprimanding 
the child for risky behaviors.

for her mother or the parent reprimanding 
the child for risky behaviors. The lack of an 
answering response to these angry outbursts 
gradually persuades the bereaved person that 
the separation is irremediable and paves the 
way for despair, helplessness, and low self-
esteem.
Attachment research (Dozier, Stovall-
McClough, & Albus, 2008; McMahon, Bar-

Children with resistant insecure patterns 
tend to dampen down their separation pro-
test when separated from their caregivers. 
The pain of separation is thus initially miti-
gated by its transposition from the external 
to the inner world. This protects the individ-
ual from the vagaries of fate, but a price has 
to be paid. Now the self is no longer nour -

to be paid. Now the self is no longer nour -

The pain of the outer actual loss is replaced 
by guilt and inner emptiness, in which one 
part of the self attacks another. 
In addition to emphasising the shift 
from an outer loss to a “loss in the ego,” 
Freud picked up on conflict between the self 
and its objects as a central theme in depres-
sion. The attachment account similarly sees 
insecure individuals in an ambivalence bind.

n depres-
sion. The attachment account similarly sees 
insecure individuals in an ambivalence bind. 
They need proximity to the object for secu-
rity; but if the object is inconsistent or aban-
doning, the attachment response will be one 
of protest and anger in an attempt to restore 
closeness. However, the insecure child fears 
that to express such protest runs the risk of 
further alienating the secure base, and at this 
point, depressive helplessness sets in.
People become depressed, this view 
suggests, because (a) they have been, or feel,

rage about this, and (c) they protect the ob-

3. Primal Emotions in Depression
Self-attack as diverted aggression can-
not be taken as a general theory of depressive 
experience.

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_48
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
Self-attack as diverted aggression can-
not be taken as a general theory of depressive 
experience. A more nuanced picture, taking 
into account individual differences is needed. 
Blatt (2008) classifies depression psycho-
analytically into “anaclitic” (object leaning) 
and “introjective” (self-absorbed) patterns. 
These map well onto attachment theory’s 
two forms of “organized insecurity”—hy-
per- and de-activating insecure attachment 
(Mikulincer & Shaver, 2008). 
The de-activating or avoidant pattern 
renders its sufferers more prone to introjec-
tive ruminations.

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_49
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
de-activating or avoidant pattern 
renders its sufferers more prone to introjec-
tive ruminations. Such people will have had 
developmental experiences in which feelings 
were damped down (de-activated) in order to 
retain a degree of protection from a stressed 
or rejecting caregiver (Ainsworth, Blehar, 
Waters, & Wall, 1978). As a way of surviv-
ing in a harsh world, these people may then 
imaginatively create an ideal inner scenario 
in which they are perfectly “good,” their 
caregiver perfectly attuned and responsive.

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_50
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
er scenario 
in which they are perfectly “good,” their 
caregiver perfectly attuned and responsive. 
When this fails, they then may turn against 
themselves in the way that the classical ac-
count describes. This sets up a typically de-
pressive gulf between real self and ideal self; 
narrowing this discrepancy is a major thera-
peutic target (Kuyken et al., 2010).
In the dependent, “anaclitic” type of 
depression, however, self-attack and anger 
are usually far less prominent (Blatt, 2008). 
These sufferers often present a mixed depres-
sive/anxiety picture.

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_51
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
less prominent (Blatt, 2008). 
These sufferers often present a mixed depres-
sive/anxiety picture. Jane’s intimate relation-
ships illustrate Blatt’s anaclitic depression. 
Her attachment pattern was one of cling-
ing adhesion to an inconstant or enigmatic 
object. This was played out in the transfer -
ence, as she tried to maneuver the therapist 
into making life decisions for her, especially 
when it came to taking anti-depressants, the 
thought of which evoked in her an irrational 
fear.

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_52
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
when it came to taking anti-depressants, the 
thought of which evoked in her an irrational 
fear. 
“Please tell me whether I should take 
those pills or not,” she pleaded.
The therapist’s response was: “The psy-
chiatrist in me thinks it would be a really 
good idea to give them a try; but as a 
psychotherapist I believe it’s vital for you 
to find the freedom to make decisions for

Given the ubiquity and obvious fitness-
reducing aspects of depression, a fundamen-
tal preliminary question is whether depres-
sion can be seen as adaptive, and therefore 
to have an evolutionary function (Neese, 
2005).

to have an evolutionary function (Neese, 
2005). Three possible approaches are com-

The psychoanalytic-attachment model 
proposed above is consistent with Simpson 
and Belsky’s (2008) “psychic pain hypoth-
esis.” Sensitivity to physical pain is an es-
sential protective mechanism for living or -
ganisms.

environment, the capacity to experience psy-

fort is spared to maintain the attachments es-
sential for security and ultimate reproductive 
success. The capacity to become depressed in 
response to irretrievable loss is the dark side 
of the life-enhancing virtues of intimate at-
tachment.

A second popular idea derives from

link this with the “affluenza” concept (James,

which envy is rife; therefore, people are more

against the strong, an antidote to dominance

SOCIAL PSYCHIATRY 
We have already seen how some of the 
most important findings in mood disorders 
came from social psychiatry research (Brown 
& Harris, 1978). These have continued with 
the Newpin project (Lederer, 2009), an in-
tervention study on the impact of befriend-
ing on depressed mothers in a deprived area 
of East London.

have shown that recovery from depression is 
fostered by the combination of befriending 
and a positive “new beginning” event, such 
as getting a job or starting a new relation-
ship—an important reminder that life events 
can be antidotes to depression as well as pre-
cipitants.

“playing” affective modules, as opposed to 
“rage” or “panic.” If therapy in Winnicott’s 
(1965) terms is “learning to play,” the re-

more positive ones is a crucial therapeutic

EPIGENETICS 
Epigenetics is strictly defined as the 
study of heritable changes in the phenotype 
transmitted by non-genomic means, but is

study of heritable changes in the phenotype 
transmitted by non-genomic means, but is 
often more widely referred to as the study 
of developmental pathways. The essential 
message is that current environmental ad-
aptations can, under some circumstances, be 
directly transmitted to offspring. The explo-
ration of epigenesis sheds new light on the 
nature-nurture debate, whose psychiatric 
76 Holmes
manifestation is the divide between “organ-
ic” and psychodynamic psychiatry.5
In the terms of this paper, the epi-
genetics of developmental psychobiology can

In the terms of this paper, the epi-
genetics of developmental psychobiology can 
be summarized by the equation:
Phe = G × E squared
6
That is, a given phenotype (Phe) is 
determined by genetic makeup (G) “times” 
the environment (E) squared—“squared” 
because the environment impacts on the 
phenotype in two distinct ways. First, the 
Ec (the current environment), through pro-
moter genes, influences the expression of the 
individual’s genetic potential.

moter genes, influences the expression of the 
individual’s genetic potential. Second, the Ed 
(the developmental environment), through 
epigenetic mechanisms, inscribes itself in an 
individual’s biology, which is then transmit-
ted to future generations.
Developmental neurobiologist Dr. 
Frances Champagne (2010, p. 564) puts it 
like this: 
[T]here is emerging evidence that 
changes in gene expression both within 
the brain and in peripheral tissues are 
associated with differences in the quality 
of the early environment and that these

developmental effects are maintained by 
epigenetic mechanisms that control the 
activity of genes involved in disease risk 
and behavioral variation. [my italics]
Epigenetics shows how, contrary to 
Darwinian dogma, acquired characteristics 
can be heritable. This is because the DNA 
base sequence is only part of the develop-
mental story. DNA is tightly bound in the 
cell to histone proteins. DNA is only avail-
able for transcription by mRNA into protein 
if the binding is sufficiently loose.

especially the psychobiologically relevant

mental influence, and this is then transmitted 
through the mother to future generations.
In addition, different environments 
switch on or off promoter genes, thereby 
determining varying phenotypic manifesta-
tions.

Exposure to abuse in infancy is associated

stress, in both humans and rodents, can be

Epigenetic variability in response to 
stress, in both humans and rodents, can be 
conceptualized as adaptive. The harsher the 
environment, the more short-term survival 
strategies take precedence over the com-

exploration. In adverse environments, high 
reactiveness (adaptive misperception: “take 
any unexpected sensation as potentially 
threatening”) and early sexual maturation 
(when life expectancy is reduced) become 
priorities.

benign relationship between vulner-

genetic polymorphisms or epigenetic 
transmission, are more vulnerable to 
environmental trauma, but also to 
psychotherapeutic amelioration.

adversity is potentially amenable to

and prolonged level if permanent

NEUROIMAGING:  
THE BRAIN IN ACTION 
Neuropsychoanalysis (Northoff, 
2011; Solms & Turnball, 2002) is an emerg-
ing discipline in our field.

chunks.text:
opsychoanalysis (Northoff, 
2011; Solms & Turnball, 2002) is an emerg-
ing discipline in our field. Aware of the limi-
tations of a purely computational approach, 
neurologists have been drawn to psychody-
namic models capable of linking experiential 
meaning with structural models of the mind.
7
Neuropsychiatrist Helen Mayberg 
(2009) sees pathology in depression as en-
tailing two related areas of dysfunction: (a) 
impedance to the normal integrated flow of 
cerebral activity across regions, and (b) fail-
ure of the regulatory function of one part of 
the brain over another.

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_98
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:

ure of the regulatory function of one part of 
the brain over another.
The structural areas implicated in de-
pression include the dorsolateral pre-frontal 
cortex (DLPFC), cingulate cortex, basal gan-
glia, amygdala, and hippocampus (Mayberg, 
2009). Three sets of findings stand out as 
particularly significant from the perspective 
of the psychodynamic clinician:
First is the well-replicated consensus 
that there is decreased dorsolateral pre-fron-
tal cortex (DLPFC) activity in depression 
(Wang et al., 2008), as measured by blood-
flow and glucose metabolism.

(Wang et al., 2008), as measured by blood-
flow and glucose metabolism. This relation-
ship is quantitative, with inverse relationship 
between severity of depression and prefron-
tal cortex function (Brody et al., 2001). The 
principal role of the DLPFC lies in planning 
and regulation of emotions.
Second, ventral prefrontal cortex 
(VPFC) and amygdala hyperactivity has

depression is associated with anxiety and ob-

particularly involved in implicit as opposed 
to episodic learning of intense, emotionally

A third region relevant to the genesis 
and treatment of depression is the subcal-
losal cingulate gyrus, and in particular area 
Cg25.

and treatment of depression is the subcal-

Cg25. Severe depression is associated with 
excessive neural activity in this region, as are 
sad mood states in normal subjects (May-

sants show reductions in blood flow in Cg25 
as their depressive symptoms remit (May-
berg et al., 2000).
A speculative model combining these 
findings with the attachment picture pro-
posed in the first part of this paper would 
suggest the following:
1.

suggest the following:
1. Decreased DLPFC activity is consis-
tent with the clinical observation of 
depressive disengagement from the 
world, moving from an object rela-
tions to a self-sufficient, “narcissistic” 
mode of functioning. Carhart-Harris, 
Mayberg, Malizia, and Nutt (2008) 
describe a “default mode network” 
(DMN) pattern of brain functioning 
that is superseded when the subject 
is engaged with some external task.

that is superseded when the subject 
is engaged with some external task. 
In depression, the DMN takes over, 
and this can be conceptualized as 
the replacement of self-other relating 
(and associated neural circuitry) with 
endogenous self-self circuits. 
2. Hyperactivity in the basal ganglia 
and amygdala can be seen as reflect-
ing “damming up” of activity arising 
from limbic system centers. With the 
DLPFC in DMN mode and diminu-
tion of planning and regulation, there 
is a failure to subject primal affects 
to regulation and reality testing.

is a failure to subject primal affects 
to regulation and reality testing. With 
the brain in DMN mode, feelings can-
not be brought into play in the inter-
personal field—hence, the salience of 
“primitive emotions” in depression.
3. Cg25 can be postulated as a repres-
sive agency, attempting to damp down 
and keep at bay impulses from lower 
centers (Carhart-Harris et al., 2008), 
which threaten to overwhelm the un-
der-functioning higher centers, such as 
the DLPFC (c.f. Mayberg, 2009).

the DLPFC (c.f. Mayberg, 2009). The 
Cg25 center acts in a superego–like 
fashion, punitively self-persecuting as 
Freud postulated, vainly attempting to 
maintain a degree of psychic equilib-
rium.
4. Given that the amygdala matures 
prior to the hippocampus, and given 
amygdala hyperactivity in depres-
sion, implicit (as opposed to episodic) 
memories of childhood trauma may 
be revived in depressive states (Renn, 
2011).

therapies (Zobel et al., 2011). The lat-

This model predicts that recovery 
from depression will entail a normalization 
of the DLPFC, Cg25, VPFC, and amygdala 
dynamic balance.

of the DLPFC, Cg25, VPFC, and amygdala 
dynamic balance. Depressed people who 
respond to antidepressants do indeed show 
concomitant increases in DLPFC activity and 
decreases in Cg25 blood flow (Mayberg et 
al., 2000). However, the converse is found in 
CBT responders, who show decreased DLP-
FC blood flow as they get better. Viewing 
brain function as a dynamic system makes 
sense of this apparently paradoxical effect.

CBT encourages patients to use their rational 
cognitive capacities to re-evaluate the primi-

(Kuyken et al., 2010). It is likely, therefore, 
that they will move from high to low PFC

AN INTEGRATIVE MODEL  
FOR DEPRESSION 
I shall now put forward a psychoan-
alytic-attachment model of depression in-
corporating the above findings and offering 
some possible mechanisms of action for psy-
choanalytic psychotherapies.
1.

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_111
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
findings and offering 
some possible mechanisms of action for psy-
choanalytic psychotherapies.
1. In a normal resting state, the individ-
ual and her/his attachment figures are 
in a dynamic equilibrium, in which 
the security and responsiveness of the 
environment facilitates exploratory 
physical and mental functioning (in-
cluding exploring one’s own and oth-
ers’ mental states, that is, “mentaliz-
ing”; Lemma et al., 2010).

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_112
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
ing exploring one’s own and oth-
ers’ mental states, that is, “mentaliz-
ing”; Lemma et al., 2010). The neural 
substrate for this entails interacting 
intersecting feedback loops between 
the DLPFC and a) the interpersonal 
environment, that is, “significant 
others” and their DLPFC, and b) the 
intrapsychic environment, represented 
by the “lower” centers, including the 
amygdala. Primal emotions, evoked 
by external events including loss, are 
filtered through the “gateway” of 
the Cg25 and processed—regulated, 
moderated, and mentalized—by the 
DLPFC.
2.

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_113
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
gh the “gateway” of 
the Cg25 and processed—regulated, 
moderated, and mentalized—by the 
DLPFC.
2. The establishment of a “good internal 
object” is the result of repeated cycles 
of need, loss, and repair throughout 
childhood. This leads to the instan-
tiation of an internalized emotion-
processing attachment representation, 
based on “good enough” security 
provision by the external environment 
in the course of emotional develop-
ment.
3.

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_114
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
ough” security 
provision by the external environment 
in the course of emotional develop-
ment.
3. The system of intersecting feedback 
is disrupted by significant loss events, 
whether actual (e.g., loss of an attach-
ment figure through death or divorce) 
or symbolic (e.g., loss of self-esteem 
following a career setback). This dis-
rupts the normal attachment response 
to loss, in which the primitive emo-
tions of mental pain trigger seeking 
out comfort from a secure base.

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_115
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
, in which the primitive emo-
tions of mental pain trigger seeking 
out comfort from a secure base. But if 
the sought-after comforter (actual or 
symbolic, e.g., career advancement) 
is the very source of security that has 
been lost, this leads to a turning away 
from the external world.
4. In the normal grieving process, there 
is still sufficient “ego strength” for the 
sufferer to replace the lost external 
relationship with an internal “good 
object,” enabling the primitive emo-
tions of mental pain, anger, guilt, and 
so forth generated in the lower centers 
to be processed.

chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
tions of mental pain, anger, guilt, and 
so forth generated in the lower centers 
to be processed. Adaptive repression 
plays a part too: under the aegis of 
Cg25, pain is modulated and dealt 
with in manageable quanta. In addi-
tion, the supportiveness of the envi-
ronment and availability of potential 
new attachment figures during and 
after grieving significantly influence 
outcome.
5.

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_117
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
f potential 
new attachment figures during and 
after grieving significantly influence 
outcome.
5. Depressive illness, rather than nor-
mal grieving, may result following 
loss, depending on developmental 
factors: (i) an insecure rather than a 
secure attachment relational disposi-
tion which compromises the capacity 
of the DLPFC to regulate primitive 
emotions, and (ii) a history of child-
hood trauma or neglect, either in the 
individual or, epigenetically, in the 
previous maternal generations.

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_118
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
ma or neglect, either in the 
individual or, epigenetically, in the 
previous maternal generations. This 
“sets” the HPA axis in ways that 
lead to excessive reactivity, with the 
potential for triggering early trauma 
schemata by current loss events.
Attachment Model of Depression 81
6. Dysregulation after loss will follow 
different patterns depending on the in-
dividual’s attachment style. In the de-
activating (avoidant) type, the subject 
withdraws from the environment and 
tries to deal with primitive emotions 
by repression.

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_119
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
subject 
withdraws from the environment and 
tries to deal with primitive emotions 
by repression. Here, excessive activ-
ity in Cg25 leads to an introjective 
pattern, with typical self-reproaches 
and rumination as elaborated on 
by Freud. In the contrasting hyper-
activating (ambivalent) pattern, the 
depressed person becomes anaclitic, 
seeking reassurance, becoming overly 
dependent, and attempting to use the 
clung-to other as an auxiliary ego in 
an effort to process the primitive emo-
tions with which she is flooded.
7.

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_120
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
as an auxiliary ego in 
an effort to process the primitive emo-
tions with which she is flooded.
7. Therapy helps move the depressed in-
dividual back onto a less dysregulated 
pathway and helps to restore normal 
responses to loss and setback in a 
number of ways:
(a) A stable, secure collaborative ob-
ject relationship, which temporarily takes 
over some of the functions of the lost object, 
is offered.
(b) The cognitive processing of emo-
tions is fostered, thereby overcoming affect 
phobia.

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_121
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
offered.
(b) The cognitive processing of emo-
tions is fostered, thereby overcoming affect 
phobia. In the introjective pattern, the intra-
psychic dynamic is opened out, lessening the 
repressive grip of the superego/Cg25, allow-
ing feelings to be felt and processed, with the 
auxiliary help of the therapist.
(c) In the anaclitic pattern, the thera-
pist gradually returns projected feelings back 
to the sufferer, re-empowering her DLPFC’s 
autonomous capacity to regulate her/his 
emotions.
(d) The intensity of primitive emotions 
“from below” is reduced.

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_122
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
ty to regulate her/his 
emotions.
(d) The intensity of primitive emotions 
“from below” is reduced. This can happen 
in a number of ways, including the gradual 
processing of implicit memories of trauma in 
psychodynamic therapy; antidepressant ther-
apy; and meditative techniques in MBCBT 
(Kuyken et al., 2010). In each case, there 
may be a gradual resetting of the HPA axis, 
with reduced glucocorticoid sensitivity, and 
thereby enhanced skillfulness in using cogni-
tion to modulate emotion.
(e) Finally, there is the instantiation 
of hope, the possibility of a new beginning,

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_123
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
ate emotion.
(e) Finally, there is the instantiation 
of hope, the possibility of a new beginning, 
and the reduction of helplessness (Bibring, 
1953). The lost object is restored to the in-
ner world, which is thereby strengthened in 
parallel with a renewed interest in external 
reality. Hope can be equated with the re-
linquishment of self-absorption (and DMN 
function), and with a renewed trust in fruit-
ful exploration, bolstered by the knowledge 
that security will be available if loss or threat 
once more supervenes.

In this survey, I have deliberately
