PRACTICE POINTS 
In this survey, I have deliberately 
avoided a focus on outcome research and the 
relative merits of different therapeutic ap-
proaches.
8 Nevertheless, the model proposed 
above has significant implications for psy-
choanalytic practitioners.
First, depression needs to be seen as 
a heterogeneous condition (Blatt, 2008), 
both in terms of severity and subtypes of 
depression.

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_125
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
s 
a heterogeneous condition (Blatt, 2008), 
both in terms of severity and subtypes of 
depression. A stepped care model (NICE, 
2005) seems appropriate, in which CBT’s 
combination of a good therapeutic relation-
ship and reactivation of cognitive function 
in the DLPFC may in many cases suffice to 
restore psychological equilibrium. Where 
there is a history of early trauma or neglect, 
the prognosis tends to be less good and the 
indications for a psychodynamic approach 
correspondingly greater (Leischenring & 
Raybung, 2011; Zobel et al., 2011).

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_126
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
sychodynamic approach 
correspondingly greater (Leischenring & 
Raybung, 2011; Zobel et al., 2011). It is im-
portant to bear this diagnostic heterogeneity 
in mind within the psychoanalytic paradigm, 
in that the standard psychoanalytic model 
of depression of “anger turned against the

self” is more applicable to introjective than 
to anaclitic patterns.
Psychodynamic practitioners will con-
sider what the unique contribution of their

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_127
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
clitic patterns.
Psychodynamic practitioners will con-
sider what the unique contribution of their 
discipline might be to the treatment of de-
pression. Three points stand out. The first, 
while not specifically psychoanalytic in itself, 
is length of treatment. There is accumulating 
evidence for the superiority of outcomes for 
longer- over short-term therapies, although 
differences do not show themselves until well 
into the third year of treatment (Knekt et al., 
2008).

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_128
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
ferences do not show themselves until well 
into the third year of treatment (Knekt et al., 
2008). Despite evidence for neuroplasticity, 
in severe cases prolonged treatments will be 
needed if the biological substrate for depres-
sion is to be reset in less pathogenic ways. 
Lessening the strength of primitive emotions, 
reducing the need for excessive repression, 
decreasing the reactivity of the HPA axis, and 
fostering the capacity of the mind to regulate 
and process painful feelings, all take time.
Second, psychoanalytic approaches 
can help transmute and modify implicit

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_129
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
feelings, all take time.
Second, psychoanalytic approaches 
can help transmute and modify implicit 
memory systems that are likely to be awry 
in individuals who have experienced trauma 
or neglect in early childhood. Within the 
boundaries of the setting, therapy offers 
new experiences of sensitivity, responsive-
ness, and the capacity for reflection in place 
of confusing, disorganizing, and controlling 
interpersonal patterns of relating.

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_130
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
lection in place 
of confusing, disorganizing, and controlling 
interpersonal patterns of relating. Becoming 
aware of these ingrained patterns, as well as 
providing a setting in which they can be re-
worked, is central to the mechanism of ac-
tion of psychoanalytic therapy (c.f. Fonagy, 
1998; Holmes, 2010, 2011; Renn, 2011).
This leads, finally, to the unique and 
specific contribution of psychoanalysis to 
psychotherapy practice—working with the 
subtleties of transference and counter-trans-
ference.

to 
psychotherapy practice—working with the 
subtleties of transference and counter-trans-
ference. Let us return to Jane and the vignette 
with which we started.
The presence of affect phobia was sig-
naled in Jane by a verbal ambiguity. The 
double meaning of “he wasn’t having 
it” exemplified how repressed primal 
emotions make their presence felt and 
the therapist’s role in identifying these 
markers of repressed meaning.

chunks.id: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf_132
chunks.source: An Attachment Model of Depression  Integrating Findings from the Mood Disorder Laboratory.pdf
chunks.text:
e their presence felt and 
the therapist’s role in identifying these 
markers of repressed meaning. The im-
plicit message from the therapist and the 
therapeutic situation was: “Your painful 
feelings are present; you aren’t con-
sciously aware of them, but they mani-
fest themselves in your speech patterns 
and perhaps in your somatic symptoms. 
It is now safe to feel those feelings in the 
secure presence of a therapist.”
Jane was in a dilemma about taking 
antidepressants.

lings in the 
secure presence of a therapist.”
Jane was in a dilemma about taking 
antidepressants. The vacuum left by her 
mother’s death meant that she found it 
difficult to make decisions for herself, 
and she tried to push the analyst into de-
ciding for her, which he initially resisted. 
At the end of one session, stung by her 
indecisiveness, and probably in a minor 
enactment, he found himself encouraging 
her to stop vacillating and to give them 
a try.
Jane returned the following week, admit-
ting that she still hadn’t been able to 
bring herself to start them.

ed the following week, admit-
ting that she still hadn’t been able to 
bring herself to start them. Her demean-
or seemed shamefaced and guilty. When 
the analyst pointed this out, she replied, 
“Oh, I thought you’d be really cross 
with me.” While noting his counter-
transference of mild exasperation, the 
analyst then explored a possible parallel 
between the sense that Jane felt she had 
to please him, that he would be annoyed 
if she didn’t take her pills, and the way 
she and her mother had related. Now, 
for the first time, ambivalent feelings 
about her mother surfaced.

d her mother had related. Now, 
for the first time, ambivalent feelings 
about her mother surfaced. Yes, mother 
was her best friend, but she could be 
demanding and difficult at times; if Jane 
crossed her in any way, she would sulk. 
Then Jane would feel utterly wretched 
and abandoned, and compelled to break 
the ice and say she was sorry, even if she 
knew in her heart that it was her mother 
who was in the wrong.
The minutiae of transference led to a 
formulation as follows.

The minutiae of transference led to a 
formulation as follows. Jane’s relation-
ship with the therapist revealed a picture 
of anaclitic depression arising out of a 
hyper-activating pattern of insecure at-
tachment. Jane’s maternal caregiver was 
inconsistent: sometimes she was available 
or even overly available, sometimes 
mysteriously absent and rejecting. This 
set up a pattern of clinging attachment in 
which Jane’s self-composure was depen-

Jane’s underlying resentment and con-
comitant fear of “biting the hand that 
feeds” underlay her defensive idealiza-

He was the “one supposed to know” 
(whether or not to take antidepressants), 
and yet she felt he really knew noth-
ing about her (her fear of side effects, 
her wish to solve her problems without

resentment into the open, it was possible 
for the underlying feelings of fear, panic, 
helplessness, and rage to be processed by 
two DLPFCs acting in concert.
In order for Jane to benefit from therapy 
(antidepressants aside), she would need 
to co-create a pattern of relationship in 
which the analyst was available but not 
controlling, and to be able to express 
disagreement and resentment towards 
him without feeling that it would lead to 
rejection.

Implicit in the above is the idea that 
the neurobiology of transference in depres-
sion depends on hypofrontality of the DLP-
FC. Instead of the normal interlocking of 
two mutually exploring minds, the sufferer’s 
appraisal functions—of both self and oth-
er—are inhibited, so that primal emotions, 
including implicit procedural memories, bio-

including implicit procedural memories, bio-

projected onto or into the therapist (anaclitic 
pattern) or sequestered within the pressure 
cooker of the psyche (introjective pattern). 
Withdrawn into herself, Jane could only see 
the analyst in terms of pre-existing mental 
structures. In both cases, the therapeutic task 
is to re-activate the DLPFC and thereby re-
duce affect phobia.

n both cases, the therapeutic task 
is to re-activate the DLPFC and thereby re-

difficult feelings are gradually returned from 
therapist to the sufferer for reappraisal; in 
the introjective pattern, the patient is encour-

order to mentalize and modulate the hitherto 
warded-off mental pain and rage. 
An example of Jane’s progress was given 
in the “reinstatement” of her mother’s

An example of Jane’s progress was given 
in the “reinstatement” of her mother’s 
dinner set. Another occurred when she 
applied for a job for which she was not 
really qualified and, unsurprisingly, failed 
to get it. Jane was immediately plunged 
into depression, self-doubt, and feelings 
of inadequacy. However, that night she 
dreamed that she was climbing a ladder 
to change a light bulb, with her mother 
at the bottom of the steps telling her to 
come down, that she was about to fall.

Discussing this dream with her analyst, 
she saw how undermining her mother’s 
“over-helpfulness” had been and how 
it inhibited her attempts to change. 
Processing her feelings of depression in 
this way (using her own and the analyst’s 
DLPFC to regulate her subcortical affect) 
seemed to alleviate her depression and 
enabled her to laugh at her thus far ill-
thought-out attempt to find a job.

In moving from an external loss to its 
meaning and significance in the inner world,

In order to understand the effects of trauma on a person’s brain chem-

The human stress response system is centered around a small organ in the
limbic system, the amygdala. The amygdala connects the sensory system,
which perceives a threat to the motor system, which then responds to the
threat (Le Doux, 1990). When a threat reaches a certain threshold, the amyg-
dala sends messages through its many projections to respond to the
stress. Projections from the amygdala to the reticularis pontis initiate
the startle response (Davis, 1992).

rojections from the amygdala to the reticularis pontis initiate
the startle response (Davis, 1992). Projections from the amygdala to the
lateral hypothalamus and then to the rostral ventral medulla stimulate
the sympathetic nervous system (Le Doux et al., 1988). Projections from
the amygdala to the stria terminalis initiate, the hypothalamic-pituitary-
adrenal (HPA) axis response (Roozendaal, Koolhaas, & Bohus, 1992).
These pathways combine to create the “flight, fight or freeze” response
typical of individuals under acute stress.

This stress response system results in the release of both catechol-
amines (epinephrine and norepinephrine) and cortisol at the time of the
acute stress. Catecholamine release causes an increase in blood flow and
glucose to skeletal muscles to prepare for fight or flight (Guyton, 1986).
Cortisol, which may be thought of as an “anti-stress hormone,” shuts down
the stress response system.

Emotion Regulation
Timothy R. Rice *
Psychiatry, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY , USA
Keywords: defense mechanisms, implicit emotion regulation, psychodynamic psychotherapy, psychoanalysis,
child development
A commentary on
The Neural Bases of Emotion Regulation
by Etkin, A., Büchel, C., and Gross, J. J. (2015) Nat. Rev. Neurosci. 16, 693–700.

chunks.id: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf_3
chunks.source: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf
chunks.text:
otion Regulation
by Etkin, A., Büchel, C., and Gross, J. J. (2015) Nat. Rev. Neurosci. 16, 693–700. doi: 10.1038/nrn4044
Amit Etkin, Christian Büchel, and James Gross make a valuable contribution in their article “The
neural bases of emotion regulation” in the November 2015 issue of Nature reviews: Neuroscience
(Etkin et al., 2015). Their review article concludes a process of gradual elevati on of implicit emotion
regulation to an equal footing with explicit emotion regulation.

chunks.id: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf_4
chunks.source: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf
chunks.text:
ual elevati on of implicit emotion
regulation to an equal footing with explicit emotion regulation. Whereas, explicit processes of
emotion regulation refers to those that demand conscious, eﬀortful application, implicit refers
to those that proceed automatically and unconsciously. In this commentary, I suggest that the
increased recognition and neural deﬁnition of implicit emotion regulation processes oﬀers a unique
opportunity for psychodynamic psychotherapy.

chunks.id: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf_5
chunks.source: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf
chunks.text:
f implicit emotion regulation processes oﬀers a unique
opportunity for psychodynamic psychotherapy. The postulated equivalence of defense mechanisms
with implicit emotion regulation (Rice and Hoﬀman, 2014) extends an opportunity to ground a key
ps
ychodynamic construct in deﬁned neural correlates.
Etkin and colleagues’ article is not the ﬁrst time that the implicit emotion regulation construct
has been identiﬁed.

chunks.id: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf_6
chunks.source: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf
chunks.text:
es’ article is not the ﬁrst time that the implicit emotion regulation construct
has been identiﬁed. In a 2011 article Etkin’s group introduced “two theoretical and empirical
spheres that organize diﬀerent areas of emotion regulation and label these as ‘explicit’ and ‘implicit”’
(Gyurak et al., 2011). The authors note that there was some precedent to this organi
 zation in the
work of Bargh and Williams’ conceptualizations of eﬀortful and automatic processes (Bargh and
W
illiams, 2007), a work preceded by Bargh’s early interests in automaticity in social cognition
(Bargh, 1994).

chunks.id: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf_7
chunks.source: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf
chunks.text:
007), a work preceded by Bargh’s early interests in automaticity in social cognition
(Bargh, 1994). The organization of Bargh and Williams’ work parallels those of Susan Andersen and
others, where the study of transference phenomenon and other unconscious processes developed a
valuable scientiﬁc base to key psychodynamic principles (Berk and Andersen, 2000; Andersen and
P
rzybylinski, 2012).
T
he explicit-implicit distinction oﬀers a similar opportunity for the psychodynamic construct
of defense mechanisms.

chunks.id: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf_8
chunks.source: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf
chunks.text:
icit distinction oﬀers a similar opportunity for the psychodynamic construct
of defense mechanisms. Gross notes that past studies of emotion regulation include Freud’s studies
of how people unconsciously defend against anxiety-inducing impulses (Gross, 2013). Etkin and
c
olleagues’ valuation of implicit process emphasizes these unconscious processes as central to
the ﬁeld of neurobiological study of emotion regulation.

chunks.id: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf_9
chunks.source: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf
chunks.text:
these unconscious processes as central to
the ﬁeld of neurobiological study of emotion regulation. The distinction between ventromedially-
mediated implicit processes and more dorsolaterally-mediated explicit processes in the prefrontal
cortex oﬀers a means to observe these distinct unconscious processes. Because implicit emotion
regulation is postulated to be equivalent to defense mechanisms ( Rice and Hoﬀman, 2014), a key
ps
ychodynamic construct gains a neural signature and a valuable place in the study of the aﬀective
neurosciences.

chunks.id: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf_10
chunks.source: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf
chunks.text:
construct gains a neural signature and a valuable place in the study of the aﬀective
neurosciences. Establishing brain-based, neurobiological correlates to traditionally psychological
constructs advances the goals of the Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) project (Insel et al., 2010)
a
nd furthers the rapprochement between psychodynamics and contemporary medicine.
Implicit regulation originates in the inhibitory action of the ventral prefrontal cortex (vPFC),
which includes the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), ventromedial PFC (vmPFC), and ventral anterior

chunks.id: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf_11
chunks.source: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf
chunks.text:
PFC),
which includes the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), ventromedial PFC (vmPFC), and ventral anterior
Rice Commentary: The Neural Bases of Emotion Regulation
cingulate cortex (vACC; Etkin et al., 2013 ). Bidirectional
inhibitory action from these centers modulates lower
brain structures including the amygdala, ventral striatum ,
hypothalamus, and brainstem nuclei. These pathways are distinct
from those in explicit emotion regulation that originate in a reas
including the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC) and t he
dorsolateral PFC (dPFC).

chunks.id: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf_12
chunks.source: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf
chunks.text:
e in a reas
including the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC) and t he
dorsolateral PFC (dPFC). The successful modulation of these
limbic and visceromotor centers by these PFC regulators lea ds
to decreased sympathetic arousal and increased parasympathet ic
or vagal tone (
Lane et al., 2009 ). This results in a measurable
neurochemical state of phenotypic calmness.
Regional diﬀerentials in synaptogenesis, myelination, and
pruning create earlier maturity in ventral as opposed to dorsal
areas (
Fuster, 2002 ), leaving children and adolescents without

chunks.id: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf_13
chunks.source: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf
chunks.text:
ty in ventral as opposed to dorsal
areas (
Fuster, 2002 ), leaving children and adolescents without
explicit cognitive emotional controls ( Casey et al., 2011 ).
Normative development in the implicit ER system thus may be
extremely important in children to promote self-regulation when
the neurobiological substrates to employ explicit ER are lack ing.
Operationalized defense analysis may progress implicit ER
development.

chunks.id: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf_14
chunks.source: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf
chunks.text:
oy explicit ER are lack ing.
Operationalized defense analysis may progress implicit ER
development. Contributions beyond Freud, particularly thos e
made in the subspecialty of child and adolescent psychoanalys is,
make the parallel between implicit emotion regulation and
defense mechanisms clear. Sigmund Freud’s daughter Anna
signiﬁcantly developed the defense mechanism construct (
Freud,
1936).

chunks.id: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf_15
chunks.source: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf
chunks.text:
igmund Freud’s daughter Anna
signiﬁcantly developed the defense mechanism construct (
Freud,
1936). The shift from understanding defenses as protecting
against theoretical, immeasurable drives to protecting aga inst
observable and measurable aﬀective states occurred through
the groundbreaking work of
Bornstein (1945, 1949) and the
subsequent generational line of child analysts to the present
(
Becker, 1974; Hoﬀman, 2007 ).

chunks.id: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf_16
chunks.source: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf
chunks.text:
d the
subsequent generational line of child analysts to the present
(
Becker, 1974; Hoﬀman, 2007 ). This shift and its contemporary
acceptance emphasize that children employ a range of defenses
to help themselves tolerate unbearable, discomforting fee lings.
The parallels between implicit emotion regulation and defens e
mechanisms is quite clear.
To date, no author has oﬀered a biological substrate to
defense mechanisms, though broader eﬀorts at deﬁning the
neural bases of the dynamic unconscious have been made (
Berlin,
2011).

chunks.id: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf_17
chunks.source: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf
chunks.text:
oader eﬀorts at deﬁning the
neural bases of the dynamic unconscious have been made (
Berlin,
2011). This makes this contribution that is made possible by
the scientiﬁc works of Etkin, Bargh, and Gross unique and
valuable.
The relative isolation of the child psychoanalytic literatu re
may have served to hinder awareness of the parallels between
defense mechanisms and implicit emotion. This may have
prevented the spread of established therapeutic intervention s
focused on defense mechanisms beyond psychoanalytic
circles.

chunks.id: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf_18
chunks.source: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf
chunks.text:
established therapeutic intervention s
focused on defense mechanisms beyond psychoanalytic
circles. The operationalization of defense analysis into a
manualized, short-term psychotherapy termed Regulation
Focused Psychotherapy for Children (RFP-C;
Hoﬀman et al.,
2016) is one means to interface this therapeutic intervention
targeting implicit ER with contemporary models of health care
provision. This approach maintains focus on the disruptive
child’s aggression as maladaptive defense mechanisms agains t
sadness, loss, loneliness, and trauma.

chunks.id: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf_19
chunks.source: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf
chunks.text:
hild’s aggression as maladaptive defense mechanisms agains t
sadness, loss, loneliness, and trauma. The approach helps the
child to recognize that the feared feelings will not overwhe lm
him or her, and that alternative strategies are available. T hrough
this approach children develop a wider range of adaptive defense
mechanisms and employ them more ﬂexibly, leading to health
and developmental progression (
Hoﬀman, 2007).
The observed parallels between defense mechanisms and
the implicit emotion regulation system ( Rice and Hoﬀman,
2014) enable us to hypothesize that this manualized procedure

chunks.id: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf_20
chunks.source: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf
chunks.text:
regulation system ( Rice and Hoﬀman,
2014) enable us to hypothesize that this manualized procedure
will strengthen implicit emotion regulation processes. Child ren
who participate in the treatment will show improvements in
validated measures of emotion regulation. Further elabora tion
of the implicit emotion regulation system and its neural
correlates and of this psychodynamic treatment may one day
enable measurement of change at the neural system level,
through electroencephalogram or functional magnetic resonance
imaging.

chunks.id: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf_21
chunks.source: Commentary -The neural bases of emotion regulation.pdf
chunks.text:
at the neural system level,
through electroencephalogram or functional magnetic resonance
imaging. The aﬀective neurosciences oﬀer rich opportunities fo r
psychodynamic psychiatry, and Etkin and colleague’s work oﬀer
a special one for defense analysis.

Commentary on ‘The case for neuropsychoanalysis ’
Dear Editor,
As a psychoanalyst intrigued by the hyphen in the neuro-psychoanalysis I
welcomed the discussion for and against ‘The case for neuropsychoanalysis’
(2015), but was rather demoralized by the absence of the ‘meeting of the
minds’ on two sides of it.

Yovell, Solms and Fotopoulou seemed to do disservice to their case of

Abstract
Freud wanted to be a scientist but fell short of this goal in several ways: first by attempting to make psychoanalysis consistent

but fell short of this goal in several ways: first by attempting to make psychoanalysis consistent 
with Newtonian physics, second by not being rigorous with the scientific method, and finally, by responding to political and 
social needs. As a result, science did not welcome psychoanalysis into its fold. Fortunately, this is changing. In the years since 
Freud’s death, two science-based psychoanalytic theories have developed: attachment theory and affect theory. They are both 
measurable and supported by social psychology, neuroscience, and infant research.

brilliance, contributed a great deal to the understanding

Reason, which directed his desire to be scientific.

Bowlby
A serendipitous fact connects Fairbairn with Bowlby. They 
were both acutely aware of the suffering of children who 
were separated from their families during World War II. 
These separations were aimed at protecting children by 
getting them out of London and away from the threat of

Davanloo, 1990; Coughlin della Selva, 1996; McCullough, 1997;
Davanloo, 2000; McCullough et al., 2003; Frederickson, 2013).
Then patients can feel their feelings without being dysregulated.
CONCLUSION
In the present paper, we explored the issue of emotion
regulation inside psychodynamic approaches and how concepts

paper, we explored the issue of emotion
regulation inside psychodynamic approaches and how concepts
of anxiety and defenses may be useful to understand patients’
DAS and we provided a framework and methodology for
an Experiential-Dynamic Emotion Regulation Methodology
(EDER) that incorporate emotion regulation science principles
into psychodynamic psychotherapy.
A number of studies in the ﬁeld of experimental psychology
and aﬀective neuroscience have collected evidence that emotion
regulation strongly contributes to psychological health (Aldao

have collected evidence that emotion
regulation strongly contributes to psychological health (Aldao
et al., 2010; Hu et al., 2014) and that some strategies produce
better health outcome than others (Gross, 2002; Gross and
John, 2003). Here, we extend these studies by considering
another important element that determines the adaptiveness
of emotion regulation: the diﬀerentiation between original
emotion and DAS.

rmines the adaptiveness
of emotion regulation: the diﬀerentiation between original
emotion and DAS. Physiological emotions should be expressed
and a regulatory function is not necessarily required, whereas
dysregulated states require regulation due to their negative
contribution to individual adaptation to the environment. At
the clinical level, this has important implications.

o individual adaptation to the environment. At
the clinical level, this has important implications. The therapist
should promote the expression of original emotions and block
DASs.
Thus, the concepts of emotion regulation and dysregulation
are consistent with the psychodynamic view of aﬀective disorders
and their therapy. In addition to cognitive-behavioral methods of
emotion regulation, we include psychodynamic forms of emotion
regulation.

ive-behavioral methods of
emotion regulation, we include psychodynamic forms of emotion
regulation. We noted that the use of techniques that implicitly
involve emotion regulation could be more eﬀective than the use
of voluntary emotion regulation strategies. Indeed, in some cases
voluntary emotion regulation strategies may compromise the free
expression of original emotions.
Despite the explicit reference to ISTDP , we consider that the
EDER concepts and techniques may be usefully incorporated into
any other psychotherapy models when working with patients
suﬀering from DASs.

lly incorporated into
any other psychotherapy models when working with patients
suﬀering from DASs. EDER principles oﬀer a trans-theoretical
approach for the understanding of situations that require the
building of the capacities for emotion tolerance and regulation,
and anxiety regulation. EDER techniques may be used to
enhance emotion tolerance as an alternative to cognitive control
techniques that may be detrimental when they support emotion
avoidance.
Despite such interesting insights concerning theoretical
models of psychotherapy, the clinical recommendation of

interesting insights concerning theoretical
models of psychotherapy, the clinical recommendation of
EDER would require an empirical evaluation of the eﬃcacy
and tolerability of the model in clinical studies. Other brief
psychodynamic approaches have been consistently aﬃrmed as
evidence-based therapies (Abbass et al., 2006, 2009; Driessen
et al., 2010). Comparative studies are strongly recommended to
add to the scientiﬁc evidence for the EDER approach, and to
identify its speciﬁc change mechanisms when compared with
other psychodynamic approaches.

chunks.text:
Emotion Regulation, Relationship and
Therapeutic Change in Analytical
Psychology and Contemporary
Psychodynamic Approaches
Christian Roesler, Freiburg, Germany
Abstract
All contemporary psychotherapies agree that (failing) emotion regulation is central to
psychological disorders and that psychotherapy is about improving emotion regulation.
In his research on the “emotion-laden” complex Jung put an emphasis on the role of
failing emotion regulation in contributing to psychological disorders as well as to
change in the process of psychotherapy, but he left this ﬁeld of research and took a very

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_1
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
ell as to
change in the process of psychotherapy, but he left this ﬁeld of research and took a very
different direction in favour of his archetype concept. Psychodynamic approaches
generally argue that changes in emotion regulation are accomplished through corrective
emotional experiences in the therapeutic relationship. Insights from affective
neurosciences and attachment research have had a major in ﬂuence on how the
therapeutic relationship is constructed in contemporary psychodynamic approaches.
There is a lack of similar developments in analytical psychology, which leads to

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_2
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
ynamic approaches.
There is a lack of similar developments in analytical psychology, which leads to
substantial differences between the models of Jungian psychotherapy in contrast to
other contemporary psychodynamic approaches. The implications of these differences
for the practice of psychotherapy and especially the role of the therapeutic relationship
are pointed out.
Keywords: affective neuroscience, analytical psychology, attachment research, emotion
regulation, psychodynamic psychotherapy, therapeutic relationship

ogy, attachment research, emotion

At the beginning of the 20th century, Jung earned his international reputation,
even before he became linked to the psychoanalytic movement, with his
research on the affective-laden complex. He could provide empirical evidence
that there are unconscious factors, fuelled by strong emotions, which are not
accessible to or controllable by consciousness but which have a major impact
on cognitive functioning and behaviour (Roesler, 2017).

the emphasis on the concept of archetypes.

In the last years, the focus on emotion regulation has gained major
importance in clinical psychology: the major schools of psychotherapy agree
that emotion regulation is the decisive factor for psychotherapy. On the one
hand, psychological disorders can be understood as speci ﬁc impairments of
emotion regulation; on the other hand, psychotherapy aims at an
improvement of this emotion regulation.

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_6
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
ion regulation; on the other hand, psychotherapy aims at an
improvement of this emotion regulation. These views have changed the
traditional orientation in cognitive approaches, which assumed that emotions
are the results of cognitions, in the sense that the cognition is before the
emotion and gives them their speci ﬁc colouration. LeDoux ( 1998) could
demonstrate that the relationship between cognitions and emotions is
characterized by a complex reciprocity.

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_7
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
te that the relationship between cognitions and emotions is
characterized by a complex reciprocity. The attempt to regulate problematic
emotions by cognitive control has turned out to be limited, whereas the
psychodynamic schools have always emphasized that the improvement of
emotion regulation takes place within the therapeutic relationship, through an
internalization of a successful interpersonal regulation of the client ’s emotions.
In this paper, the parallels as well as the differences in the view on emotion
regulation in analytical psychology, in the other psychodynamic schools and

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_8
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
in the view on emotion
regulation in analytical psychology, in the other psychodynamic schools and
in contemporary theories of emotion are investigated with special emphasis
on how this impacts different approaches to psychotherapy and the role of
the therapeutic relationship.
Complexes
Complexes are, according to Jung, affective laden unconscious factors. They are
organized around strong emotions, and they trigger strong emotions when
activated, which adversely in ﬂuences behaviour, e.g., cognitive processing and
memory (Jung, 1959, para. 4).

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_9
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
which adversely in ﬂuences behaviour, e.g., cognitive processing and
memory (Jung, 1959, para. 4). Pathological complexes are what has to be
focused on in psychotherapy, and they have formed through problematic
relationship experiences with caregivers which results in unresolved emotions,
or, to put it in contemporary terms, poor emotion regulation. The theory of
complexes is well proven empirically, and it was already in Jung ’s time. Jung
received international reputation as a scientist and researcher because of his
studies with the Association experiment.

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_10
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
al reputation as a scientist and researcher because of his
studies with the Association experiment. Already in this research he was able
to provide evidence for the existence of unconscious emotional factors which
inﬂuence behaviour. In the last decades, more research was conducted which
conﬁrms the concept of complexes as unconscious emotional factors, for
example in fMRI studies (for an overview see Roesler & van Uffelen, 2018).
It is also con ﬁrmed by developmental and attachment research, which has
demonstrated that attachment patterns are formed during development

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_11
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
attachment research, which has
demonstrated that attachment patterns are formed during development
around emotional experiences with caregivers (see below). An example is A.
Damasio’s( 2012) concept of somatic markers. The neuroscientist was able to
demonstrate that there is an emotional memory system which stores
emotional experiences. It does so by connecting them with somatic markers,

i.e., bodily feelings. If the person is again in a similar situation, emotional
memory is activated via the somatic markers. This is useful as it can support
decision-making if several options are available. If the earlier experience was
connected with negative emotion, in a similar later situation this emotion is
activated by somatic markers and serves as protection against decisions with
painful consequences; the whole process operates on an unconscious level.

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_14
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
on against decisions with
painful consequences; the whole process operates on an unconscious level.
This supports Jung ’s concept of complexes. It also explains why psychic
disorders based on earlier painful experiences and the accompanying
dysfunctional patterns in cognition and behaviour are so dif ﬁcult to change
by psychotherapy. To provide therapeutic change, psychotherapy has to reach
the level of these embodied emotional memories.
Basic Emotions as Signalling Systems
The neuroscientist Joseph LeDoux ( 1998, 2012) and his research tradition

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_15
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
ons as Signalling Systems
The neuroscientist Joseph LeDoux ( 1998, 2012) and his research tradition
argue that emotions are signalling or information systems which point to
unmet needs in the organism. This is also the reason why there are innate
speciﬁc emotions, as they point to basic needs essential for the survival of the
organism (see below). Moser ( 2023) argues that the basic function of
emotions in this information theory perspective is to cause an interruption in
mental processing so as to regulate an internal or external relationship.

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_16
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
cause an interruption in
mental processing so as to regulate an internal or external relationship. In
addition, there is also a totally unconscious emotion regulation on the limbic
level, which guarantees a relatively automated behavioural response, in the
sense of top-down control to down-regulate the amygdala. It seems that in
strong pathological complexes these regulatory processes could not develop,
or they break down, as a consequence of unresolved early experiences and the
accompanying strong emotions (Panksepp et al., 2017).

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_17
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
uence of unresolved early experiences and the
accompanying strong emotions (Panksepp et al., 2017).
Panksepp ( 1998, 2011) identi ﬁed seven “basic affective systems ” (the idea
was already put forward by Darwin in 1871): SEEKING (expectancy), FEAR
(anxiety), RAGE (anger), LUST (sexual excitement), CARE (nurturance),
PANIC/GRIEF (sadness), PLAY (social joy). These basic emotion systems are
in a certain sense lifesavers, since they circle around existential needs and
situations. The theory is extremely well empirically founded.

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_18
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
y circle around existential needs and
situations. The theory is extremely well empirically founded. The mainstream
in the neurosciences agrees with the basic tenets of this approach, which has
been called neuroaffective theory or theory of basic emotional systems.
Neuropsychological systems such as Panksepp ’s basic systems are called
bottom-up processes in cognitive neurosciences; in humans they are regulated
and modulated by top-down mechanisms, e.g., controlled by the prefrontal
cortex, up to the point that they can be totally inhibited.

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_19
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
sms, e.g., controlled by the prefrontal
cortex, up to the point that they can be totally inhibited. These regulatory
mechanisms are fully dependent on one ’s individual history of experiences,
ﬁrst of all in primary caregiver relationships.

Emotions are Relational
In line with Panksepp, Ekman ( 1992) identi ﬁed basic emotion expressions in
the face, which form universal speci ﬁc signalling systems.

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_21
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
identi ﬁed basic emotion expressions in
the face, which form universal speci ﬁc signalling systems. He described
practically the same basic emotions as pointed out above but put the focus in
his research on the facial expressions of these emotions and how they can be
identiﬁed by other humans. He found that these basic emotions are expressed
by universal facial expressions which can also be found in primates.

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_22
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
e basic emotions are expressed
by universal facial expressions which can also be found in primates. These
emotions and the connected facial expressions have a speci ﬁc physiology and
a hardwired coherence between detecting a speci ﬁc facial expression and the
according emotional reaction. Since they are universal they are expressed and
can be understood similarly in all cultures in the world.

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_23
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
they are universal they are expressed and
can be understood similarly in all cultures in the world. Now the interesting
point is that even newborn babies are able to show these facial expressions
and to read them correctly in the face of another person (Hardy 2009); they
can even imitate them if seen on the face of another person (Meltzoff &
Moore, 1977).
Based on these insights, Ekman developed a theory about the functions of
these basic emotions and their expressions.

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_24
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
sights, Ekman developed a theory about the functions of
these basic emotions and their expressions. Emotions inform the individual
about their own current inner state and signal to others about unmet needs.
Thus, emotions prepare the organism for action, they activate in a speci ﬁc
way. This activation is directed towards others, this is a biologically
preformed general human attitude. Humans make use of others and the
relationship to them to regulate their emotions and to communicate their
needs, which, as far as it refers to the basic emotions, are directed to other
persons (see Table 1).

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_25
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
eds, which, as far as it refers to the basic emotions, are directed to other
persons (see Table 1). Thus, emotions are relationship oriented.
In this sense, emotions are a signalling system which plays a crucial role in
self-regulation and relationship regulation.
This interpersonal system of emotion regulation was further investigated
by the infant researchers in the context of the Boston Process of Change
Study Group (Stern, 1985).

by the infant researchers in the context of the Boston Process of Change
Study Group (Stern, 1985). They found that in infancy and early childhood
the child and its caregiver together form a shared emotional regulation system
which communicates via the universal basic facial expressions of emotions

(Tronick, 1989). The genetic makeup of humans is oriented towards interaction
with other human beings and sociality —the “social embedded brain ”
(Northoff, 2015).

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_29
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
s interaction
with other human beings and sociality —the “social embedded brain ”
(Northoff, 2015). The most elaborate theory resulting from these
considerations is attachment theory and attachment research.
Attachment
Human infants would not be able to survive without the care of a more
experienced adult who is able to regulate their basic physiological needs as
well as their stress levels, because young infants cannot take care of these basic
physiological and psychological needs by themselves.

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_30
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
young infants cannot take care of these basic
physiological and psychological needs by themselves. The early environment
of evolutionary adaptiveness among humans required the basic ability to
become emotionally attached in order to survive and enhance inclusive ﬁtness.
Since the environment of humans consists mainly of situations with a high
need of cooperation and complex social interaction, these are the competencies
which human children must be prepared for.

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_31
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
d complex social interaction, these are the competencies
which human children must be prepared for. Thus, the evolutionary
adaptiveness of humans involves the acquisition of complex social and
interactive competencies, which is only possible through experiences in a social
network itself, it cannot be pre-formed by genes. The genetic makeup only
prepares the infant to be highly sensitive for social interaction (Simpson &
Belsky, 2018).

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_32
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
up only
prepares the infant to be highly sensitive for social interaction (Simpson &
Belsky, 2018). Following this model, it also can be assumed that the mating
model of long-term pair bonds seems to be the most reasonable, since it
provides the most suitable environment for the development of complex social
competencies. On the other hand, this implies that the quality of the
environment early in life can exert long-lasting effects on psychosocial
development, including social competency and the development of speci ﬁc
mating and parenting strategies in both males and females.

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_33
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
mpetency and the development of speci ﬁc
mating and parenting strategies in both males and females.
On the other hand, depending on the quality of these early social interactions
provided mainly by the caregivers, …
Infants differ rather drastically in the quality of their attachment relationships, and
attachment theory hypothesizes that this attachment performance is largely, albeit
not exclusively, environmentally determined … as a consequence of childrearing
experiences with parents and other caregivers …. The parallel to language
development is useful here.

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_34
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
periences with parents and other caregivers …. The parallel to language
development is useful here. Every child is born with the capacity to learn a language,
but the speci ﬁc language environment determines the kind of language to be learned.
(Bakermans-Kranenburg & van Ijzendoorn, 2018,p . 155)
The ﬁndings of attachment research point to the fact that the development of
the self of human beings is almost exclusively based on interpersonal
processes.

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_35
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
the development of
the self of human beings is almost exclusively based on interpersonal
processes. The newborn infant has just some basic abilities to draw the
caregiver into a form of interaction, e.g., by imitating the face expression
(therefore Ekman ’s universal face expressions), or giving other signals which
are then interpreted by the caregiver as an initiative to communication. Here,

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_37
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
almost totally on a caregiver who is aware of the signals and responds to
them in a sensitive way. If this happens, the child can increasingly rely on the
presence of the caregiver and use the adult person to regulate its needs and
emotions. The way in which the adult caregiver responds, i.e., sensitive or
not, will determine the internalized representations of these interactions
(Daniel Stern: representations of interactions generalized). So, the self which is
formed in such processes is constituted by interpersonal processes, by
interactions.

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_38
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
self which is
formed in such processes is constituted by interpersonal processes, by
interactions. There is no way that the child could develop his/herself
individually and independently. Even when children have formed an early
form of the self, they still apply what is called social referencing: when
confronted with a new experience, the ﬁrst thing they do is to look on the
face of the caregiver for emotional cues as to how to interpret this experience.
These ideas have been put together in the theory of the social brain

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_39
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
to interpret this experience.
These ideas have been put together in the theory of the social brain
(Pfaff, 2013), which basically points out that the brain of humans is largely a
social construction.
Consequences for Contemporary Psychoanalytic Theories
From these insights, in psychoanalysis, the relational and intersubjective schools
have developed, which are based on the infant research conducted by the
Boston Process of Change Study Group, employing concepts such as Stern ’s
representations of interactions that have been generalized (Stern, 1985).

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_40
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
concepts such as Stern ’s
representations of interactions that have been generalized (Stern, 1985). The
general idea here is that the psyche is structured and practically built from the
early interactional experiences of the child in its relationships with caregivers.
It also has to be noted that the term drive, so fundamental to orthodox
psychoanalysis, meanwhile has been discarded in the contemporary schools of
the Freudian tradition, and has been reformulated as the concept of
motivations (e.g., Lichtenberg, Lachmann & Fosshage, 2009):

chunks.text:
has been reformulated as the concept of
motivations (e.g., Lichtenberg, Lachmann & Fosshage, 2009):
Post-Freudians, for instance, have replaced Freud ’s pleasure principle as the primary
biological drive with the idea of the need for relationship and relatedness as our
most basic human longing. Wherever we turn across the psychodynamic spectrum,
we see therapy more concerned with engagement, and more critical of all forms of
disengagement, especially narcissism and other disorders of relatedness.
(Tacey, 1998,p .

speciﬁc motivations; they activate the organism in a speci ﬁc way and at the
same time inform the social environment about the current inner state of the
person. This enables humans to show affective attunement and, on a higher

level, mentalization. In this sense, the basic emotions are primarily adaptive,
which means, when they are activated they lead to adaptive behaviours,
individually as well as socially. Therefore, contemporary psychotherapy
approaches, as for example Emotionally Focused Therapy, focus on these
basic or primary emotions as their activation is in itself therapeutic.
For relational analysts, the social aspect of our being is fundamental to psychological
life—it is not an add-on or a separate domain of our existence.

the relational context in which it is embedded. (Colman, 2018,p .

subsequent to and contingent upon
the relational context in which it is embedded. (Colman, 2018,p . 130)
Archetypes and Emotions: Jung ’s Developmental Model
These ideas are more or less the contrary of how Jung imagined the
development of a person, putting the emphasis mainly on what comes out of
the individual ( “the myth of the isolated mind ”). Archetypes here are
considered to be preformatted patterns and structures, which develop
independently from experiences in interactional relationships (Roesler, 2021),
what Jung calls “autochthonous development ”.

chunks.text:
ences in interactional relationships (Roesler, 2021),
what Jung calls “autochthonous development ”. In contrast to the above
model, Jung conceptualizes psychic energy, libido, as a general,
undifferentiated emotional energy, which is behind all psychological
processes. The archetypes provide the speci ﬁc colouration to this general
undifferentiated emotional energy.

interpretation determined by the situational context. In contrast to this, the

For Jung, archetypes are channels for emotions or psychic energy in general,
which give the energy a certain shape and direction (Jung, 1976, para. 589). In
Jung, the general idea is that archetypes shape a universal, preformatted process
of transformation in which emotions are the energy.

chunks.text:
hetypes shape a universal, preformatted process
of transformation in which emotions are the energy. Jung believed that the
archetypes connected with emotions are similar to instincts in animals, in the
sense that a speci ﬁc symbol (representing an archetype) triggers a speci ﬁc
meaning or emotion, in the same manner as the innate release mechanism in
behavioural biology triggers an instinctually ﬁxated pattern of behaviour.
Contemporary neuroscience contradicts this notion: there are no universal
signals triggering speci ﬁc emotions in humans.

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_54

chunks.text:
nce contradicts this notion: there are no universal
signals triggering speci ﬁc emotions in humans. Emotions in humans are
always the result of subjective interpretations, based on earlier experiences
and individual emotion regulation. In Ethology/Behavioural Biology
(Bischof, 1985/2020) an instinct/pattern of behaviour is clearly de ﬁned and
has three components:
1. a trigger mechanism (innate release mechanism IRM), which means that
there is a speci ﬁc stimulus in the environment which can be detected by
the individual, which then
2. activates a drive, which leads to
3.

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_55

chunks.text:
ronment which can be detected by
the individual, which then
2. activates a drive, which leads to
3. an inherited automatic coordinated action pattern.
There is no such thing in human beings (for more details see Roesler, 2023).
It also has to be noted that the ﬁndings around these basic emotion systems
clearly show that, in contrast to Jung ’s thoughts (and as argued recently by
Alcaro et al., 2017), the genetic information does not directly activate
behaviour patterns, but it activates affect and emotion, which is consciously
experienced and then initiates actions.

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_56
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
, but it activates affect and emotion, which is consciously
experienced and then initiates actions.
In this context, it is again important to consider that much of the massive neocortical
expansions since human divergence from greater apes was substantially controlled by
a single gene variant, ARHGAP 11 B. We think such ﬁndings provide little leeway for
robust and speci ﬁc genetic control of various high-end neocortical primary sensory
and affective functions [ …] (Panksepp et al., 2017,p .

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_57

chunks.text:
arious high-end neocortical primary sensory
and affective functions [ …] (Panksepp et al., 2017,p . 199)
So, there is no direct path from genes to behaviour, but the path goes from genes
via emotions to behaviour (Solms, 2015). The ﬁxated patterns also do not react
to trigger stimuli, as instinctual behaviour in animals does. In contrast to
instincts, the basic emotion systems in humans are signalling systems for
existential needs and lead to typical behaviour directed mostly towards the
caregivers, e.g., attachment behaviours.

Jung regarding archetypes:

Consequences for the Practice of Psychotherapy

Consequences for the Practice of Psychotherapy
The above insights, of course, have far-reaching implications for the practice of
Jungian psychotherapy. In contrast to the classical school, where the therapist
waits for an autochthonous development to unfold out of the person
independently, based on biologically/genetically imprinted archetypes, should
the emphasis not be much more on creating a certain quality of relationship,
as the relational schools in psychoanalysis suggest? But if so, what is the

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_63
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
uality of relationship,
as the relational schools in psychoanalysis suggest? But if so, what is the
relationship between the idea of archetypes and an archetypal development of
the person in the course of psychotherapy on the one side, and the
contribution of the therapeutic relationship on the other? It seems to me that
this relationship is not really clari ﬁed even in contemporary schools of
Jungian psychology.
It is interesting that recent accounts of the process which is assumed to unfold
in Jungian psychotherapy often largely ignore the classic model of archetypes.

generalized” (Boston Change Process Study Group, Stern 1985), but describes
the psychotherapeutic process, although she calls it archetypal, without any

The Role of the Therapeutic Relationship
In Jung’s perspective, development of the personality happens almost exclusively
from inside the individual, autonomously, relationships do not play a role
beyond their being a projection screen (Healy, 2017). For example: “At the
heart of marriage is the question whether one can live his true nature, and if
one can give the other —being it husband or wife —the freedom for their
individuation” (Jung in Jaffé, 2021,p . 57; author ’s translation).

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_68
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
or wife —the freedom for their
individuation” (Jung in Jaffé, 2021,p . 57; author ’s translation). This means a
relationship, at best, is not an obstacle to individuation.
This attitude is in drastic contrast to the state-of-the-art in human and social
sciences (the “relational self ”), as presented above —and in practically all the
other psychodynamic schools —that relationships are at the very beginning of
individual development and are absolutely essential for the development of
the personality.

chunks.text:
ning of
individual development and are absolutely essential for the development of
the personality. There is a lack of clarity in the theory of analytic psychology
as to where development comes from, which role relationships play in the
matter and what that means for the therapeutic relationship.
Analytical Psychology as elaborated by Jung and his immediate followers did not focus
on the depth psychological aspects of the early infant and childhood development.
Neither was there much attention paid to the usefulness of understanding the

childhood development.
Neither was there much attention paid to the usefulness of understanding the
varieties of relationship that can occur in the consulting room between patient and
analyst.… The lack of a clinical and theoretical tradition of investigation in these two
important areas … with the resulting lack of interest in understanding their
interrelationship via the analysis of the infantile transference, left AP impoverished in
an important way. This would need to be recti ﬁed if AP was to go on developing as a
creditable professional and clinical endeavor. (Solomon, 1997,p .

f AP was to go on developing as a
creditable professional and clinical endeavor. (Solomon, 1997,p . 119)
There has been some theoretical development regarding the conceptualization
of the transference and its role in psychotherapy, mainly in the British —
so-called developmental —school of analytical psychology —but there is no
match to the theoretical developments in the Freudian tradition (e.g., object
relations theory, self-psychology, infant observation etc.).

n the Freudian tradition (e.g., object

analyst and patient, in which both descend into mutual unconscious

differing perceptions of the nature of the unconscious. (Knox, 2009,p .

Knox points out that beginning with the object relations school in
psychoanalysis, all of the contemporary relational approaches in
psychoanalysis agree on the three fundamental developmental tasks that have
to be accomplished in a successful therapy:
1. affect regulation
2. the capacity for mentalization
3.

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_84
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
be accomplished in a successful therapy:
1. affect regulation
2. the capacity for mentalization
3. a sense of self agency
These capacities, especially affect regulation and the capacity for mentalization
directly result from the relational interaction with the therapist/analyst:
especially “the emotional regulation offered by the relationship creates the
conditions necessary for the neuronal development in the orbitofrontal cortex
and other areas on which affect regulation depends ” (Knox, 2009,p .

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_85
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
nt in the orbitofrontal cortex
and other areas on which affect regulation depends ” (Knox, 2009,p . 10).
Psychotherapeutic change comes about through the experience of being
mentalized in an emotionally safe and valued relationship. In one of his latest
papers, Peter Fonagy (Fonagy et al., 2022) even presents the viewpoint that
all the psychological problems that need psychotherapy are rooted in
experiences of being insuf ﬁciently mentalized in the course of development,
and can, therefore, be treated effectively by a mentalization focused approach.

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_86
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
rse of development,
and can, therefore, be treated effectively by a mentalization focused approach.
Incidentally, this corresponds to what Shedler ( 2022)d e ﬁnes as the basic
elements of modern psychodynamic psychotherapy: Focus on emotion,
emotional expression; exploration of patient ’s attempts to avoid distressing
thoughts and feelings (defences); identi ﬁcation of recurrent patterns;
exploration of past experiences; focus on interpersonal relationships; focus on
therapy relationship; exploration of fantasies.
These tasks are very different from what Jung thought to be the aims of

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_87
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
; exploration of fantasies.
These tasks are very different from what Jung thought to be the aims of
therapy. Here, the relational model speaks of mental capacities of emotion
regulation, whereas Jung speaks of clearly de ﬁned stages of a process —which
has a parallel in Jung ’s view of biologically inherited qualities, i.e., archetypes,
as being speci ﬁed by their content (e.g., anima, the wise old man etc.) versus
contemporary insights in innate qualities being mainly capacities for relating
and interpersonal emotion regulation.

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_88
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
ghts in innate qualities being mainly capacities for relating
and interpersonal emotion regulation. Contemporary developmental models
put the emphasis on capacities and not on content, whereas Jung ’s idea was
that content patterns were preformatted. It also has to be noted that, based on
the research which found that inborn capacities consist of interaction and
relationship abilities, in contemporary psychodynamic approaches the self in
development is always conceptualized as “Self-being-with-other” (Stern, 1985)

Self-Righting
I would like to conclude with reference to a concept developed in the context of
Kohut’s self psychology, the capacity of self-righting (Milch, 2022). By this is
meant an intrinsic tendency of the organism to recover from a de ﬁcit and to
make a developmental advance even when external conditions were
obstructive. A normal developmental step that was hindered or missing
altogether becomes possible later.

Toutes les psychothérapies actuelles s ’accordent sur le fait que la régulation (défaillante)
de l ’émotion est au centre des désordres psychologiques et que la psychothérapie vise à
améliorer la régulation de l ’émotion. Dans sa recherche sur le « complexe à haute
charge émotionnelle », Jung a mis l ’accent sur le rôle de la régulation défaillante de
l’émotion comme participant aux désordres psychologiques ainsi qu ’au changement
dans le processus de psychothérapie.

dans le processus de psychothérapie. Mais il a abandonné ce champ de recherche et
pris une direction très différente, y préférant son concept de l ’archétype. Les approches
psychodynamiques plaident généralement en faveur de l ’idée que les changements dans
la régulation de l ’émotion sont atteints par les expériences émotionnelles corrective
dans la relation thérapeutique.

thérapeutique est construite dans les approches psychodynamiques actuelles. De tels
développements font défaut dans la psychologie analytique, ce qui conduit à des
différences considérables entre les modèles de psychothérapie jungienne en contraste
avec les autres approches psychodynamiques actuelles.

Tutte le psicoterapie contemporanee concordano sul fatto che la (fallita) regolazione
delle emozioni è centrale per i disturbi psicologici e che la psicoterapia riguarda il
miglioramento della regolazione delle emozioni.

chunks.id: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf_123
chunks.source: EMOTION REGULATION, RELATIONSHIP AND THERAPEUTIC CHANGE.pdf
chunks.text:
turbi psicologici e che la psicoterapia riguarda il
miglioramento della regolazione delle emozioni. Nella sua ricerca sul complesso
“carico di emozioni ”, Jung ha posto l ’accento sul ruolo della fallita regolazione delle
emozioni nel contribuire ai disturbi psicologici e al cambiamento nel processo della
psicoterapia, ma ha poi abbandonato questo campo di ricerca ed ha preso una
direzione molto diversa, centrata sul suo concetto di archetipo.

chunks.text:
o campo di ricerca ed ha preso una
direzione molto diversa, centrata sul suo concetto di archetipo. Gli approcci
psicodinamici generalmente sostengono che i cambiamenti nella regolazione delle
emozioni avvengono tramite esperienze emozionali correttive nella relazione
terapeutica. Le intuizioni delle neuroscienze affettive e della ricerca sull ’attaccamento
hanno avuto un ’inﬂuenza importante sul modo in cui la relazione terapeutica è
costruita negli approcci psicodinamici contemporanei.

chunks.text:
te sul modo in cui la relazione terapeutica è
costruita negli approcci psicodinamici contemporanei. C ’è una mancanza di analoghi
sviluppi nella psicologia analitica, che porta a differenze sostanziali tra i modelli della
psicoterapia junghiana, in contrasto con altri approcci psicodinamici contemporanei.

utilainen 1*, Pentti Henttonen 2, Mikko Kahri 1, Niklas Ravaja 3, Mikko Sams 4 and
