findings regarding motivation reveal the biological substrate of motivations,
not their psychological structure” (p. 27). Neuroscience doesn’t discover an
appetitive drive or an attachment drive. Rather there is observed appetitive
or attachment like behaviour and neuroscience can describe what underlies
this behaviour on the level of the biology of the brain.

agree, and acknowledge that the biological level is not a crucial one; that

f attachment and appetitive drives.
But here lies the fallacy that we pointed to in our 2007 paper. It is only
when one takes what we referred to as a ‘biologistic’ stance and assumes
that the biological substrate of motivations reveals their true and basic
structure that one could conclude this. We explain:
Psychology attempts to construct theories of motivation by studying mani-
festations of motives and attempting to meaningfully organize them in terms
of psychological considerations and categories.

of psychological considerations and categories. People express a huge num-
ber of specific motives (e.g., to get home on time, to succeed in an exam, to
receive a hug, to go shopping) and many readily generalized ones (e.g., to
have a family, to earn money, to succeed at work, to be loved, to avoid criti-
cism). Psychological theories reveal and highlight less apparent psychological
connections between the more apparent motives.

chunks.id: Further evidence for the case against neuropsychoanalysis  How Yovell  Solms  and Fotopoulou s response to our critique confirms the irrelevance and h.pdf_122

connections between the more apparent motives. The motives to succeed on
an exam or to go shopping are not regarded as basic psychological motiva-
tions, which can, in and of themselves, well explain important aspects of
human behavior. In contrast, to survive, to be socially accepted, to be loved,
to be powerful, to gain mastery, to understand, to find meaning, as well as
to satisfy instinctual drives and to be attached are a few of the motives that
different psychological theories have, over the years, proposed as being more
basic.

different psychological theories have, over the years, proposed as being more

person’s behavior, experience and psychic functioning.

the category is the extent to which it enhances our meaningful understanding

tion. Moreover, it has chosen to consider the person insofar as he is shaped
by certain kinds of psychological motivations.

hosen to consider the person insofar as he is shaped
by certain kinds of psychological motivations. These are determined by the
specific insights into psychic functioning, behaviour and experience that psy-
choanalysis comes to from its specifically psychoanalytic perspective. This
means that psychoanalysis’ choice of its perspective, of how it understands
what psychoanalysis is all about, also plays a crucial role in determining the
motivations that it highlights (not the mere existence of a motivation and
definitely not its biological correlates).

definitely not its biological correlates). Freud has expressed this very clearly

Unintelligent opposition accuses us of one-sidedness in our estimate of the sexual
instincts. ‘Human beings have other interests besides sexual ones,’ they say. We have
not forgotten or denied this for a moment. Our one-sidedness is like that of the che-
mist, who traces all compounds back to the force of chemical attraction.

Mechanisms
Understanding how and why psychological treatments work is
important for a number of reasons. Firstly, although there is
evidence that psychotherapy is helpful for many people who
report psychological distress, there is considerable variation
between individuals in terms of the amount of change
experienced as a result of engaging with therapy ( 4).

measures or reduction or increases in identi ﬁed behaviors.
Indeed, for some clients, engaging with psychotherapy actually
seems to lead to negative outcomes such as a deterioration in
functioning ( 5).

CONCLUSION
We argue that, for psychotherapy to improve its effectiveness and
efﬁciency, the standard for what is accepted as a useful
mechanism needs to be raised substantially.

therapeutic interventions. The current state of the evidence
shows that the science has some distance to progress before
we can be certain of the functional mechanisms

Background: Repression is considered as a central defense mechanism in
psychodynamic theory. It refers to the process by which “unbearable” mental contents
(e.g., those related to internal conﬂicts) are kept out of consciousness. The process
of repression is probably closely related to concepts of emotion regulation derived
from a different theoretical background. This relationship is particularly relevant because
it relates repression to current research in the affective neurosciences as well as
to experimental studies on emotion regulation.

chunks.text:
t research in the affective neurosciences as well as
to experimental studies on emotion regulation. Due to its complex and highly
individual nature, repression has been notoriously difﬁcult to investigate. We investigated
repression with an individualized experiment in healthy subjects in order to establish
methods to study repression in clinical populations. To this end we operationalized
repression using individualized experimental conditions, and then studied potential
behavioral [memory and reaction time (RT)] and psychophysiological correlates [skin
conductance response (SCR)].

chunks.text:
emory and reaction time (RT)] and psychophysiological correlates [skin
conductance response (SCR)].
Method: Twenty-nine healthy female subjects were asked to freely associate to
individualized cue sentences. Sentences were generated from individual psychodynamic
interviews based on operationlized psychodynamic diagnosis (OPD), and were
comprised of three different types: positive, negative non-conﬂictual, and negative
conﬂict-related sentences. Subjects were asked to name the ﬁrst three associations
coming into their mind.

chunks.text:
-related sentences. Subjects were asked to name the ﬁrst three associations
coming into their mind. Afterward, the remaining time was used for free association.
SCR during each association trial and RT of the ﬁrst given association were recorded.
The memory for the ﬁrst three associations was subsequently tested in an unexpected
recall.
Results: Associations to conﬂict-related cue sentences were associated with longer
RTs and increased SCRs.

INTRODUCTION
Repression is a central concept of psychodynamic theories
on psychosomatic and neurotic symptoms.

chunks.text:
N
Repression is a central concept of psychodynamic theories
on psychosomatic and neurotic symptoms. It refers to the
mechanism by which mental contents that are related to internal
conﬂicts are made unconscious (Freud, 1957a; Person et al.,
2005; Wöller and Kruse, 2014). Repressed mental contents are
less accessible to conscious processing and still underlie dynamic
processes. They might, for instance, generate associated material
and intrude into awareness.

chunks.text:
namic
processes. They might, for instance, generate associated material
and intrude into awareness. In the case, that repressed material
gains access to consciousness, it elicits a secondary repression
excluding it once more from consciousness.
Throughout our lifetimes various internal conﬂicts arise, e.g.,
conﬂicts of self-value, or conﬂicts between the desire for autarchy
and the need for care.

e, e.g.,
conﬂicts of self-value, or conﬂicts between the desire for autarchy
and the need for care. Of course, not all of these conﬂicts
lead to pathological symptoms, but if the theme of such a
conﬂict is touched upon in a real-life situation, it induces a
plethora of reactions on the behavioral, cognitive, emotional, and
somatic levels (at the very least, physiological arousal).

reactions typically call for regulatory processes, ranging from
deliberate and conscious emotion regulation (e.g., reappraisal;
Gross, 2002), to less conscious defense mechanisms (e.g.,
repression; Brenner, 1982; Mentzos, 1984; Person et al., 2005).
Repression is considered a major defense mechanism and hence
an important concept guiding psychodynamic therapy (Person
et al., 2005).

fense mechanism and hence
an important concept guiding psychodynamic therapy (Person
et al., 2005). As one of the ﬁrst defense mechanisms postulated
by Sigmund Freud and Josef Breuer repression was initially
closely associated to “hysteria, ” where symptoms (e.g., paralysis
or involuntary seizure-like motor symptoms) were interpreted as
a bodily converted form of oedipal unwanted feelings, thoughts
or desires (Freud, 1955).

rpreted as
a bodily converted form of oedipal unwanted feelings, thoughts
or desires (Freud, 1955). This conceptualization of repression
was later modiﬁed and extended by Freud, when he deﬁned
it as the process “of rejecting and keeping something out of
consciousness” (Freud, 1957a). Accordingly, it was also attributed
to other psychopathologies such as phobias and obsessive
neuroses.

ordingly, it was also attributed
to other psychopathologies such as phobias and obsessive

from other defense mechanisms (Freud, 1992) such as, for
example, aﬀect isolation (i.e., a subject does not experience
the aﬀective valence of a thought or a memory), displacement
(i.e., a subject relocates an important issue, e.g., anger about
someone, toward another person) or splitting (i.e., a subject
fails to integrate two, perhaps contradicting, sides of a person).
In general, the assessment of defense mechanisms is a central

In general, the assessment of defense mechanisms is a central
part of psychodynamic diagnosis, where they are additionally
evaluated with regards to their ﬂexibility and the ensuing costs
of reality check. In our study, we deﬁne repression technically
as a defense mechanism and thematically broadly in the original
sense of “rejecting and keeping something out of consciousness”
(Freud, 1957a). It is hence associated with a reduced memory for
unpleasant or forbidden thoughts, aﬀects and wishes.

Historically, the scientiﬁc study of repression in a clinical
context started with Jung’s (1918) experiments.

chunks.text:
ly, the scientiﬁc study of repression in a clinical
context started with Jung’s (1918) experiments. Jung assumed
that the physiological arousal and hesitation that accompanied
subjects’ free association to certain cue words indicated that
those words were related to internal conﬂicts, and that the
contents triggered by those words were automatically repressed.
His ﬁndings are consistent with recent studies of repression
and internal conﬂicts, which have been found to be associated
with autonomic arousal (Person et al., 2005).

chunks.text:
rnal conﬂicts, which have been found to be associated
with autonomic arousal (Person et al., 2005). Also in this
vein, Levinger and Clark (1961), Rossmann (1984), and Köhler
and Wilke (1999) found impaired declarative memory for free
associations that were accompanied by high levels of autonomic
arousal.
The central idea in these studies is that the technique
of free association reduces censorship (Freud, 1957b), which
allows previously repressed memory contents, besides their above
mentioned dynamic properties, to intrude into consciousness,

mentioned dynamic properties, to intrude into consciousness,
i.e., to “emerge.” These memories then lead to increased
autonomic arousal and the secondary repression of those
contents (i.e., the repressed memory contents and their
associations), which become less accessible for subsequent recall.
Indeed, Köhler and Wilke (1999) noted that a limitation of
these studies was that eﬀects were only analyzed on a group
level, which excludes ideas about the subjective impact of the
repressed material.

level, which excludes ideas about the subjective impact of the
repressed material. The authors addressed this issue in their
work by analyzing intraindividual associations among the three
dependent variables. However, another approach, which we
wanted to address with this study, was to investigate subjectively
meaningful and individually tailored material for each of the
subjects.
Expanding on these early ﬁndings, we investigated the
behavioral, physiological, and neural correlates of free
associations to cue words and to conﬂict-related cue sentences

in two functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies
(Schmeing et al., 2013). In both studies, high autonomic arousal
[measured via increased skin conductance responses (SCRs)]
and delayed responses [longer reaction times (RTs)] during
free association predicted forgetting of these associations
in a subsequent recall task, conﬁrming previous ﬁndings.
Interestingly, associations to conﬂict-related sentences were
accompanied by increased activation of the anterior cingulate

an individualized experimental paradigm. Twenty-nine healthy
female subjects were interviewed by an expert clinician according
to the system of operationalized psychodynamic diagnosis (OPD;
OPD-Task-Force, 2008) yielding personally relevant life events
and individual conﬂict themes. This complex material was then
used to derive stimulus sentences to be presented in the MRI
scanner.

DISCUSSION
In our study, N= 29 healthy female subjects were meticulously
interviewed according to the OPD (OPD-Task-Force, 2008)
criteria, in order to extract positive, negative and conﬂict-
related life events, which were used to create individualized cue

chunks.text:
t positive, negative and conﬂict-
related life events, which were used to create individualized cue
sentences. Conﬂict-related life events were related to a typical
psychodynamic conﬂict, i.e., individual “sore-spots.” While freely
associating to conﬂict-related sentences, subjects had longer RTs,
higher SC responses and impaired memory for the associations
produced in an unexpected subsequent recall when compared
with positive and negative sentences.

Our work expands upon a line of studies starting with

Our work expands upon a line of studies starting with
C. G. Jung’s early experiments on free associations to cue
words (Jung, 1918), which were later replicated by other teams
(Levinger and Clark, 1961; Rossmann, 1984; Köhler and Wilke,
1999), as well as in our own previous works (Kehyayan et al.,
2013; Schmeing et al., 2013). The study presented here further
developed this paradigm by using individualized stimuli derived
from an OPD interview.

chunks.id: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf_106
chunks.source: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf
chunks.text:
here further
developed this paradigm by using individualized stimuli derived
from an OPD interview. Overall, generating individualized
stimuli was very time-consuming and closely matched to a
clinical context. The reason for this eﬀort lay in the overarching
goal of our venture: we attempted to operationalize a clinically
meaningful concept – repression as a major defense mechanism
according to psychodynamic theory – under experimental
conditions with healthy subjects, in order to make it assessable
in clinical populations in the future.

chunks.id: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf_107
chunks.source: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf
chunks.text:
itions with healthy subjects, in order to make it assessable
in clinical populations in the future. Psychosomatic or neurotic
patients, whose disorders could be connected to psychodynamic
conﬂicts, may beneﬁt from the detection of such conﬂicts via an
experimental procedure similar to the one applied in this study.
The derivation of individualized stimuli from a psychodynamic
clinical interview was seen as a necessary intermediate step to the
eventual realization of this goal, and therefore worth the added
eﬀort.
As in previous studies (Kehyayan et al., 2013; Schmeing

chunks.text:
goal, and therefore worth the added
eﬀort.
As in previous studies (Kehyayan et al., 2013; Schmeing
et al., 2013), prolonged RTs and higher SCR were considered

to be indirect markers of the ongoing resistance and autonomic
arousal that is elicited by conﬂict-related stimuli, which lead to
repression.

chunks.id: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf_109
chunks.source: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf
chunks.text:
stance and autonomic
arousal that is elicited by conﬂict-related stimuli, which lead to
repression. Our observations in the present study are consistent
with our previous ﬁndings that used standardized conﬂict-related
sentences. Thus, the present study expands upon these ﬁndings
by showing the same eﬀects when using individually tailored
stimuli, which arguably target an individual’s conﬂict themes
more speciﬁcally.
Previous research on behavioral responses to highly arousing
negative and positive stimuli has been heterogeneous.

chunks.id: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf_110
chunks.source: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf
chunks.text:
ch on behavioral responses to highly arousing
negative and positive stimuli has been heterogeneous. While
some studies show that arousal facilitates stimulus processing
irrespective of valence (Schacht and Sommer, 2009), others
suggest that emotionally negative (Zinchenko et al., 2015) or
positive (Herbert et al., 2009) stimuli are processed preferentially.
Unexpectedly, we also obsereved increased SC responses for
positive as compared to negative sentences (see Figure 2).

chunks.id: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf_111
chunks.source: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf
chunks.text:
lso obsereved increased SC responses for
positive as compared to negative sentences (see Figure 2). While
we do not have a clear explanation for this eﬀect, it may
be (in line with the above mentioned heterogenous ﬁndings)
due to the high perceived salience of the positive events, even
though these events evoked smaller SC respones than the
conﬂict-related experiences. Besides this, we introduce a further
dimension of pivotal ecological relevance: the relatedness of
negative stimuli to autobiographical conﬂicts.

chunks.id: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf_112
chunks.source: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf
chunks.text:
of pivotal ecological relevance: the relatedness of
negative stimuli to autobiographical conﬂicts. The results of the
present study suggest that particularly ego-threatening and self-
relevant stimuli (for example, those that elicit shame or guilt) are
accompanied by longer RTs, which is consistent with previous
studies on the RT eﬀects of psychodynamic conﬂicts (Shevrin,
1990).
Importantly, subjective ratings of emotional valence and
arousal did not diﬀer between conﬂict-related and negative
sentences.

chunks.id: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf_113
chunks.source: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf
chunks.text:
ings of emotional valence and
arousal did not diﬀer between conﬂict-related and negative
sentences. This may indicate that the diﬀerences in autonomic
arousal (and RTs) were not paralleled by diﬀerences in conscious
processing of valence and/or arousal, but might rather be
considered correlates of unconscious or preconscious processing
of valence and arousal. In this vein, we investigated two
other possible confounds, the vividness and recollection of
sentences.

chunks.id: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf_114
chunks.source: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf
chunks.text:
is vein, we investigated two
other possible confounds, the vividness and recollection of
sentences. Although positive sentences were rated to be more
vivid, there was no diﬀerence in vividness between negative
and conﬂict-related sentences. The diﬀerences in memory
performance between negative and conﬂict-related sentences
can thus not simply be explained by vividness.

chunks.id: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf_115
chunks.source: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf
chunks.text:
mance between negative and conﬂict-related sentences
can thus not simply be explained by vividness. Interestingly,
positive and conﬂict-related sentences were equally frequently
recollected since the interview, but conﬂict-related sentences
were still remembered worse in the recall experimental session.
Hence, diﬀerences in experimental (i.e., relative short-term)
memory performance might not be attributed to mere eﬀects of
remembering sentences per se over time.
We found no association between experimental eﬀects and
results from personality questionnaires, especially not for a

chunks.id: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf_116
chunks.source: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf
chunks.text:
ation between experimental eﬀects and
results from personality questionnaires, especially not for a
measure of repressive coping style. Again, this appears to indicate
that the conscious self-appraisal of being more or less vigilant
toward unpleasant stimuli, or of suppressing thoughts about
unpleasant stimuli, does not correlate with the concept of
repression, as it is operationalized in, e.g., Jung’s (1918) early
experiments or in recent clinical concepts (Person et al., 2005).
Concerning the limitations of this study, the main issue

chunks.id: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf_117
chunks.source: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf
chunks.text:
t clinical concepts (Person et al., 2005).
Concerning the limitations of this study, the main issue
is expressed in the antagonism between a naturalistic versus
laboratory perspective: is the design naturalistic enough? Is
it possible to capture complex psychodynamic processes like
the reaction to conﬂict-related material and the defense
mechanism of repression with any experimental (i.e., controlled)
design?
On the other hand, is the design controlled enough? Subjects’
associations, and their respective memory performances, are not
under the experimenter’s control.

chunks.id: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf_118
chunks.source: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf
chunks.text:
’
associations, and their respective memory performances, are not
under the experimenter’s control. The associations themselves
are – naturally – highly variable, and hence pose diﬃculties for
the experimental design and analytic approach.
Furthermore, as mentioned in the introduction, other studies
on repression also considered the return of the repressed
by showing that neurological patients with anosognosia can
overcome their unawareness of the paralysis (Ramachandran,
1995; Nardone et al., 2008; Turnbull et al., 2014).

chunks.id: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf_119
chunks.source: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf
chunks.text:
eir unawareness of the paralysis (Ramachandran,
1995; Nardone et al., 2008; Turnbull et al., 2014). In these
studies, anosognosia was not interpreted as a mere cognitive
deﬁcit in attention, but rather as resulting from defense
against unbearably painful aﬀects associated with paralysis.
Psychodynamic interventions based on this reconceptualization
of anosognosia were able to relieve symptoms in several
patients (Kaplan-Solms and Solms, 2000), and there was some
evidence that patients were implicitly aware of their deﬁcits
(Fotopoulou et al., 2010).

chunks.id: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf_120
chunks.source: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf
chunks.text:
e was some
evidence that patients were implicitly aware of their deﬁcits
(Fotopoulou et al., 2010). Moreover, anosognosia has been
conceptually linked to impairments of a brain system for emotion
regulation (Turnbull et al., 2014), inducing regression to the more
premature, and dysfunctional, process of repression.
According to the cognitive approach to repression,
“suppression” (Anderson and Green, 2001), a comparative
study is needed for a more diﬀerentiated conceptualization
of repression.

chunks.id: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf_121
chunks.source: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf
chunks.text:
een, 2001), a comparative
study is needed for a more diﬀerentiated conceptualization
of repression. Here, the diﬀerences (e.g., return of the target
material) and similarities (e.g., form of emotion regulation via
memory control) of these two mechanisms warrant further
analysis to improve our understanding of these forms of
emotion- and self-regulation. Additionally, as diﬀerent sorts of
defense mechanisms tend to overlap, further research is needed
to compare our operationalization of repression to other closely
related defense mechanisms like denial.

chunks.id: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf_122
chunks.source: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf
chunks.text:
mpare our operationalization of repression to other closely
related defense mechanisms like denial. Importantly, in our
OPD assessment, we focused on neurotic conﬂicts rather than
structural deﬁcits (i.e., those related to narcissistic or borderline
states) because we were primarily interested in repression rather
than dissociative phenomena. We cannot exclude, though, that
some of the subjects we included also suﬀered from structural
deﬁcits, even though we screened them for current psychiatric
diseases.

chunks.id: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf_123
chunks.source: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf
chunks.text:
lso suﬀered from structural
deﬁcits, even though we screened them for current psychiatric
diseases. We believe that future studies directly comparing
repression and dissociative phenomena will be important.
Finally, it should be noted that our indirect markers for
resistance and repression can by no means be considered
exclusive indicators of such complex processes. In this study
we focused on resistance and an involuntarily induced memory
inhibition induced by individualized conﬂict-related material
for a working deﬁnition of repression.

chunks.source: Investigating behavioral and psychophysiological reactions to conflict-related and individualized stimuli as potential correlates of repression.pdf
chunks.text:
nhibition induced by individualized conﬂict-related material
for a working deﬁnition of repression. In future studies,
the inclusion of more physiological and neurophysiological
measures (i.e., heart rate, electromyography, EEG), which are
not inﬂuenced by conscious processes, could strengthen the
idea that we actually capture unconscious or preconscious
processes.

idea that we actually capture unconscious or preconscious
processes. These ﬁndings should also be independently replicated
and investigated in a clinical population, which, if successful,

the Analytic Relationship . Hove, East Sussex; New York: Routledge, 2014.
Pp. 213. Pbk. £25.32 / $45.95
This book provides us with 12 complex, nuanced accounts of struggles at once
highly personal and involving all who work in this ﬁeld. It is a collection of
ﬁrst-person accounts by psychoanalytically-oriented clinicians who write of
their experiences with traumatic ruptures in analytic relationships and the
ripplings outward of these in analytic institutions; I cannot recall anything like

ionships and the
ripplings outward of these in analytic institutions; I cannot recall anything like
it in its directness. The death of an analyst, the loss of an analyst after the
analyst’s boundary violation of another patient, the loss of a patient to suicide
—the authors speak into the silences that surround these and other traumatic
ruptures in analytic relationships. Many of the papers centre on the experience
of candidates in training, by authors re ﬂecting back on their early-career
experiences.

of candidates in training, by authors re ﬂecting back on their early-career
experiences. I felt appreciation and —at times —awe for the authors ’ efforts to
engage with and think about these deeply painful experiences.
Traumatic Ruptures is part of the Relational Perspectives Book Series, a series
which originated under Stephen A. Mitchell ’s editorial overseeing and is now
under the editorial supervision of Lewis Aron and Adrienne Harris. The
authors in this volume are largely from North America.

Psychoanalysis.
The book is divided into four parts, each taking up a different aspect of
rupture. Part 1, ‘Ruptured Subjectivity, Lost and Found ’, includes two papers.
In the ﬁrst, Adrienne Harris explores the question ‘What kind of analyst am I
now?’ when her identity as an analyst is ruptured after her husband ’s sudden
death and where ‘the central instrument of … her work is deeply charged with

The Red Book reﬂects Jung ’s midlife crisis, which —at a personal level —has
been associated with his rupture with Freud and a probable psychotic
breakdown, and —at a collective level —with the prelude to World War I.
However, as Thomas Kirsch ( 2014) states in his Introduction to The Red
Book: Re ﬂections on C.G. Jung ’s Liber Novus ,ad e ﬁnitive interpretation of it
may never be possible.

chunks.text:
: Re ﬂections on C.G. Jung ’s Liber Novus ,ad e ﬁnitive interpretation of it
may never be possible. I believe that the complexity of Jung ’s process of
individuation and his extraordinary, almost mediumistic, powers of intuition
make conclusions dif ﬁcult. With such a rich symbolic content, it is inevitable
that The Red Book will inspire different interpretations of the inner life of the
author, his individuation process and the rediscovery of his soul.
In clinical practice, when we attempt to understand the individuation process

chunks.text:
iscovery of his soul.
In clinical practice, when we attempt to understand the individuation process
as expressed in dreams, fantasies or active imaginations, we link these to
signiﬁcant people, events or contexts in a life story as well as to archetypal
patterns that express human nature and psychological development. As The
Red Book reﬂects Jung ’s individuation process, it is natural and enriching to
ﬁnd connections with his personal life, historical context and people who
inﬂuenced him, be they intellectual references, relatives, close friends or
colleagues.

people who
inﬂuenced him, be they intellectual references, relatives, close friends or
colleagues. Insofar as it re ﬂects Jung ’s theory of individuation, the content of
The Red Book is a symbolic representation of his own individuation process.
By this I mean that we can read in it Jung ’s psychological dynamics, con ﬂicts
and needs.
Murray Stein ( 2012) states that ‘The Red Book can be, and is read, from the
perspectives of three different contexts: the personal and biographical one, the

consider the context of Jung ’s personal life at the time he began The Red

ause it grounds the work in the author ’s deep existential engagement with
himself and his world ’. The focus of Guerra ’s book deepens this perspective,
highlighting Jung ’s relationship to Toni Wolff and his wife Emma.
Some will ﬁnd Guerra ’s courageous exploration of Jung ’s personal love
drama highly provocative. Her research included detailed reports by Sonu
Shamdasani, Barbara Hannah and Deirdre Bair, as well as Jung ’s own
writings in Memories, Dreams, Re ﬂections and other works.

chunks.id: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf_33
chunks.source: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf
chunks.text:
and Deirdre Bair, as well as Jung ’s own
writings in Memories, Dreams, Re ﬂections and other works. As Carlos
Byington, Guerra ’s husband, writes in his introduction, she discovered in this
material an Ariadne ’s thread ‘that gives an absolute personal storyline, the
light and the shadow, charged with seeking, suffering, guilt and self-
realization, that could link the content of The Red Book as a whole to an
individual myth, to Jung ’s process of individuation, to existential details that
really characterize life as it is ’.

chunks.text:
Jung ’s process of individuation, to existential details that
really characterize life as it is ’.
Authors including Susan Rowland and Deirdre Bair have described the role
played by Toni Wolff in Jung ’s life. Guerra emphasizes Wolff ’s role in Jung ’s
search for his lost soul, which she connects with the search for real love. The
importance of Wolff and Sabina Spielrein in Jung ’s search for love is
undeniable, and this book is seminal for understanding the role of Eros in
Jung’s individuation process.
The book is divided into ﬁve sections in which the author concentrates on

chunks.text:
’s individuation process.
The book is divided into ﬁve sections in which the author concentrates on
Jung’s visions, dreams and inner experiences as they appear in The Red Book .
She interprets these in the light of his relationship with Toni Wolff and his
struggle to stay with his family and wife Emma, his search for love and ﬁnally
his encounter with love.
After a brief introduction to The Red Book , in the second section Guerra
deepens the study of Jung ’s marriage and affair with Sabina Spielrein to
conclude that ‘I therefore consider the essence of The Red Book to be the result

chunks.text:
abina Spielrein to
conclude that ‘I therefore consider the essence of The Red Book to be the result
of Jung ’s simultaneous relationships with Toni Wolff and Emma Jung, and of
the feelings and emotions arising from it. My aim is to bring to light this
essence by studying in detail the content of Jung ’s formidable book ’ (p. 26).
Continuing her analysis of Liber Primus and
Liber Secundus , she maintains
that the awakening of the spirit of the depths with Jung ’s yearning for the soul,
as it appears in the ﬁgures of anima, is the backbone of The Red Book and

chunks.id: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf_37

chunks.text:
’s yearning for the soul,
as it appears in the ﬁgures of anima, is the backbone of The Red Book and
must be associated with the woman who touched Jung ’s soul deeply, Toni
Wolff. Guerra notes that following his anima was not without crisis and that
many of the visions and dreams in Liber Primus and Liber Secundus refer to
this con ﬂict. She shows how Jung got in touch with his feelings, his dilemma,
and ﬁnally by the end of Liber Secundus how he reached a transformation of
his experience of love when Salome ’s blindness is healed.

chunks.source: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf
chunks.text:
undus how he reached a transformation of
his experience of love when Salome ’s blindness is healed. At the end of the
section on Liber Secundus, Guerra states that, because Jung allowed himself to
live his drama deeply, he was able to overcome his desire for pleasure and the
power of seduction and to develop his capacity to love.

In a brief conclusion, Guerra recalls an interview with the Chilean writer
Miguel Serrano in 1959 in which Jung speaks about the importance of love
in the life of a man. She also reminds the reader that ‘Jung wrote what he
lived and, in this sense, knew what he said.

chunks.id: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf_40
chunks.source: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf
chunks.text:
. She also reminds the reader that ‘Jung wrote what he
lived and, in this sense, knew what he said. Perhaps for this reason his
theory is spreading increasingly throughout the world, each one of us feeling
and intuiting the deep truth of the ordeals of someone who experienced
them’ (p. 103); I think this was Guerra ’s aim in writing the book.
Guerra describes an affectionate, even passionate, personality, who was
acclaimed for his brilliant thinking and intuition but who followed the
archetype of the anima and whose individuation process was guided
essentially by his feeling function.

chunks.id: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf_41
chunks.source: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf
chunks.text:
hetype of the anima and whose individuation process was guided
essentially by his feeling function. Is this dif ﬁcult or even impossible to admit?
The future will decide. We cannot deny the fact that love is always a very
important healing factor. Jung began The Red Book with a wound that needed
to be healed: he had lost his soul, he was depressed and empty, and he was
looking for a new way.

chunks.id: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf_42
chunks.source: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf
chunks.text:
d
to be healed: he had lost his soul, he was depressed and empty, and he was
looking for a new way. The picture of love and its transformation given in
Guerra’s book introduces the dimension of human love in the comprehension
of Jung’s individuation process.
Jung had a very strong internal experience of love during his confrontation
with the unconscious, and this is very clearly revealed in The Love Drama of
C.G. Jung . He had the courage to live his individuation process, confronting
tradition with love and even adultery through following his heart.

chunks.id: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf_43
chunks.source: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf
chunks.text:
dividuation process, confronting
tradition with love and even adultery through following his heart. His wife
Emma had the courage and alterity to understand this. Barbara Hannah
(1997)i n Jung: His Life and Work says that Emma told him, ‘You see, he
never took anything from me to give to Toni, but the more he gave her the
more he seemed able to give me ’ (p. 119).
I think that it is possible to delineate other Adriane ’s threads in The Red Book
that refer to Jung ’s personal life or to the more impersonal archetypal domain,
and I look forward to reading about them.

chunks.id: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf_44
chunks.source: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf
chunks.text:
ersonal life or to the more impersonal archetypal domain,
and I look forward to reading about them. But, whether or not the reader agrees
with the interpretation presented in Guerra ’s book, what should be
acknowledged is the erudition, admiration and affectionate consideration for
Jung with which she undertook her research.

Junkers, shines a light on the uncomfortable
topic of ageing and the ending of an analyst ’s life. Exploring the subject from a
number of perspectives, so metimes with a laser focus and sometimes with a
broader, more encompassing view, the authors in this collection of essays create a
comprehensive picture of the personal and institutional challenges that are being
initiated by our ageing population and changing social conditions.
The empty couch, which was chosen to symbolize our analytic work, evokes
an immediate personal, emotional response and directs our attention to the

chunks.id: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf_48

chunks.text:
ur analytic work, evokes
an immediate personal, emotional response and directs our attention to the
possibility of an emptiness in our future lives, a time when the intensity of our
analytic practice and the opportunity it provides to immerse ourselves in the
mysteries of another person ’s psyche is no longer available. What substitutes
will we ﬁnd to replace it? Who will we be then and what will we call ourselves?
I’m personally aware that the Empty Couch is fast becoming more of a reality
among my colleagues and, as an ageing analyst, it creates an uncomfortable

chunks.id: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf_49

chunks.text:
coming more of a reality
among my colleagues and, as an ageing analyst, it creates an uncomfortable
nudge that the same situation is in my near future. My reluctance to confront
this possibility was revealed in the approach-avoidance dynamic that I
experienced in reading the book. At the same time, I noticed a sense of relief
that the topic was being addressed, because even though the subject of ageing
is gaining momentum in the collective, in my experience there is little
discussion of these issues in analytic circles.

in the collective, in my experience there is little
discussion of these issues in analytic circles. The paucity of articles pertaining
to retirement, possible illness or death of analysts is also striking.

between Guiseppe Civitarese and Antonio Ferro about couches, and the

Whether it is to burnout, ageing or illness, analysts gradually, through their
professional lives, begin to lighten the weight of the couch.

ss, analysts gradually, through their
professional lives, begin to lighten the weight of the couch. As ageing and
losses begin to shake up the steadiness of one ’s personal and professional
identity, the actuality of the empty couch begins to emerge, often with
some accompanying anxiety. The emotional investment, as well as the time
and energy, given to ﬁlling the couch makes it dif ﬁcult to imagine a time
when it is truly empty.

chunks.id: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf_52
chunks.source: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf
chunks.text:
and energy, given to ﬁlling the couch makes it dif ﬁcult to imagine a time
when it is truly empty. But there is no escaping this eventual reality, and
the growing awareness of nothingness and death requires an active
recognition of our own ﬁnitude.
The essays in Part 1 focus on an array of topics that deal with the tasks
implicit in facing this reality. Several authors emphasize the need for
institutions to rethink the role that elderly analysts can and should ful ﬁl in the
last period of their lives.

chunks.id: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf_53
chunks.source: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf
chunks.text:
to rethink the role that elderly analysts can and should ful ﬁl in the
last period of their lives. For example, the focus of an older person often
turns from ‘having and producing ’ to the importance of the values related to
‘being’ and one of the more important roles an older person may play is in
imparting the richness of these values to younger people. Elderly analysts also

have rich psychoanalytic experiences that may be shared with younger
colleagues through teaching, supervision and writing.
But it is also vital for ageing analysts to recognize and be aware when a
diminishment of capabilities and functions occur.

chunks.id: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf_55
chunks.source: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf
chunks.text:
ageing analysts to recognize and be aware when a
diminishment of capabilities and functions occur. Many of the authors point
to the dif ﬁculties that can arise and the harm that may be done to patients if
this is avoided. Role reversals and care-taking by the patient; re-traumatization
and lingering pain caused by the disruption of analysis; an altered capacity for
critical self-re ﬂection and containment; impaired understanding and memory
on the part of the analyst are a few examples.

chunks.id: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf_56
chunks.source: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf
chunks.text:
n and containment; impaired understanding and memory
on the part of the analyst are a few examples. These potential dif ﬁculties raise
questions for the ageing analyst regarding his responsibility about undertaking
a long-term analysis. When does one say no? Or when is it time for a Society
or training institute to step in if an analyst refuses to relinquish his role or does
not realize he is no longer able to work? Unfortunately, there is often a
collusion of not acknowledging the disturbing symptoms, tolerating the
situation and deciding to ‘wait it out ’ in order to protect a colleague,

chunks.id: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf_57
chunks.source: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf
chunks.text:
symptoms, tolerating the
situation and deciding to ‘wait it out ’ in order to protect a colleague,
abandoning a situation that is damaging to both the individual and his
patients and trainees.
Essays addressing questions of how we apply our analytic capacity to our
very own ageing issues, namely our own concrete transience, were
particularly thought provoking. Successful ageing requires a growing
acceptance of temporal time, a recognition of the historical dimension of
one’s life and a relinquishment of omnipotent thinking.

chunks.id: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf_58
chunks.source: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf
chunks.text:
recognition of the historical dimension of
one’s life and a relinquishment of omnipotent thinking. But there are speci ﬁc
conditions that exist in analytic work that may make this acceptance of
temporal time particularly dif ﬁcult. One is the timeless perspective in which
analysis takes place, a world in which linear time is suspended. Analysts may
also hold an unconscious idea that their own analysis confers a kind of
immunity to the problems that affect others.

chunks.id: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf_59
chunks.source: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf
chunks.text:
nscious idea that their own analysis confers a kind of
immunity to the problems that affect others. Believing that their own analysis
has also given them the tools to undertake an ongoing self-analysis, some
analysts may be surprised to discover that, when the end is in view, old
problems, anxieties and defense mechanisms are once again in the forefront.
Becoming an analyst also requires huge investments.

chunks.id: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf_60
chunks.source: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf
chunks.text:
nse mechanisms are once again in the forefront.
Becoming an analyst also requires huge investments. Whether the choice to
become an analyst stemmed from one ’s narcissism, a real passion for the
emotional and intellectual work, omnipotent needs or idealization of the
analytic situation, that investment may leave little room for recognition of
one’s limitations and failing analytic abilities.

chunks.id: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf_61
chunks.source: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf
chunks.text:
vestment may leave little room for recognition of
one’s limitations and failing analytic abilities. And if the analytic identity has
served to prop up a fragile personal identity, retirement can indeed be
experienced as a painful loss, reviving feelings of exclusion, aloneness, and the
need to be liked, loved and admired. But if a person has succeeded in
developing a solid sense of personal identity and a ‘psychic home ’, they may
be more successful in actively shaping the withdrawal and ending that is
demanded by the ageing process.

chunks.id: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf_62
chunks.source: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf
chunks.text:
re successful in actively shaping the withdrawal and ending that is
demanded by the ageing process. Gabriele Junkers, in her essay entitled
‘Later, Perhaps’ sums up the challenge and needed response of acknowledging
one’s own transience in this way, ‘To enable us to live with the knowledge of
our own ﬁnitude, we need defence and acknowledgement in equal measure …

we must continue to plunge into the river of life, while also contemplating the
end’ (p 24).
The focus of essays in Part II of the book are related to illness in the analyst:
how it in ﬂuences the ability to practise analysis; the psychological processes

chunks.id: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf_64
chunks.source: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf
chunks.text:
ess in the analyst:
how it in ﬂuences the ability to practise analysis; the psychological processes
that a severe illness can set in motion; how a foreseeable end is best dealt
with; and how abandoned patients may be helped.
Authors reveal opposing attitudes toward questions regarding the analyst ’s
revelation of illness to their patients. Analysts taking the position of
informing patients about an illness are especially attuned to unconscious
communication between patient and analyst, and believe that many patients,
regardless of diagnostic category, perceive subtle changes in the analyst ’s

chunks.id: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf_65
chunks.source: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf
chunks.text:
ve that many patients,
regardless of diagnostic category, perceive subtle changes in the analyst ’s
bodily and emotional states. They believe a factual disclosure to patients can
be used in the service of the analytic practice. Others recommend abstention,
suggesting that continuing analytic work under such circumstances allows
patients the opportunity to unfold their fantasies and eliminates the potential
situation of patients feeling that they have to care for the analyst.
Three essays in this part of the book provide illuminating personal accounts

chunks.id: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf_66
chunks.source: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf
chunks.text:
care for the analyst.
Three essays in this part of the book provide illuminating personal accounts
of the impact of an analyst ’s illness on his/her patients. One analyst writes about
dealing with a severe illness and her own observations of its impact on her
patients. Another essay provides a distressing picture of a training candidate ’s
experience with an analyst whose declining health left lasting regrets and
distress that affected her own professional activity. The third essay explores
the re-traumatization and suffering that occurred after one person suffered the
death of two analysts.

chunks.id: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf_67
chunks.source: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf
chunks.text:
re-traumatization and suffering that occurred after one person suffered the
death of two analysts. These personal stories serve to heighten awareness of
how important it is for analysts to thoroughly analyze their fears of illness
and death in order to be able to come to terms with them realistically in their
relationships with patients.
Chapters in Part III highlight the need for the institution to come to terms with
its own ‘ageing’.

chunks.id: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf_68
chunks.source: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf
chunks.text:
Chapters in Part III highlight the need for the institution to come to terms with
its own ‘ageing’. Changing demographic situations, such as the increase of older
members, as well as older training candidates, and an increased life expectancy,
are forcing a need for ethical, administrative and structural changes. Suggestions
about how to meet some of these institutional challenges are offered and
debated, such as imposing age limits on future trainees; providing other
options in the institutions or societies for ageing analysts to keep up their

chunks.id: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf_69
chunks.source: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf
chunks.text:
nees; providing other
options in the institutions or societies for ageing analysts to keep up their
professional identity without working directly with patients; providing
external oversight for retirement; and creating an Assistance Committee to
identify and provide assistance to analysts who may be functioning at an
impaired level due to illness. Another way that individuals and professional
organizations can take responsibility for patient care and con ﬁdentiality in the
event of an analyst ’s death is to prepare a Professional Will.

chunks.id: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf_70
chunks.source: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf
chunks.text:
ent care and con ﬁdentiality in the
event of an analyst ’s death is to prepare a Professional Will. A model of such a
will is provided.
This book makes an important contribution to the literature on the topic of
the ageing and retiring analyst. The provocative questions and thoughtful
discussions presented by the authors offer insights about our fears and denial

Considering how many times the spirit Mercurius is mentioned in Jung ’s
writings and how large an importance Jung clearly attaches to this ﬁgure, not
the least in writings after 1928, it is remarkable how little the ﬁgure actually
appears in secondary literature. Apart from individual chapters from loyal
colleagues such as Emma Jung and Marie-Louise von Franz, Mercurius is as
good as gone.

chunks.id: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf_75

chunks.text:
s from loyal
colleagues such as Emma Jung and Marie-Louise von Franz, Mercurius is as
good as gone. This is remarkably contrary to ﬁgures such as Christ or
Hermes, and contrary to the status of a psychological-mythological ﬁgure
such as Philemon who has entered the Jungian world in recent years.
Mather’s book therefore opens a forgotten area of Jung ’s writings, and brings
it forth in modern, intellectual-academic research.

forgotten area of Jung ’s writings, and brings
it forth in modern, intellectual-academic research. As such, the book is more
than welcome.
One could choose to address the topic of Mercurius in the currently revived
research into esoteric traditions in Western history, as rejected knowledge in
the history of philosophy, and in the history of ideas and sciences, or as
hermetic philosophy.

chunks.id: J Analytical Psychology - 2015 - Wilkinson - Memory and Healing  Neurocognitive and Psychodynamic Perspectives on how.pdf_77

in
the history of philosophy, and in the history of ideas and sciences, or as

and the theory and practice of rituals such as the kabbala and gnosis are
constantly undergoing serious and profound reinterpretations. From a
different perspective, one could choose to analyse the Mercurius ﬁgure in

On the argument for (and against) neuropsychoanalysis
Dear Editor,
I read with interest the recent contributions of Yovell, Solms and Fotopou-
lou (2015) and the response of Blass and Carmeli (2015). Blass and Carmeli
are particularly critical of the clinical material pointing out the supportive
nature of the intervention.

chunks.id: On the argument for  and against  neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_2
chunks.source: On the argument for  and against  neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
ticularly critical of the clinical material pointing out the supportive
nature of the intervention. They also argue that the familiar psychological
finding regarding the fallibility of memory relegates the neuroscientific
research to no more than a biological correlate of what is common knowl-
edge amongst psychoanalysts. Blass and Carmeli (2007) previously observed
that the importance of focusing on recollecting facts of past events in treat-
ment was a ‘debated issue’ with the trend in contemporary practice support-
ing a more limited role for such approaches.

chunks.id: On the argument for  and against  neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_3
chunks.source: On the argument for  and against  neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
ssue’ with the trend in contemporary practice support-
ing a more limited role for such approaches. I offer a brief vignette
illustrating the use of neuro-scientific research on traumatic memory during
the course of a four time per week analysis. I argue that such research can
be relevant and helpful, though, in ways that are neither categorical nor
predictable.
Many years ago as a candidate I struggled in my work with an adult ana-
lysand whose belief her mother had sexually abused her in certain ways as a
young child allowed her to feel integrated as ‘victim’.

chunks.id: On the argument for  and against  neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_4
chunks.source: On the argument for  and against  neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
ad sexually abused her in certain ways as a
young child allowed her to feel integrated as ‘victim’. The focus in supervi-
sion was on working with her ‘psychic reality’ – the analysand’s experience
reflecting some admixture of fantasy and historical reality. In the transfer-
ence, the experience of victimization was enacted when attempting to
explore her reality as over-determined by internal and external factors.
Attempts to explore what she believed happened left her feeling criticized
and attacked as she had been in childhood – my efforts were equated with

chunks.id: On the argument for  and against  neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_5
chunks.source: On the argument for  and against  neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
eft her feeling criticized
and attacked as she had been in childhood – my efforts were equated with
either my disbelief or thinking she was ‘stupid’ as her father had called her.
At the time, I was reading about the neuro-scientific research on memory
and trauma (specifically hippocampal damage due to early trauma impacted
declarative memory systems). It served an unintended supervisory function
in helping me see that the clinical surface demanded an exploration of how
she remembered (with conviction) rather than what she remembered.

chunks.id: On the argument for  and against  neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_6
chunks.source: On the argument for  and against  neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
ce demanded an exploration of how
she remembered (with conviction) rather than what she remembered. It
helped me see that I had unconsciously become the container for an uncer-
tainty she had split off. The research (which raised questions about what
could be explicitly remembered from childhood abuse) helped me formulate
what otherwise had escaped me (and my supervisor). Interpreting her cer-
tainty as a defense helped bring the patient’s deeply shameful and guilt pro-
voking pedophilic urges into the treatment. The interpretation made no
reference to her brain or brain research.

chunks.id: On the argument for  and against  neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_7
chunks.source: On the argument for  and against  neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
ilic urges into the treatment. The interpretation made no
reference to her brain or brain research. We could now look at her wish to
victimize others including me.
Blass and Carmeli (2007, p. 23) have commented on how the focus on
reconstruction has given way to heightened attention on the “patient’s ten-
dencies to recollect in a certain way” in the setting of transference. This is
precisely what happened for me – a consequence of reading the neuro-scien-
tific research on memory.

chunks.source: On the argument for  and against  neuropsychoanalysis.pdf

vant or dangerous. This is a position taken up by Leuzinger-Bohleber

Is neuroscience relevant to psychoanalysis? Here was a neuroscientific
fact (Bremner et al. , 1997) that helped me understand my analysand’s mind
and the transference countertransference situation. It informed my interpre-
tation of defense and deepened the analytic process. I am arguing for rele-
vance, not necessity.

chunks.id: On the argument for  and against  neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_10
chunks.source: On the argument for  and against  neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:

tation of defense and deepened the analytic process. I am arguing for rele-
vance, not necessity. Other fledgling candidates, perhaps with a different
supervisor, would have arrived at an understanding of the analysand’s mind
without recourse to memory research. In addition, the memory research,
however consonant with analytic trends, is not the final word on recon-
struction.
The categorical position of Blass and Carmeli that neuroscience has ‘com-
plete’ irrelevance for psychoanalysis (and endangers it) distinguishes it from

chunks.id: On the argument for  and against  neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_11
chunks.source: On the argument for  and against  neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
uroscience has ‘com-
plete’ irrelevance for psychoanalysis (and endangers it) distinguishes it from
other interdisciplinary efforts with philosophy, humanities, art, and religion
that have long enriched our field. While I see many of the concerns they
raise as legitimate, the conviction with which Blass and Carmeli (2015)
embrace their point of view blinds them (yes, in my eyes) to the complexity
of the situation and creates an unfortunate antagonism.

chunks.id: On the argument for  and against  neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_12
chunks.source: On the argument for  and against  neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
ds them (yes, in my eyes) to the complexity
of the situation and creates an unfortunate antagonism. I believe there are
unique challenges that exist in relating neuroscience to psychoanalysis but
the authors’ conclusion is, at best, premature.
It may be, as Blass and Carmeli suggest, that the artist is not helped by
knowledge of the chemistry of the paints she uses. And it may be that
knowing about the brain’s functioning is unnecessary and, at times, inter-
feres with exploring the analysand’s mind.

chunks.id: On the argument for  and against  neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_13
chunks.source: On the argument for  and against  neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
brain’s functioning is unnecessary and, at times, inter-
feres with exploring the analysand’s mind. But if I am neither the artist nor
the chemist but one engaged in the restoration of art then knowing chem-
istry may come in handy at times.

regard to telepathic dreams, and specifically those related to
Klein’s projective identification and latterly developed by Bion and
Grinberg, the author reviews some concepts associated with the
theory of intersubjectivity.

Conclusions
I consider it to be evident that a mind can transmit content to another mind, and that this
other mind can work through it in dream formation. This process is unconscious and forms
a part of what Freud called “unconscious communication. ” It is communication with
“dream thoughts ”—level C in Bion ’s Grid.
The fundamental unconscious psychological mechanisms of this dream communi-
cation are normal and abnormal projective identification and counter-identification.

dream communi-

analysand’s evacuative PI, as has generally been considered; rather, there is also a
normal PCI in both the analyst and the analysand, which allows them a level of communi-
cation typical of the depressive position, thanks to “alpha-function.”
The intersubjective process promotes the creation of these dreams due to the peculiar
syntonic communication between the unconsciouses of the analytic pair.

QUO VADIS? THE FUTURE OF PSYCHOANALYSIS
Mauricio Cortina
Although contemporary psychoanalysis is split into different 
schools and traditions, there is growing support for some of the 
main tenets of contemporary psychodynamic thinking from at-
tachment theory, infant research, developmental psychopathol-

emotional regulation, and the discovery of different implicit and 
explicit memory systems. These tenets, which psychodynamic cli-
nicians of all stripes encounter in their daily work with clients, are 
the following: (1) that large footprints are left over from infancy 
and childhood which involved insensitive, intrusive, frightening, 
or shaming care; (2) the carryover of these relational experiences

Many findings from infant research, attachment theory, and new 
models of motivation and neuroscience have developed alongside 
the intersubjective and relational turn in psychoanalysis in the last 
sixty years.
