Response to Kessler, Sandberg, and Busch: The case for and against
neuropsychoanalysis
Dear Editor,
In our 2015 paper, “Further evidence for the case against neuropsychoanal-
ysis” as well as in our earlier work on this topic (Blass and Carmeli, 2007;

chunks.id: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_2
chunks.source: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
ainst neuropsychoanal-
ysis” as well as in our earlier work on this topic (Blass and Carmeli, 2007;
Carmeli and Blass, 2013), we present arguments that show that despite the
existence of obvious and proven ties between brain and mind, neuroscience
has no contribution to psychoanalysis; moreover, it can never have any.
Luba Kessler in her letter states that something must be amiss with our
position, but only offers yet another formulation of the tie between brain
and mind.

chunks.id: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_3
chunks.source: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
amiss with our
position, but only offers yet another formulation of the tie between brain
and mind. She does not take issue with a single one of our arguments
regarding the irrelevance of such ties to psychoanalysis and thus her reflec-
tions don’t really address our critique.
For example, her comments about how a neuroscientifically informed
psychoanalyst would understand Ms A do not in any way support the idea
that being so informed is worthwhile. She speaks of Ms A’s trauma as a
known fact which “undoubtedly” had certain specific effects both psycho-
logical and physiological.

chunks.id: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_4
chunks.source: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
known fact which “undoubtedly” had certain specific effects both psycho-
logical and physiological. However, from the description of the case the
reality of this trauma was precisely what was in doubt. But even assuming
it happened (and we accept that it may have) how should the specific neu-
roscientific findings on the effects of trauma on the hippocampus impact us
as psychoanalysts? An example of how neuroscience might shape what the
analyst says or does in the treatment of Ms A would have been most help-
ful here.

chunks.id: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_5
chunks.source: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
t shape what the
analyst says or does in the treatment of Ms A would have been most help-
ful here. Instead, Kessler offers a very general theoretical comment, which
does not advance our understanding. She agrees with us that the “psycho-
analyst needs to preserve the conceptual and clinical integrity of her clinical
and theoretical discipline”, but at the same time maintains that there is
some “conceptual richness offered by judiciously managed insights from the
neurosciences” that remains to be gained.

chunks.id: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_6
chunks.source: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
richness offered by judiciously managed insights from the
neurosciences” that remains to be gained. Her comments on the crucial
question of the nature of this richness were, unfortunately, unintelligible to
us. She writes that biology enriches “both fields of inquiry”,
because it encompasses the body AND the psyche. Indeed one can argue that the
care of psychoanalytic rigor is especially important BECAUSE the psyche is deeply
implicated in the homeostatic management of the human organism it inhabits.

chunks.id: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_7
chunks.source: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
SE the psyche is deeply
implicated in the homeostatic management of the human organism it inhabits. The
fact that same may apply to the neuronal structure such as the hippocampus does
not replace it but rather serves to illuminates [ sic].
A convincing clinical illustration or a more cogent argument is needed to
meaningfully counter the detailed position we offered in our paper regard-
ing the irrelevance of physiological findings – however, well-founded they
may be – to the analyst’s clinical work.
Larry S. Sandberg, in his letter, believes that he provides just such an
illustration.

chunks.id: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_8
chunks.source: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
inical work.
Larry S. Sandberg, in his letter, believes that he provides just such an
illustration. He describes how reading neuroscientific literature which ques-
tioned what could be explicitly remembered following trauma helped him
Int J Psychoanal (2016) 97:1155–1158 doi: 10.1111/1745-8315.12576
Copyright © 2016 Institute of Psychoanalysis

take note of his patient’s defensive sense of certainty and projection into
him of uncertainty, which could then be interpreted.

chunks.id: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_9
chunks.source: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
fensive sense of certainty and projection into
him of uncertainty, which could then be interpreted. However, the specific
neuroscientific finding mentioned in his reading, namely, on how “hip-
pocampal damage due to early trauma impacted declarative memory sys-
tems” seems to serve here no more than an inspirational role; it stimulated
Sandberg’s associative processes. Perhaps the fact that it’s a scientific find-
ing, authoritative in its own field, made it particularly stimulating for Sand-
berg, but it did not in any direct way actually shape his interpretation.

chunks.id: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_10
chunks.source: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
rly stimulating for Sand-
berg, but it did not in any direct way actually shape his interpretation. In
other words, the fact that Sandberg’s interpretation was inspired by neuro-
science says nothing about the real value of neuroscience to psychoanalysis
and, in fact, does not rely on any real research having been carried out.
E.g., if the question regarding memory were raised in the book without
mentioning neuroscience, or if the results were fabricated it could, in princi-
ple, have been just as inspiring, just as consequential.

chunks.id: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_11
chunks.source: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
sults were fabricated it could, in princi-
ple, have been just as inspiring, just as consequential.
In another of our papers (Carmeli and Blass, 2013) we discussed precisely
this kind of misguided attempt to support the relevance of neuroscience to
psychoanalysis, focusing on Norman Doidge’s claim that neuroscientific
findings have been used to develop rehabilitation programmes for psycho-
logical deficiencies.

chunks.id: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_12
chunks.source: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
ific
findings have been used to develop rehabilitation programmes for psycho-
logical deficiencies. Reviewing his presentation of the case of Barbara
Arrowsmith Young we concluded that “Barbara’s reading about brain
research apparently had an impact on her rehabilitation process, but it was
not the neuroscientific contents of what she read that played the crucial
role” (p. 395).

chunks.id: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_13
chunks.source: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
ut it was
not the neuroscientific contents of what she read that played the crucial
role” (p. 395). Rather she was inspired by the research: “It served for Bar-
bara as a sort of motto: ‘the brain could be modified’” (ibid.).
Here it is important to recognize that there are innumerable things that
can be helpful to analytic practice in this inspirational kind of way without
the effect being “categorical or predictable” and that neuroscience has no
special status in this regard.

chunks.id: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_14
chunks.source: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
fect being “categorical or predictable” and that neuroscience has no
special status in this regard. Relaxation, exercise, and various forms of lei-
surely activities are common sources of inspiration that can further insight-
ful analytic thinking. Like these practices, the study of neuroscience should
not be discouraged. However, it should be clear that like these practices
there is no reason at all for psychoanalysis to encourage it either.
And yet Sandberg seems to award neuroscience some special status.

chunks.id: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_15
chunks.source: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
oanalysis to encourage it either.
And yet Sandberg seems to award neuroscience some special status. It
were as though he can’t let go of a belief that neuroscience must have some
special value for psychoanalysis; that there is a baby there that is in danger
of getting tossed out with the bathwater as a result of our critique. How
else can one understand how Sandberg, (similarly to Kessler), refers to our
antagonism to neuroscience, while failing to provide any evidence at all to
back up his claim that the complete rejection of the relevance of neuro-

chunks.id: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_16
chunks.source: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
ide any evidence at all to
back up his claim that the complete rejection of the relevance of neuro-
science to psychoanalysis is premature? To actually ground his claim he
would have to seriously take issue with our argument (which we develop in
detail in all our papers) that the essential relationship between the fields is
such that by definition neuroscience can never be relevant to psychoanalysis
(Blass and Carmeli, 2007, 2015; Carmeli and Blass, 2013).
In fact, Sandberg’s final comment, which makes a parallel between the

chunks.id: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_17
chunks.source: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
15; Carmeli and Blass, 2013).
In fact, Sandberg’s final comment, which makes a parallel between the
analyst and the art restorer, brings to the fore his gross neglect of this argu-
ment. Our argument makes clear why the analyst’s role is precisely not com-
parable to that of the art restorer; how the nature of the analyst’s concern
1156 Letter to the Editor
Int J Psychoanal (2016) 97 Copyright © 2016 Institute of Psychoanalysis
with meaning is such that the understanding of physical matter and how it
can be manipulated is irrelevant to him.

chunks.id: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_18
chunks.source: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
such that the understanding of physical matter and how it
can be manipulated is irrelevant to him. Indeed, the analyst might be said
to aim at restoration but, as we explain, this is a restoration of meaning for
which analytic understanding alone is needed (just as the artist needs artistic
capacities). The physical restoration that might be possible through neuro-
surgery or medication and relies on neuroscientific knowledge is what’s
analogous to the role of the art restorer.

chunks.id: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_19
chunks.source: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
cation and relies on neuroscientific knowledge is what’s
analogous to the role of the art restorer. In failing to distinguish between
what we have shown in our paper to be two very different senses of restora-
tion, and in analogy of cure, Sandberg simply ignores our most basic point.
Frederic N. Busch’s letter similarly overlooks our key points. He main-
tains that our negative attitude towards neuroscience is like the negative
attitude analysts used to have towards medication being introduced into
analytic treatment.

chunks.id: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_20
chunks.source: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
egative
attitude analysts used to have towards medication being introduced into
analytic treatment. But medication is now commonly and beneficially
applied in analytic treatments. He goes on to assert that the effectiveness of
medication impacts the understanding of intrapsychic dynamics and that
medication should be regarded as an analytic intervention. However, at the
very heart of our paper is the claim that the fact that medication can reduce
symptoms of the kind that may also be effected by analytic interventions
says nothing about the relevance of biology for analytic understanding, or

chunks.id: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_21
chunks.source: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
y analytic interventions
says nothing about the relevance of biology for analytic understanding, or
about the analytic nature of biological interventions. Our paper offers
detailed arguments explaining why, even though the individual may always
be understood in terms of his neurology and his state of mind may often be
impacted neurologically, neuroscience cannot deepen our understanding of
unconscious meanings. And it is precisely the understanding of unconscious
meanings that is the essence of the analytic process.

chunks.id: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_22
chunks.source: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
is precisely the understanding of unconscious
meanings that is the essence of the analytic process. To analyze is to choose
to understand the person in this way over other available ways of under-
standing him. Unfortunately, Busch does not take issue with our arguments,
nor does he offer evidence that opposes our positions.
Perhaps this has to do with his problematic basic assumption regarding
the nature of the person and of psychoanalysis.

chunks.id: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_23
chunks.source: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
do with his problematic basic assumption regarding
the nature of the person and of psychoanalysis. Busch seems to think that
the kind of understanding that should be applied to deal with human
predicaments is determined by the nature of the predicament. The person
may have neurological problems or psychoanalytic ones (he may have a
defective piano or be a defective pianist). When neurology is applicable the
analyst needs to expand his role to include it.

chunks.id: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_24
chunks.source: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
efective pianist). When neurology is applicable the
analyst needs to expand his role to include it. This assumption runs counter
to the view that we have argued for in our paper; namely, that the person is
always open to being understood in multiple ways: neurological, psychoana-
lytical, behavioral, sociological, philosophical, theological, etc. Except for
situations in which the person is so severely damaged that he is not capable
of generating meaning, neurological or psychoanalytical intervention is a
matter of choice.

chunks.id: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_25
chunks.source: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
capable
of generating meaning, neurological or psychoanalytical intervention is a
matter of choice. Crucial here is the fact that Busch doesn’t consider the
move to the neurological level, which we agree at times may be necessary,
to be extra-analytic, but rather integral to psychoanalysis. But here one
must ask: What definition of psychoanalysis does he adopt to support this
view? Does he regard as analytic any intervention that alleviates symptoms
(including behavioral methods)? Anything that furthers the analytic process

chunks.id: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_26
chunks.source: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
hat alleviates symptoms
(including behavioral methods)? Anything that furthers the analytic process
(e.g., including the patient getting a job which allows him to pay for the
analysis)? Or is it specifically biological understanding and intervention that
Letter to the Editor 1157
Int J Psychoanal (2016) 97Copyright © 2016 Institute of Psychoanalysis
must be considered psychoanalytic? Busch doesn’t explicitly present his defi-
nition of psychoanalysis.

chunks.id: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_27
chunks.source: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
be considered psychoanalytic? Busch doesn’t explicitly present his defi-
nition of psychoanalysis. But it is clear that if one adopts his limited posi-
tion on how the person can be understood (whereby the nature of the event
determines the kind of understanding that is possible) together with very
broad position on the nature of psychoanalysis of the kind that he suggests,
then the relevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis is clear and even obvi-
ous, but it also tells us nothing meaningful.

chunks.id: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_28
chunks.source: Response to Kessler  Sandberg  and Busch  The case for and against neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
euroscience to psychoanalysis is clear and even obvi-
ous, but it also tells us nothing meaningful. Nothing uniquely psychoana-
lytic remains to which neuroscience could be relevant.
Sincerely,
Rachel Blass and Zvi Carmeli
13 Gikhon St., Jerusalem, Israel

chunks.text:
Book Review
The Present Moment in Psychotherapy and Everyday Life.
Daniel M. Stern. New York: W. W. Norton and Company, 2004. 247
pages, hardbound, $29.95.
Once again, Daniel N. Stern writes a book that is relevant and inclusive
of the ﬁeld of Dance/Movement Therapy. In his 1985 publication of The
Interpersonal World of the Infant: A View from Psychoanalysis and
Developmental Psychology, he addresses the phenomenon of attunement
in a manner that afﬁrms and illuminates what dance therapists know
about that subject.

chunks.id: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf_1
chunks.source: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf
chunks.text:
f attunement
in a manner that afﬁrms and illuminates what dance therapists know
about that subject. He gives credit in a footnote to the work of Kestenberg
and Sossin in the microanalysis of mother/infant interactions. In his
recent publication, The Present Moment in Psychotherapy and Everyday
Life (2004), he studies the nature, temporal architecture and organiza-
tion of nowness using a phenomenological approach and using language
that has great relevance to and overlap with the ﬁeld of dance/movement
therapy.

chunks.id: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf_2
chunks.source: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf
chunks.text:
and using language
that has great relevance to and overlap with the ﬁeld of dance/movement
therapy. He again acknowledges Judith Kestenberg, as well as Warren
Lamb, Rudolf Laban and Emile Dalcroze, and their contributions to the
study of movement analysis. Stern has a deep understanding of how
their work helps to delineate the micro-world of the present moment as
‘‘lived experience’’ (p. xiii) which is the focus of his book.
Stern’s book is divided into three parts.

chunks.id: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf_3
chunks.source: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf
chunks.text:
ed experience’’ (p. xiii) which is the focus of his book.
Stern’s book is divided into three parts. In Part One, entitled
Exploring the Present Moment , he studies the characteristics of the
present moment as a process unit that is about perceptual, subjective,
psychological, and lived (as opposed to verbal) experience in the here
and now. In chapter three Stern compares the duration of the present
moment as it is conceived in music, movement, dance, nonverbal mo-
ther-infant interactions, and in general mental operations.

chunks.id: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf_4
chunks.source: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf
chunks.text:
n music, movement, dance, nonverbal mo-
ther-infant interactions, and in general mental operations. He describes
the temporal dynamics of moments as vitality affects that unfold as the
101
American Journal of Dance Therapy
Vol. 27, No. 2, Fall/Winter 2005
DOI: 10.1007/s10465-005-9004-x
/C2112006 American Dance
Therapy Association
moment unfolds. He refers to the choreographer’s attempts to get at the
artistry of expression rather than just the technique, as that matches
his own interest in vitality affects which have more to do with feeling
than with the actual movement.

chunks.id: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf_5
chunks.source: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf
chunks.text:
own interest in vitality affects which have more to do with feeling
than with the actual movement. Stern is talking about the ‘‘how’’ of
movement that is thoroughly addressed both in LMA and in the
Kestenberg Movement proﬁle.
Stern wants us to think of the present moment as a short stretch of
consciousness in which felt experience is expressed through vitality
affects (effort/shape) and to consider such moments as offering the
greatest potential for authenticity and change.

chunks.id: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf_6
chunks.source: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf
chunks.text:
shape) and to consider such moments as offering the
greatest potential for authenticity and change. He states that these
moments of vitality affects are where the ‘‘magic in a therapy session or
in intimate relations’’ (p. 67) resides. He challenges the clinical, behav-
ioral and neurosciences to work to understand more fully phenomenal
experience, i.e., the subjective experience of vitality affects.
As dance/movement therapists, we might feel some momentary frus-
tration or excitement that Stern expresses explicitly what we know
implicitly.

chunks.id: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf_7
chunks.source: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf
chunks.text:
some momentary frus-
tration or excitement that Stern expresses explicitly what we know
implicitly. We are very familiar with lived experience as it unfolds mo-
ment-by-moment and movement-by-movement in a Chacian group or
authentic movement process. This irritation or excitement might aug-
ment as one reads further, as Stern urges the ‘‘beyond talking’’ (p. 142)
therapies not only to stay focused on the ‘‘micro-temporal structure of the
process’’ (p. 143), but also to pay more attention ‘‘to its detailed
description and conceptualization.’’ (p.

chunks.id: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf_8
chunks.source: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf
chunks.text:
(p. 143), but also to pay more attention ‘‘to its detailed
description and conceptualization.’’ (p. 143)
In Part II, Contextualizing the Present Moment , Stern further ex-
plores the present moment through the lens of intersubjectivity and asks
how the present moment is experienced by dyads and groups when it is
co-created and shared in a moment of intersubjective contact. He is most
interested in, and wants the reader to be interested in, the feeling/
experiencing realm.
Stern outlines the neuroscientiﬁc evidence of ‘‘mirror neurons’’ (p.

chunks.id: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf_9
chunks.source: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf
chunks.text:
e feeling/
experiencing realm.
Stern outlines the neuroscientiﬁc evidence of ‘‘mirror neurons’’ (p. 78)
and the neurobiological mechanisms, which allow one to read, empathize
and resonate with another person’s state of mind, intentions, experience,
or movement. He raises the question of how a present moment that is
implicitly grasped becomes conscious. He contrasts the introspective, or
reﬂective, consciousness that takes place verbally in most therapies with
the phenomenal consciousness ‘‘usually synonymous with enactments’’
(p.

chunks.id: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf_10
chunks.source: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf
chunks.text:
ally in most therapies with
the phenomenal consciousness ‘‘usually synonymous with enactments’’
(p. 125) stressed in movement, drama and other ‘‘existentially oriented
therapies.’’ He suggests a new form of consciousness, which he calls
intersubjective consciousness, in which the phenomenal consciousness of
one overlaps with that of another, out of which an intersubjective expe-
rience, or a ‘‘shared feeling voyage’’ (p. 173) is co-created. The participants
have a social experience of sharing similar landscapes of feeling (p. 246)
that feels mutually validating.

chunks.id: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf_11
chunks.source: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf
chunks.text:
social experience of sharing similar landscapes of feeling (p. 246)
that feels mutually validating. Reﬂective consciousness, states Stern,
happens when one experiences the other’s experience of one’s experience.
102 Book Review
From the perspective of a dance/movement therapist, reading this
section of the book might cause a sense of ‘‘of course.’’ Marion Chace
developed a whole method of therapy and change based on the ability to
connect through kinesthetic empathy and attunement to the vitality af-
fects and felt experience of others.

chunks.id: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf_12
chunks.source: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf
chunks.text:
through kinesthetic empathy and attunement to the vitality af-
fects and felt experience of others. Some of what Stern talks about we
take for granted; nevertheless, there can also be an exhilarating sense of
validation that the neurosciences are catching up to us and that our ﬁeld
can now come into its own.
In Part Three, Views from a Clinical Perspective , Stern urges clini-
cians to put the present moment on ‘‘center stage’’ in the clinical setting,
so as to see the richness of intimate human relations and psychotherapy
at the micro level of moments that occupy a subjective now.

chunks.id: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf_13
chunks.source: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf
chunks.text:
imate human relations and psychotherapy
at the micro level of moments that occupy a subjective now. Stern cites
the work of the expressive therapies for their focus on what is unfolding
at the present centered interaction as the context of the emerging
material. He makes a criticism that often we then proceed to do what
most verbal therapies do; i.e., move into the content or the explicit and
therefore lose much of the ‘‘wholeness, felt truth, richness, and honesty’’
of the lived moment.

chunks.id: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf_14
chunks.source: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf
chunks.text:
nd
therefore lose much of the ‘‘wholeness, felt truth, richness, and honesty’’
of the lived moment. Stern becomes quite impassioned here as he an-
swers his self-imposed question of whether he is giving action and/or
joint action precedence over thought and language. He reminds himself
and us that such a question is irrelevant when we understand the cog-
nitive sciences’ proposal that the mind is not an independent disem-
bodied entity. ‘‘Rather, thinking itself requires and depends upon
feelings emanating from the body.’’ (p.

chunks.id: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf_15
chunks.source: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf
chunks.text:
entity. ‘‘Rather, thinking itself requires and depends upon
feelings emanating from the body.’’ (p. 145) Change, he says, can come
not only through interpretation (psychoanalytic) in the explicit domain,
but also through shifts in implicit knowing. As implicit knowing is given
more importance, so also more importance is given to action and non-
verbal present moments in which intersubjective contact takes place
through mutual gaze, postural shifts, gestures, facial expressions,
respiratory changes or changes in vocal tone or strength.

chunks.id: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf_16
chunks.source: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf
chunks.text:
ral shifts, gestures, facial expressions,
respiratory changes or changes in vocal tone or strength.
The ﬁnal chapters document therapy as a co-created journey in which
it is understood that the client brings a desire to be known and a desire
for intersubjective contact that both drives the psychotherapeutic process
forward and also regulates it. Stern reveals his keen interest in dance
and movement process as he couches and speaks of the therapeutic
process in choreographic language and uses such phrases as ‘‘the moving
along process, relational moves, process ﬂow, missteps in the dance,

chunks.id: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf_17
chunks.source: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf
chunks.text:
s such phrases as ‘‘the moving
along process, relational moves, process ﬂow, missteps in the dance,
presentness ﬁlls the time and space, choreography of intention move-
ments.’’ The dance that Stern describes is one in which the implicit is at
the forefront and which culminates in a peak experience that he calls a
‘‘moment of meeting.’’ (p. 151) These moments take place in kairos,a
Greek term for time in which there is an emergent sense of something
coming into being.

chunks.id: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf_18
chunks.source: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf
chunks.text:
in kairos,a
Greek term for time in which there is an emergent sense of something
coming into being. This something is experienced affectively through the
103Book Review
expression of vitality affects and intersubjectively as ‘‘doing something
together’’ (p. 176), whether it is mental, affective or physical.
Stern uses the wonderful phrase, ‘‘interweaving the implicit and ex-
plicit’’ (p.

chunks.id: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf_19
chunks.source: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf
chunks.text:
tive or physical.
Stern uses the wonderful phrase, ‘‘interweaving the implicit and ex-
plicit’’ (p. 187), to describe a client expressing herself, and the therapist
listening and participating in the experience, as it gets relived explicitly
through words, but also through the implicit expression of ‘‘ease, difﬁ-
culty, groping, hesitating, blocking, frustration, effort, changes in ﬂow,
speed, volume and force...’’ (p. 193).

chunks.id: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf_20
chunks.source: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf
chunks.text:
, hesitating, blocking, frustration, effort, changes in ﬂow,
speed, volume and force...’’ (p. 193). Stern aptly names this as a perfor-
mance that evokes in both the listener and the teller a stream of implicit
experiencing.
This section of the book lays to rest the many discussions I have been
privy to among dance/movement therapists regarding whether words are
necessary to process the experience.

chunks.id: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf_21
chunks.source: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf
chunks.text:
to among dance/movement therapists regarding whether words are
necessary to process the experience. Our job, according to Stern, is to pay
attention and respond to the implicit experience, to the felt experience, to
the vitality affects or effort/shape expression, whether in the form of
language or movement. It is the now moments followed by a moment of
meeting, in which the participants are focused on the presentness of the
current lived moment, that change happens in relationships.
Reading Stern offers the dance/movement therapist an opportunity

chunks.id: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf_22
chunks.source: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf
chunks.text:
t change happens in relationships.
Reading Stern offers the dance/movement therapist an opportunity
for an experience of parallel process, or perhaps more accurately, a kind
of virtual moment of meeting in the intersubjective matrix. His under-
standing of dance and movement process serves as metaphor for his new
views on what is essential and meaningful in human interaction and in
the change process of psychotherapy. His writing mirrors what the ﬁeld
of dance/therapy knows implicitly and struggles to express in explicit
forms.

chunks.id: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf_23
chunks.source: Review ofThe present moment in psychotherapy and everyday life.pdf
chunks.text:
mirrors what the ﬁeld
of dance/therapy knows implicitly and struggles to express in explicit
forms. Stern lets us know that we are at the cutting edge of the neuro-
science of interpersonal relating. We need to take our rightful place and
to enter into an intersubjective dialogue in which we share our knowl-
edge and respond/contribute to this exciting new ‘‘moment of meeting.’’
Margaret L. Mason

Book Review Essay
The case against neuroplastic analysis: A further
illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to
psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge ’s
The Brain that Changes Itself
Zvi Carmeli and Rachel Blass
The Department of Psychology, The Hebrew University of Jerusalem,
Israel 91905 – zcarmeli@gmail.com
Heythrop College, The University of London, 23 Kensington Square,
London, W8 5HN, UK – rblass@ucl.ac.uk
In a previous paper, we critically examined claims put forth by proponents

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_3
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
N, UK – rblass@ucl.ac.uk
In a previous paper, we critically examined claims put forth by proponents
of the growing neuropsychoanalytic trend (Blass and Carmeli, 2007). In par-
ticular, we called into question the claim that neuroscientific findings are
relevant and important for the development and justification of psychoana-
lytic theory and practice. We pointed to some of the intuitions that have led
to the popularity of such neuropsychoanalytic claims, and then exposed the
fallacies that underlie both the claims and the intuitions.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_4
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
hoanalytic claims, and then exposed the
fallacies that underlie both the claims and the intuitions.
We also showed how the neuropsychoanalytic trend modifies the basic
aims of the analytic process, shifting away from the unique psychoanalytic
concern with the understanding of meanings and the role of interpersonal dis-
course in discerning and justifying these meanings. As such it was having a
negative impact on the development of psychoanalytic thinking and practice.
The present paper expands on and further grounds these conclusions.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_5
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
analytic thinking and practice.
The present paper expands on and further grounds these conclusions. It
responds to claims put forth in the neuropsychoanalytic literature regarding
an area of neuroscientific interest that we did not address in our previous
work. This area of interest is the brain’s plasticity (neuroplasticity). In short,
brain plasticity denotes the capacity of the brain’s structure and function to
be altered by experience and input from the environment.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_6
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
y of the brain’s structure and function to
be altered by experience and input from the environment. Contemporary
investigators of this plasticity offer evidence regarding the various forms of
change that the brain remains open to throughout life, even in adulthood. It
is often stressed that these findings challenge a view of the brain as immuta-
ble after a critical period during early childhood (Rakic, 2002).
Evidence associated with the notion of the brain’s plasticity has recently
been presented as supporting the idea that neuroscience can significantly

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_7
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
s plasticity has recently
been presented as supporting the idea that neuroscience can significantly
influence psychological understanding and theoretical development. It has
also been claimed that neuroplasticity is very relevant to psychoanalysis.
Here, we show that the evidence associated with neuroplasticity in fact dem-
onstrates the opposite: psychological understanding and theoretical develop-
ment are in no way significantly influenced by the evidence marshalled to

The present study is based on an examination of the line of argument put

ng of an analytic process.
The present study is based on an examination of the line of argument put
forth in the widely acclaimed and best-selling book The Brain that Changes
Itself. The book was written by Canadian analyst and psychiatrist Norman
Doidge (2007). While not a scientific publication per se , it has been cited
and reviewed in analytic contexts and has been influential in shaping com-
mon opinion of the relationship between psychoanalysis and neuroscience
(as evidenced, for example, by the fact that in 2008 Norman Doidge
received the prestigious Sigourney Award).

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_10
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
ced, for example, by the fact that in 2008 Norman Doidge
received the prestigious Sigourney Award).
The brain that changes itself
Doidge’s book is yet another in the flood of recently published texts on the
relationship between neuroscience and mental activity (e.g. Baron-Cohen,
2011; Churchland, 2011; Damasio, 2010; Ramachandran, 2011; Shermer,
2011). The book focuses primarily on the possibility of rehabilitation of people
who for a variety of reasons have been seriously damaged in terms of their
daily functioning.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_11
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
eople
who for a variety of reasons have been seriously damaged in terms of their
daily functioning. It tells the gripping narratives of patients and professionals
who have heroically and creatively struggled – and to a considerable extent
succeeded – to overcome the limitations with which they were faced. These are
stories of strong-willed patients who fought to re-establish normal lives despite
their supposedly hopeless prognoses, and of visionary researchers who in the
face of common wisdom and practice maintained that the brains of these

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_12
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
onary researchers who in the
face of common wisdom and practice maintained that the brains of these
patients could change and thus rehabilitation could be brought about.
Into these stories, Doidge weaves neuroscientific empirical findings and
theoretical considerations. Thus, while reading of truly amazing accounts of
cure and rehabilitation, we are also told of how these breakthrough pro-
cesses of change are a consequence of the understanding of the brain’s pre-
viously unfathomed plasticity.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_13
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
of change are a consequence of the understanding of the brain’s pre-
viously unfathomed plasticity. In this context Doidge writes:
The idea that the brain can change its own structure and function through thought
and activity is, I believe, the most important alteration in our view of the brain
since we first sketched out its basic anatomy and the workings of its basic compo-
nent, the neuron. Like all revolutions, this one will have profound effects...
(pp.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_14
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
ts basic compo-
nent, the neuron. Like all revolutions, this one will have profound effects...
(pp. ix –xx)
Some of the book’s chapters deal with astonishing accounts of physical
rehabilitation: the rehabilitation of balance in a woman with inner ear dam-
age (Chapter 1), the rehabilitation of functions that were lost due to stroke
(Chapter 5) and the overcoming of phantom pain among amputees (Chap-
ter 7).

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_15
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
ere lost due to stroke
(Chapter 5) and the overcoming of phantom pain among amputees (Chap-
ter 7). Other chapters are focused on cognitive rehabilitation: rehabilitation
in cases in which intellectual, linguistic and learning capacities were dam-
aged (Chapters 2, 3, 11) or in which elderly individuals could preserve and
even improve their cognitive abilities despite the aging process they were
undergoing (Chapter 10). Other chapters deal with emotional and impulsive
disorders and how these and their debilitating effects are dramatically over-
come (Chapters 4, 6).

e and their debilitating effects are dramatically over-
come (Chapters 4, 6).

In all these instances, alongside the stories, Doidge introduces underlying
neuroscientific explanations. The reader is invited to consider the value of
the dialogue to be had between the brain sciences and a range of therapeu-
tic fields, physical and psychical in nature.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_17
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
d between the brain sciences and a range of therapeu-
tic fields, physical and psychical in nature. Doidge also acquaints us with a
wide range of terms, concepts, and principles from the different sciences
and fields and in a way that is both clear and captivating.
Chapter 9 is of special interest to the analytic reader as it offers a case
illustration of rehabilitation through psychoanalytic treatment.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_18
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
nalytic reader as it offers a case
illustration of rehabilitation through psychoanalytic treatment. Here Doi-
dge’s point is that psychoanalysis, from its very start in Freud to the pres-
ent day, is a treatment which is actually guided by an implicit recognition
of the brain’s plasticity and by attempts to facilitate the brain’s potential
for change.
Thus, while the topics of the book are varied, they all are aimed at dem-
onstrating that successful treatments are actually founded on what we now
know to be the brain’s plasticity.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_19
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
g that successful treatments are actually founded on what we now
know to be the brain’s plasticity. More importantly, they are all used to
support the claim that the newly found knowledge regarding this plasticity
allows for cures that could have never been dreamt of in the past and
explains existing cures. This knowledge has therefore initiated a kind of
therapeutic revolution.
In our view, however, the book is also fundamentally flawed.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_20
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
ated a kind of
therapeutic revolution.
In our view, however, the book is also fundamentally flawed. This has to
do with the very problematic nature of its theoretical assumptions and
claims, implicit and explicit, regarding the relationship between the biologi-
cal and the mental spheres, and invalid inferences made from findings in
one sphere to the other. These problems have for the most part been over-
looked in the many very positive reviews this book has received both in the
general press
1 as well as in the supportive references to the book in analytic
contexts (e.g.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_21
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
the
general press
1 as well as in the supportive references to the book in analytic
contexts (e.g. Fertuck, 2008; Frank, 2008) 2. In drawing attention to them
here we will argue that Doidge is misguided in portraying the treatment
innovations and improvements as being derived from or based on develop-
ments in the field of brain research.
The fact of the matter is that neuroscientific findings have had no mean-
ingful impact on the nature of the treatments or their success.
3 This
becomes blatantly clear from a critical examination of the cases that Doidge

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_22
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
their success.
3 This
becomes blatantly clear from a critical examination of the cases that Doidge
presents to demonstrate this purported impact. One may presume that the
dramatic changes that he describes involve changes in the brain, and neuro-
scientific techniques may be able to show this. The changes themselves,
however, in no way rely on neuroscientific findings.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_23
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
be able to show this. The changes themselves,
however, in no way rely on neuroscientific findings. Nor do retrospective
1See the author’s website: http://www.normandoidge.com/normandoidge/REVIEWS.html
2In Deutsch and Deutsch’s review (2007) the authors acknowledges that the book has limitations, but
nevertheless emphasize its overall importance for psychoanalytic thinking. Also, Doidge’s book has been
cited in psychoanalytic and psychotherapeutic papers where it is described as advancing psychoanalysis
and psychotherapeutic thinking (see, for example, Hall, 2008, p. 847).

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_24
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
as advancing psychoanalysis
and psychotherapeutic thinking (see, for example, Hall, 2008, p. 847). A noted exception to this trend is
a review by McManus (2009), a UCL Professor of Psychology and Medical Education who offers a very
brief but scathing critique of the book. This critique and the kind of opposition it poses to neuropsycho-
analysis has not, however, been acknowledged within the analytic literature.
3As we shall see, unfounded beliefs regarding the value and relevance of neuroscientific findings may
influence choice and course of treatment.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_25
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
g the value and relevance of neuroscientific findings may
influence choice and course of treatment. But this points to the value and relevance of the beliefs rather
than to the value and relevance of the findings themselves. To highlight that our study investigates the
latter, at times, we refer to the ‘ meaningful’ impact of the findings and their ‘ fundamental’ relevance.
