findings regarding the neuronal changes that took place provide informa-
tion relevant to future treatment.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_26
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
regarding the neuronal changes that took place provide informa-
tion relevant to future treatment. Also, focusing on the way in which the
book presents the tie between brain research and psychoanalytic theory and
practice, we will show that the misapplication of neuroscientific ideas to the
mental sphere shapes how clinical phenomena are regarded in a way that
leaves little room for a truly psychoanalytic approach.
On wrongly attributing mental/functional improvement to
theories or findings regarding neuroplasticity
Let us now examine some of Doidge’s case studies to see the fundamental

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_27
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
s regarding neuroplasticity
Let us now examine some of Doidge’s case studies to see the fundamental
irrelevance of the neuroscientific findings to the therapeutic processes that
he describes and how, despite this, he presents the findings as crucial to the
therapy.
Some illustrations
In Chapter 2, entitled ‘Building her own Brain’, Doidge reports the fascinat-
ing case of Barbara Arrowsmith Young. As a child, Barbara was brilliant in
some fields – her visual and auditory memory were in the 99th percentile –
but there were some fields in which she was significantly limited.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_28
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
ry were in the 99th percentile –
but there were some fields in which she was significantly limited. Doidge
adds: “Because the part of her brain that helps to understand the relation-
ships between symbols wasn’t functioning normally, she had trouble
understanding grammar, math concepts, logic and cause and effect” (p. 29).
Barbara thought that these could not be improved.
At a certain point, on the advice of a friend, Barbara read about the
research of Alexander Luria.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_29
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
At a certain point, on the advice of a friend, Barbara read about the
research of Alexander Luria. Luria described someone who had similar
mental difficulties to Barbara’s although, in that person’s case, the difficul-
ties were derived from brain damage. Luria’s research left Barbara feeling
hopeless since it did not offer any course of treatment.
Barbara then heard of a study conducted by Mark Rosenzweig from the
University of California at Berkeley.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_30
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
a then heard of a study conducted by Mark Rosenzweig from the
University of California at Berkeley. Doidge explains:
[He] had studied rats in stimulating and nonstimulating environments, and in post-
mortem exams he found that the brains of the stimulated rats had more neurotrans-
mitters, were heavier, and had better blood supply than those from the less
stimulating environments.
(p. 35)
This study, according to Doidge’s description of the course of events, led
Barbara to attempt to change her brain structure and thus to change.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_31
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
n of the course of events, led
Barbara to attempt to change her brain structure and thus to change. While
reading Rosenzweig’s research “lightning struck” ( ibid.). Linking Rosen-
zweig’s research, which showed that activity could change the brain’s struc-
ture, with Luria’s research that showed that mental difficulties may be
associated with brain damage, she initiated a rigorous regime of exercising her
weaker mental capacities and the effort indeed led to dramatic improvement.
Doidge not only considers this a good use of neuroscientific findings; he

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_32
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
to dramatic improvement.
Doidge not only considers this a good use of neuroscientific findings; he
also goes as far as to affirm that Barbara made an important discovery
about the brain. In Doidge’s words:
394 Z. Carmeli and R. Blass
Int J Psychoanal (2013) 94 Copyright © 2013 Institute of Psychoanalysis
The scientists who make important discoveries about the brain are often those
whose own brains are extraordinary, working on those whose brains are damaged.
It is rare that the person who makes an important discovery is the one with the
defect, but there are some exceptions.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_33
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
person who makes an important discovery is the one with the
defect, but there are some exceptions. Barbara Arrowsmith Young is one of these.
(p. 27)
These conclusions are, however, completely unfounded. She neither made
a discovery regarding the brain nor did she make real use of existing find-
ings.
Barbara’s reading about brain research apparently had an impact on her
rehabilitation process, but it was not the neuroscientific contents of what
she read that played the crucial role.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_34
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
process, but it was not the neuroscientific contents of what
she read that played the crucial role. It may be seen, for example, that the
study that influenced her did not refer to someone with similar disabilities,
and did not suggest any particular course for improving mental abilities. It
did not even demonstrate that damaged brains could be rehabilitated or
developed. It dealt with the normal brains (of rats) and showed that these
brains develop in a stimulation-rich environment.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_35
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
the normal brains (of rats) and showed that these
brains develop in a stimulation-rich environment. It thus could not be an
inference from the method or findings of the neuroscientific study per se
that affected Barbara’s course of action and its successful outcome.
It would seem, rather, that the study served as a general source of inspi-
ration. It served for Barbara as a sort of motto: ‘the brain could be modi-
fied’.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_36
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
source of inspi-
ration. It served for Barbara as a sort of motto: ‘the brain could be modi-
fied’. With that in hand (not any new or old neuroscientific knowledge), she
went ahead and devised her rigorous regime of exercises for her weakened
functions which ultimately led to her improvement. To highlight the point:
had Rosenzweig merely found that providing rats with stimulating environ-
ments improves their mental activities, without offering any information
regarding the state of the rats’ brains, Barbara would have had just as much
reason to devise her regime.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_37
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
ing the state of the rats’ brains, Barbara would have had just as much
reason to devise her regime. The fact regarding the brain does not play any
directly meaningful role. Barbara may have been influenced emotionally by
Rosenzweig’s reference to changes in the brain, but the actual content of his
findings regarding these changes are irrelevant to her situation and could
not have had any effect.
It is important to note that the course of Barbara’s treatment is not
described as having been determined by information regarding a specific
area of her brain. This is not surprising.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_38
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
ving been determined by information regarding a specific
area of her brain. This is not surprising. As we have seen, the brain is irrele-
vant to the connections she made between the limitations of her mental
functioning and the training she developed to overcome them. Even if Bar-
bara were to have associated her limitations with a certain area of the brain
(as Doidge does in a very general way), this would not have had clear-cut
predictive implications for the effectiveness of the training programme.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_39
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
uld not have had clear-cut
predictive implications for the effectiveness of the training programme. As
is well known, (a) the same mental functioning could be determined by dif-
ferent areas of the brain and (b) training could lead to the development of
capacities through affecting other areas of the brain without modifying the
areas associated with the limitation (Levin and Grafman, 2000).
In fact, Doidge himself illustrates this point in another of the cases he
describes, that of Michelle (Chapter 11).

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_40
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
himself illustrates this point in another of the cases he
describes, that of Michelle (Chapter 11). This case, too, provides evidence
of the irrelevance of the neuroscientific findings to the therapeutic process.
Michelle was born with only a right brain hemisphere. She suffered from
The case against neuroplastic analysis 395
Copyright © 2013 Institute of Psychoanalysis Int J Psychoanal (2013) 94
certain mental and physical developmental impairments but she overcame
many of them and was able to develop mental functions usually associated
with the left hemisphere.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_41
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
many of them and was able to develop mental functions usually associated
with the left hemisphere. This occurred naturally, without any special train-
ing, and Michelle’s family and doctors were unaware (for a number of
years) of the fact that part of her brain was missing. A CAT scan per-
formed when Michelle was 3 ½ years old made them aware of this fact. No
expert on neuroplasticity was brought in to help at that point; however, her
functioning continued to improve.
Although Michelle’s case illustrates the brain’s plasticity, it also illustrates

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_42
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
tinued to improve.
Although Michelle’s case illustrates the brain’s plasticity, it also illustrates
how knowledge regarding the brain and its plasticity is irrelevant to the
understanding of the process of mental development in cases like hers. It is
clear from Doidge’s description that in such cases, in which a substantial
part of the brain is missing, one cannot predict which brain areas will take
over which mental functions. This will depend to a large extent on the
patient’s life experiences and the ways in which the brain is activated by
those experiences.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_43
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
n the
patient’s life experiences and the ways in which the brain is activated by
those experiences. Doidge, however, does not recognize the implications of
this – if factors external to the brain significantly determine its functionality
and the degree of its plasticity, this sets limits on what can be known from
the study of the brain itself about how the brain will develop. Even more
so, it limits what we can learn from such studies about mental functioning.
We turn now to yet another illustration of this.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_44
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
learn from such studies about mental functioning.
We turn now to yet another illustration of this. Doidge describes how
Michael Merzenich, “the world’s leading researcher on brain plasticity”
(p. 46), and three associates “formed … the nucleus of a company, ‘Scientific
Learning’, that is wholly devoted to using neuroplastic research to help people
rewire their brains” (p. 70). This company developed a “series of plasticity-
based computer programs, Fast ForWord ” for dealing with learning and lan-
guage disabilities.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_45
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
ity-
based computer programs, Fast ForWord ” for dealing with learning and lan-
guage disabilities. According to Doidge, this software works on principles that
are “consistent with the laws that govern brain plasticity” (p. 47).
When one examines Doidge’s description of Merzenich’s computer pro-
grams, however, it becomes apparent that, aside from the use of jargon
associated with brain research, the programs have no tie to neuroscientific
findings or principles of any kind.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_46
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
ith brain research, the programs have no tie to neuroscientific
findings or principles of any kind. For example, we are told that Fast For-
Word is disguised as a children’s game that responds in a funny and encour-
aging way when the child being treated attains one of the goals that are set.
Doidge explains the underlying neuroscientific principles thus:
This ‘reward’ is a crucial feature of the program, because each time the child is
rewarded, his brain secretes such neurotransmitters as dopamine and acetylcholine,
which help consolidate the map changes he has just made.
(p.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_47
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
mitters as dopamine and acetylcholine,
which help consolidate the map changes he has just made.
(p. 71)
This may indeed be an accurate description of neurological correlates of
rewarding situations. Moreover, such jargon may impress parents consider-
ing the program, and the program may indeed be the most successful ever.
4
But the idea that rewarding children is conducive to their learning is not a
consequence of any neurological finding.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_48
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
rewarding children is conducive to their learning is not a
consequence of any neurological finding. It is known and validated indepen-
4While Doidge presents this program in a very positive light, other researchers have revealed a more
mixed picture (Borman et al ., 2009; Gillam et al ., 2008).
396 Z. Carmeli and R. Blass
Int J Psychoanal (2013) 94 Copyright © 2013 Institute of Psychoanalysis
dently of any knowledge of brain secretions or neural networks.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_49
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
© 2013 Institute of Psychoanalysis
dently of any knowledge of brain secretions or neural networks. In fact,
any parent or teacher knows that positive responses may be motivating or
arousing, and that, in general, a happy child is a child more willing and bet-
ter able to learn. The principles involved are basic principles of learning,
based on the study of the cognitive, psychological processes involved when
a child learns – not neuroscientific ones.
5
There is yet another flawed example that Doidge brings to demonstrate
how neuroscientific findings significantly advance our understanding of

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_50
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
oidge brings to demonstrate
how neuroscientific findings significantly advance our understanding of
mental processes. Doidge writes:
Merzenich and Jenkins also found that as neurons are trained and become more
efficient, they can process faster. This means that the speed at which we think is
itself plastic.
(p. 67)
But clearly the inference here is not from a neuroscientific finding to human
activity. Rather, it is the other way around. We all know that when a per-
son (not a neuron) practices a certain activity, including certain kinds of
thinking, he becomes faster at it.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_51
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
neuron) practices a certain activity, including certain kinds of
thinking, he becomes faster at it. This plasticity of thinking is an obvious
behavioural fact and is not based on or derived from any neuroscientific
findings provided by Merzenich and Jenkins. Based on this observed
behavioural fact one may make inferences regarding the processing speed
and efficiency of neurons.
In other words, here, too, the researchers do not discover plasticity
through their neuroscientific studies as they and Doidge claim.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_52
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
earchers do not discover plasticity
through their neuroscientific studies as they and Doidge claim. They merely
discover the neuronal correlates of an obvious and presupposed plasticity.
As a result, the program that they propose is not derived in any significant,
necessary way from neuroscientific evidence regarding the brain’s plasticity.
This fallacy – whereby well-known or presupposed psychological and
behavioural facts are presented as though they are findings derived from
neuroscientific research regarding the brain’s plasticity – permeates the
book.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_53
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
ndings derived from
neuroscientific research regarding the brain’s plasticity – permeates the
book. We are led to believe that such research teaches us something new
about vision, learning processes, or physiological capacities (such as the use
of damaged limbs following stroke). However, for the same kinds of reasons
described above, this is not at all the case.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_54
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
owing stroke). However, for the same kinds of reasons
described above, this is not at all the case. At the very most, what we learn
from this research is about some neuroscientific correlates of mental and
functional facts.
The negative impact of understanding in terms of
neuroplasticity
The misguided use of brain research terminology that we have pointed to
here may be appealing and inspirational to some.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_55
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
brain research terminology that we have pointed to
here may be appealing and inspirational to some. Unfortunately, it also has
5In analogy: we understand our preference for sugar in our coffee independently of the explanations,
however interesting they may be, of the neurological effects of sugar. Moreover, if we would want to
understand the experience of sweetness in a specific individual (as a private chef might) we would have
no interest in general findings about brain correlates. We would rather be concerned with the individ-
ual’s lived experience of different foods, e.g.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_56
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
tes. We would rather be concerned with the individ-
ual’s lived experience of different foods, e.g. how he reacts to the different foods we offer and what he
says to his past experiences with food.
The case against neuroplastic analysis 397
Copyright © 2013 Institute of Psychoanalysis Int J Psychoanal (2013) 94
a negative impact on the way the mental sphere comes to be regarded (see
Blass and Carmeli, 2007). This impact may be seen clearly throughout Doi-
dge’s book.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_57
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
regarded (see
Blass and Carmeli, 2007). This impact may be seen clearly throughout Doi-
dge’s book. In the following examples, we will first describe how the notion
of plasticity is wrongly applied to the explanation of therapeutic processes.
We will then show the broader negative effects of this misuse.
Chapter 6 deals with Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD). After
describing the disorder Doidge notes that medication and behavioural ther-
apy are only partially helpful for many people. In contrast, we are told, a
form of therapy developed by the UCLA psychiatrist Jeffrey M.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_58
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
y people. In contrast, we are told, a
form of therapy developed by the UCLA psychiatrist Jeffrey M. Schwartz
has been found to be effective. This therapy developed out of Schwartz’s
study of brain images of OCD patients and a notion of the brain’s plasticity
that emerged from it. Doidge states that this was “ … the first time, to my
knowledge, that such brain scans as the PET helped doctors both to under-
stand a disorder and to develop a psychotherapy for it” (2007, p.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_59
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
PET helped doctors both to under-
stand a disorder and to develop a psychotherapy for it” (2007, p. 169).
The model of OCD and its treatment that Schwartz proposed is based on
an examination of the psychological process that occurs when one makes a
mistake, and of the correlates of that process in the brain. He points to
three things that happen. First, we feel that we made a mistake. Brain imag-
ing has shown that the detection of the mistake underlying this feeling
occurs in the orbital frontal cortex. The more obsessive one is, the more
activated one’s orbital frontal cortex becomes.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_60
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
frontal cortex. The more obsessive one is, the more
activated one’s orbital frontal cortex becomes. Second, we grow anxious,
which leads us to try to correct the mistake. Brain imaging has shown that
the cingulated gyrus, which is informed about the mistake by the orbital
frontal cortex, triggers the dreadful anxiety that something bad is going to
happen by sending signals “to both the gut and the heart (p. 169). Finally,
when we have corrected the mistake, an automatic process occurs which
allows us to move on to the next thought or action.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_61
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
the mistake, an automatic process occurs which
allows us to move on to the next thought or action. The feeling of having
made a mistake and the anxiety associated with it disappear. The area
responsible for this shift is the caudate nucleus.
In people suffering from OCD this shift does not occur. Schwartz
explains:
The orbital frontal cortex and the cingulate turn on and stay on as though locked
in the ‘on position’ … Because the caudate doesn’t ‘shift the gear’ automatically,
the orbital frontal cortex and the cingulate continue to fire off their signals, increas-

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_62
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
atically,
the orbital frontal cortex and the cingulate continue to fire off their signals, increas-
ing the mistake feeling and the anxiety. Because the person has already corrected
the mistake, these are, of course, false alarms. The malfunctioning caudate is prob-
ably overactive because it is stuck and is still being inundated with signals from the
orbital frontal cortex.
(p.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_63
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
because it is stuck and is still being inundated with signals from the
orbital frontal cortex.
(p. 170)
Schwartz’s treatment is aimed at changing this problematic course of brain
activity, this incapacity to shift gears which accounts for the OCD function-
ing, by releasing the over intense tie between the orbital frontal cortex and
the cingulate and normalizing the activity of the caudate nucleus. The treat-
ment is comprised of two steps. First the patient learns to re-label what is
happening to him.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_64
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
eat-
ment is comprised of two steps. First the patient learns to re-label what is
happening to him. He understands that his obsessive thoughts are not real
(for example, he has not contracted an incurable disease), but rather that
398 Z. Carmeli and R. Blass
Int J Psychoanal (2013) 94 Copyright © 2013 Institute of Psychoanalysis
they are an expression of an OCD episode. In this way he forms an emo-
tional distance from them and can feel calm instead of anxious.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_65
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
isode. In this way he forms an emo-
tional distance from them and can feel calm instead of anxious. As part of
this he has to remind himself (in various ways) that the reason that the epi-
sode does not pass is the problematic connections in his brain. Focusing on
the structure of the obsession rather than its content, according to Sch-
wartz, is essential to this process.
The second step of this treatment involves the patient focusing on posi-
tive and pleasurable activities (for example, gardening, music, helping oth-
ers) whenever an obsessive episode occurs.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_66
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
activities (for example, gardening, music, helping oth-
ers) whenever an obsessive episode occurs. It is necessary to do something
distracting and in this way initiate the gearshift. Repeated practice of initi-
ating the shift creates flexibility in this mental capacity.
As in our previous illustrations, however, here too it may be seen that
brain research did not actually determine this model or the treatment in any
way. Any lay person who encountered someone with OCD would recognize
his ‘stuckness’, his inability to let go of ideas even though they are mis-
taken.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_67
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
would recognize
his ‘stuckness’, his inability to let go of ideas even though they are mis-
taken. At best, what Schwartz adds here is information regarding these
events’ correlates in the brain. Moreover, the therapeutic method of suggest-
ing to the patient that these brain correlates are responsible for the obses-
sive ideas is not in any way derived from brain research, but rather from
psychological understanding of what allows for emotional distancing.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_68
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
rain research, but rather from
psychological understanding of what allows for emotional distancing. The
claim that in this case PET scans “helped doctors both to understand a dis-
order and to develop a psychotherapy for it” (Doidge, 2007, p. 169) is com-
pletely groundless.
Schwartz, as well as Doidge, doubts the efficacy of alternative therapies,
pointing to their limited outcomes but more importantly to their limited
logic.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_69
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
ernative therapies,
pointing to their limited outcomes but more importantly to their limited
logic. They oppose a behavioural approach, which involves exposure to
anxiety arousing stimuli while preventing the obsessive-compulsive responses
to them (‘exposure and response prevention’) because it tends to increase
anxiety and for many patients arouses resistance. Thus it is helpful only to
half of those who suffer from OCD and even for them only to a limited
degree.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_70
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
it is helpful only to
half of those who suffer from OCD and even for them only to a limited
degree. Schwartz (and Doidge) also opposes cognitive approaches that
encourage directly confronting the irrationality of the obsessive thoughts
since the patients are aware of their irrationality. The problem is in the
emotional sphere. To teach someone to say ‘my hands are not dirty’ will
only involve him repeating something that he already knows, and will not
affect his feeling that they are.
This critique of alternative treatments of OCD further highlights the irrel-

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_71
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
feeling that they are.
This critique of alternative treatments of OCD further highlights the irrel-
evance of neuroscience to Schwartz’s treatment. For it may be seen that the
therapeutic approaches that Schwartz rejects are just as based (or rather un-
based) as his own on neuroscientific findings regarding plasticity. The pro-
viders of these treatments also think that the patient’s problem is that he is
stuck in his thoughts and actions and that their treatments offer him a way
to let go of these.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_72
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
is
stuck in his thoughts and actions and that their treatments offer him a way
to let go of these. The therapies they offer also rest on the notion that the
brain is plastic, that is, open to change. The therapies may differ from Sch-
wartz’s in their measured effectiveness, and they definitely do differ in
regard to the method applied to bring about change. But these differences
arise from different understandings of the kinds of human interactions that
The case against neuroplastic analysis 399
Copyright © 2013 Institute of Psychoanalysis Int J Psychoanal (2013) 94

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_73
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
t neuroplastic analysis 399
Copyright © 2013 Institute of Psychoanalysis Int J Psychoanal (2013) 94
create emotional distance and relieve ‘stuckness’. These are understandings
of a psychological rather than a neuroscientific kind.
In the context of alternative treatments, Doidge also mentions the
psychoanalytic treatment of OCD. He writes:
Psychoanalysts too have focused on the content of the symptoms, many of which
deal with troubling sexual and aggressive ideas.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_74
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
used on the content of the symptoms, many of which
deal with troubling sexual and aggressive ideas. They have found that an obsessive
thought, such as “I will hurt my child”, might express a suppressed anger at the
child, and that this insight might, in mild cases, be enough to make an obsession
go away. But this often does not work with moderate or severe OCD. And while
Schwartz believes that the origins of many obsessions relate to the kind of conflicts
about sex, aggression, and guilt that Freud emphasized, these conflicts explain only
the content, not the form of the disorder.
(p.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_75
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
that Freud emphasized, these conflicts explain only
the content, not the form of the disorder.
(p. 172)
It is here that we may begin to see that the brain research adduced in
favour of Schwartz’s treatment is not only, as we have shown, irrelevant to
it, but also has a negative impact on our capacity to understand the ways in
which disorders may be treated. This is because Schwartz’s focus on neural
correlates precludes the possibility of ever coming up with a content-
oriented explanation of OCD. Areas in the brain are associated with functions,
not with contents.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_76
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
-
oriented explanation of OCD. Areas in the brain are associated with functions,
not with contents. Recognizing the involvement of a certain area of the
brain may tell us that we are doing a mathematical calculation, but it can-
not tell us what the numbers involved in it are. It may tell us that we are
thinking of something frightening, but not that the frightening thought is of
white wolves rather than a big black spider.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_77
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
rightening, but not that the frightening thought is of
white wolves rather than a big black spider. This is not a limitation of the
state of the art of neuroscience, but inherent to the possibility of inferring
from biological states to specific thoughts (see Blass and Carmeli, 2007,
p. 25).
Thus, while therapists and researchers such as Doidge may regard Sch-
wartz’s brain research as evidence for a functional explanation of OCD, for
the preference of a form-oriented model over one of content, the fact of the
matter is that no such evidence is provided.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_78
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
rm-oriented model over one of content, the fact of the
matter is that no such evidence is provided. Schwartz does not find that
form is more important than content, but rather, in choosing a method of
investigation that examines neural correlates of OCD, he is limiting himself
to formal explanations; he is assuming rather than finding that they are
preferable.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_79
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
miting himself
to formal explanations; he is assuming rather than finding that they are
preferable. The value of content-oriented explanations are automatically
downplayed; they are regarded as possibly interesting, but not really a
sound basis for an effective cure, which from the neuroscientific standpoint
would have to be a form-oriented one.
The fact that content-oriented explanations are given short shrift is par-
ticularly strange in the context of OCD. This is because, while the OCD
patient may be more inclined to get stuck than others, he does not get
equally stuck on all ideas.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_80
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
patient may be more inclined to get stuck than others, he does not get
equally stuck on all ideas. Clearly, obsessive-compulsive tendencies tend to
find expression especially in relation to certain contents. So, prima facie ,
there seems to be very good reason to pay attention to content. To fail to
do so would be like explaining one’s love for a specific painting in terms of
a highly developed area in the brain that corresponds to an aesthetic capac-
ity. Such an explanation would be blatantly flawed since it would not
400 Z. Carmeli and R.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_81
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
capac-
ity. Such an explanation would be blatantly flawed since it would not
400 Z. Carmeli and R. Blass
Int J Psychoanal (2013) 94 Copyright © 2013 Institute of Psychoanalysis
explain why this painting is the object of the desire. To explain the specific
desire it would make sense to take into account something having to do
with the content of the painting.
It may also be seen that, in following the neuroscientific focus on form
rather than content, Doidge adopts a certain notion of what constitutes a
positive outcome of treatment – only symptom reduction, behavioural
change.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_82
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
n of what constitutes a
positive outcome of treatment – only symptom reduction, behavioural
change. Other kinds of treatment outcomes, such as self-integration or self-
understanding, require a concern with meaning. Here the opposition
between Doidge and the psychoanalytic perspective is pronounced. Psycho-
analysis is not only concerned with meanings and their integration, but
rather from a psychoanalytic perspective it would be wrong to steer the
patient away from content, or even further, as Schwartz does in the case of

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_83
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
d be wrong to steer the
patient away from content, or even further, as Schwartz does in the case of
obsessive thoughts and activities, to try to convince the patient that what
goes on in his mind and what he does are meaningless. It is part of the ana-
lytic task to understand these self-expressions and to do so in a way
that allows the patient to think, rather than be taught how he should be
thinking.
The differences between Doidge’s and Schwartz’s view and that of psy-
choanalysis are not due to any research findings.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_84
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
een Doidge’s and Schwartz’s view and that of psy-
choanalysis are not due to any research findings. Rather, they reflect a
choice about what constitutes valuable therapeutic development. The fact
that this is a choice gets lost when the focus on form rather than content is
presented as the approach better grounded in the hard science of brain
research. This is yet another detrimental effect of brain research on the
understanding and treatment of mental states.
Psychoanalysis and brain plasticity
The chapter that Doidge devotes specifically to psychoanalysis offers the

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_85
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
ysis and brain plasticity
The chapter that Doidge devotes specifically to psychoanalysis offers the
most striking example of negative consequences entailed by thinking of
human experience in neuroscientific terms. Because of its specific focus on
psychoanalysis, we will discuss this chapter in greater detail. First, we will
show how Doidge’s claims regarding the relevance of neuroplasticity to psy-
choanalysis are mistaken.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_86
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
ow how Doidge’s claims regarding the relevance of neuroplasticity to psy-
choanalysis are mistaken. We then discuss the negative consequences of
maintaining these mistaken claims.
In attempting to establish the connection between psychoanalysis and
brain research, Doidge relies heavily on a series of studies conducted by the
Nobel Prize laureate Eric Kandel. In one study, Kandel revealed the neural
correlates of learning processes (for example, learning to avoid shock) in
giant marine snails of the genus Aplysia. He went on to show how the snails
develop long- and short-term memory.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_87
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
snails of the genus Aplysia. He went on to show how the snails
develop long- and short-term memory. Later, together with molecular biolo-
gist James Schwartz, he revealed the molecular processes involved in the
development of long-term memory in these snails. Doidge writes:
They showed that in the snails, for short-term memories to become long-term, a
new protein had to be made in the cell. The team showed that a short-term mem-
ory becomes long-term when a chemical in the neuron, called protein kinase A,
moves from the body of the neuron into its nucleus, where genes are stored.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_88
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
alled protein kinase A,
moves from the body of the neuron into its nucleus, where genes are stored. The
protein turns on a gene to make a protein that alters the structure of the nerve end-
ing, so that it grows new connections between the neurons. Then Kandel, Carew,
The case against neuroplastic analysis 401
Copyright © 2013 Institute of Psychoanalysis Int J Psychoanal (2013) 94
and colleagues Mary Chen and Craig Bailey showed that when a single neuron
develops a long term memory for sensitization, it might go from having 1300 to

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_89
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
when a single neuron
develops a long term memory for sensitization, it might go from having 1300 to
2700 synaptic connections, a staggering amount of neuroplastic change.
(2007, p. 220)
Doidge then presents the conclusion drawn from this study. This conclusion
regards the effects of learning on the expression of our genes:
The same process occurs in humans. When we learn, we alter which genes in our
neurons are ‘expressed,’ or turned on …. Most people assume that our genes shape
us – our behavior and our brain anatomy.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_90
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
,’ or turned on …. Most people assume that our genes shape
us – our behavior and our brain anatomy. Kandel’s work shows that when we learn
our minds also affect which genes in our neurons are transcribed. Thus we can
shape our genes, which in turn shape our brain’s microscopic anatomy.
(p. 220)
Doidge then ties this to the process of psychotherapy. He writes:
Kandel argues that when psychotherapy changes people, “it presumably does so
through learning, by producing changes in gene expression that alter the strength

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_91
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
resumably does so
through learning, by producing changes in gene expression that alter the strength
of synaptic connections, and structural changes that alter the anatomical pattern of
interconnections between nerve cells of the brain.” Psychotherapy works by going
deep into the brain and its neurons and changing their structure by turning on the
right genes.
(p. 221)
It is here that the assumed link between psychoanalysis and neuroscience
emerges.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_92
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
t genes.
(p. 221)
It is here that the assumed link between psychoanalysis and neuroscience
emerges. The analyst is viewed as one who recognizes the plasticity of the
brain and, through the analytic treatment, attempts to alter neuronal net-
works. He is, so to speak, a “microsurgeon of the mind” (p. 221).
Following up on Kandel’s insight, Doidge tries to show that Freud him-
self emphasized the plastic nature of the brain and had knowledge in this
context that only much later was formally discovered by neuroscience.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_93
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
ain and had knowledge in this
context that only much later was formally discovered by neuroscience. For
example, he writes that: “The first plastic concept Freud developed is the
law that neurons that fire together wire together” (p. 221). Similarly, Doi-
dge says that: “To be changed, Freud argued, memories had to be con-
scious and become the focus of our attention, as neuroscientists have since
shown” (p. 225).

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_94
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
e con-
scious and become the focus of our attention, as neuroscientists have since
shown” (p. 225). “Most important”, Doidge explains:
Freud discovered that transference of early traumatic scenes could often be altered
if he pointed out to the patient what was happening when the transference was acti-
vated and the patient was paying close attention. Thus, the underlying neuronal
networks, and the associated memories, could be re-transcribed and changed.
(ibid.)
Doidge goes on to present not only Freud, but psychoanalytic theory in

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_95
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
scribed and changed.
(ibid.)
Doidge goes on to present not only Freud, but psychoanalytic theory in
general, as supportive of the notion of the plasticity of the brain.
While the detailed quotes from Kandel’s work in this context imply a
close tie between psychoanalysis and neuroscience, the fact is that the con-
nections are ambiguous and superficial. What Kandel’s studies clarified are
the neurological processes that are involved in memory formation and
402 Z. Carmeli and R.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_96
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
fied are
the neurological processes that are involved in memory formation and
402 Z. Carmeli and R. Blass
Int J Psychoanal (2013) 94 Copyright © 2013 Institute of Psychoanalysis
change and in the processes of learning. One could argue that psychother-
apy entails a learning process and changes in regard to memories and there-
fore also changes in the brain. But this tells us nothing meaningful about
psychoanalysis, nor does it point to how a neuroscientific approach affected
Freud’s psychoanalytic thinking, as Doidge claims it did.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_97
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
o how a neuroscientific approach affected
Freud’s psychoanalytic thinking, as Doidge claims it did.
Doidge stresses correlations between Freud’s analytic ideas and those of
neuroscientists. For example, both recognize the importance of making
memories conscious in order to facilitate change. However, these correla-
tions do not point to significant connections between the fields.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_98
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
e change. However, these correla-
tions do not point to significant connections between the fields. Neuroscien-
tists may recognize that memories have to be made conscious in order to be
changed (whatever that may mean), but this is not a neuroscientific finding.
So the fact that Freud also recognized this has no bearing on his relation-
ship to neuroscience.
To use an analogy: neuroscientists may recognize that one needs water to
live, but this does not mean that all those who recognize this necessity are
neuroscientists or support neuroscience.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_99
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
s not mean that all those who recognize this necessity are
neuroscientists or support neuroscience. Similarly, neuroscientists may
choose to describe the neuronal correlates of psychological phenomena that
Freud identified, such as transference, but this could not possibly be
regarded as evidence of Freud’s affiliation with neuroscience. If it were, and
one accepts that all psychological phenomena have neuronal correlates, then
all psychologists would be, by definition, equally affiliated with neurosci-
ence.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_100
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
correlates, then
all psychologists would be, by definition, equally affiliated with neurosci-
ence. In other words, it makes no sense to point to a special affiliation of a
psychological approach with neuroscience on the basis of the fact that the
phenomena it describes have neuronal correlates. One may assume that all
psychological phenomena have such correlates.
Another way in which Doidge ties psychoanalysis to neuroscience is
through pointing to the neuronal effects of psychoanalysis.
6 In this context
he cites Kandel’s statement that: “There is no longer any doubt … that psy-

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_101
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
ysis.
6 In this context
he cites Kandel’s statement that: “There is no longer any doubt … that psy-
chotherapy can result in detectable changes in the brain” (p. 233). But here
too one must question whether such effects point to a significant tie. For if
indeed all psychological events have neuronal correlates, then any psycho-
logical change would involve a change on the neuronal level. The question
would only be whether or not it is identified.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_102
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
involve a change on the neuronal level. The question
would only be whether or not it is identified. Moreover, pace Doidge, neu-
roscience’s ability to identify such changes following psychoanalysis contrib-
utes little to its validation as a form of treatment. If a psychological change
took place following analysis and no neuronal correlates were found, we
would not deny the effect; rather, we would assume that the available tech-
nology failed to identify it.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_103
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
not deny the effect; rather, we would assume that the available tech-
nology failed to identify it. Conversely, if changes in the brain were noticed
after treatment despite the fact that no meaningful psychological change
could be seen, we would hardly call it a success. Ultimately, what matters
in determining the effectiveness of a treatment is the psychological, not the
neurological, level of change.
Doidge, through a case report, further develops and illustrates his think-
ing regarding the relevance of neuroscience (and specifically its findings

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_104
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
d illustrates his think-
ing regarding the relevance of neuroscience (and specifically its findings
6It should be noted that the evidence that Doidge brings in this context are from studies of interpersonal
psychotherapy based on the approaches of Bowlby and Sullivan. And one may question whether it is
legitimate on the basis of such studies to draw conclusions regarding the effects of psychoanalysis.
The case against neuroplastic analysis 403

regarding plasticity) to psychoanalysis.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_105
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
013 Institute of Psychoanalysis Int J Psychoanal (2013) 94
regarding plasticity) to psychoanalysis. It is helpful to take a closer look at
this case since it allows us to gain insight into the negative impact of turn-
ing to neuroscience in the effort to understand mental phenomena. The case
is that of Mr L, a man in his 50s, incapable of forming significant emo-
tional ties. As soon as he would get romantically involved, he would start
backing off, feeling that: “There is a better woman elsewhere whom I’m
being denied” (p. 216).

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_106
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
tart
backing off, feeling that: “There is a better woman elsewhere whom I’m
being denied” (p. 216). He had been unfaithful to his wife and as a result
lost his marriage, an outcome he greatly regretted. At the same time, he
respected his wife and was not sure why he was unfaithful to her. And,
although he was devoted to his children, he felt attached to them through a
sense of duty rather than joyful affection.
Doidge describes Mr L’s difficult background. His mother died when he
was just over 2 years old, while giving birth to his sister.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_107
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
lt background. His mother died when he
was just over 2 years old, while giving birth to his sister. He then became ill
and was sent off to be looked after by relatives. Although he had suffered a
series of traumatic losses, Mr L did not think that these events had any real
influence on his life and did not feel any sadness about them. He had no
memories from age 4 or earlier, remembered little from his teenage years,
and spoke as though nothing that had happened to him had registered.
Nevertheless, there were clues that his losses did register: as he told his story

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_108
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
m had registered.
Nevertheless, there were clues that his losses did register: as he told his story
it seemed as though he was still in shock, and he was haunted by dreams in
which he was always searching for something.
To explain Mr L’s predicament, Doidge turns to developmental research.
He suggests that:
[An] important critical period lasts from approximately ten or twelve months to six-
teen or eighteen months, during which a key area of the right frontal lobe is devel-
oping and shaping the brain circuits that will allow infants both to maintain

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_109
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
rontal lobe is devel-
oping and shaping the brain circuits that will allow infants both to maintain
human attachments and to regulate their emotions. This maturing area … is called
the right orbitofrontal system .
(p. 226)
Doidge describes this developmental process on two levels, the first interper-
sonal and the second neuronal. This allows him to offer the following expla-
nation:
For children to know and regulate their emotions, and be socially connected, they
need to experience this kind of interaction many hundreds of times in the critical

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_110
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
connected, they
need to experience this kind of interaction many hundreds of times in the critical
period and then to have it reinforced later in life. Mr L lost his mother only a few
months after he completed development of his orbitofrontal system. So it fell on
others, who were themselves grieving and probably less attuned to him than his
mother would have been, to help him use and exercise his orbitofrontal system, lest
it begin to weaken … If others cannot help him soothe himself and regulate his own
emotions as his mother did, he learns to ‘autoregulate’ by turning off his emotions.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_111
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
gulate his own
emotions as his mother did, he learns to ‘autoregulate’ by turning off his emotions.
When Mr L sought treatment, he still had this tendency to turn emotions off and
trouble maintaining attachments.
(p. 227)
It should be clear by now that this kind of emphasis of neuronal correlates
of phenomena that are known through psychological study adds nothing to
our understanding. For example, we know because of infant observation,
404 Z. Carmeli and R.
