chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
ing to
our understanding. For example, we know because of infant observation,
404 Z. Carmeli and R. Blass
Int J Psychoanal (2013) 94 Copyright © 2013 Institute of Psychoanalysis
not the observation of brains, when what is considered to be normal devel-
opment takes place.
But beyond the irrelevance of the turn to neuroscience, this emphasis also
constricts Doidge’s ability to think about the patient, as may be seen in the
clinical material he goes on to present. Neuroscientific models constrict ana-
lytic thinking in two major ways.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_113
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
rial he goes on to present. Neuroscientific models constrict ana-
lytic thinking in two major ways. First, and as we already saw above, it
leads the analyst to focus on mental functions to which he can find brain
correlates. In this way he will tend to think about his patient’s problem in
terms of deficits – for example, the absence of some emotional ability as a
consequence of an undeveloped brain area – and ignore complicated con-
flicts between meaningful ideas (see Deutsch and Deutsch, 2007).

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_114
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
area – and ignore complicated con-
flicts between meaningful ideas (see Deutsch and Deutsch, 2007). Second,
even when focused on content rather than the form of his patient’s words,
he will tend to understand his problems in terms of simple associations
between well-defined ideas. This is because the subject of neuroscience being
physical matter is concerned as it is with well-defined and discrete observa-
ble events.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_115
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
nce being
physical matter is concerned as it is with well-defined and discrete observa-
ble events. It cannot address complex associations between ideas, symbols
and phantasies, because these rely on contexts of meaning that are holistic
rather that discrete in nature (see Davidson, 1980). Consequently, an ana-
lyst inspired by neuroscientific research will seek similarly simple explana-
tions and will be predisposed to make connections only between discrete
phenomena, such as between two cognitive functions.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_116
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
posed to make connections only between discrete
phenomena, such as between two cognitive functions. His interpretations
too will be focused on well-defined and discrete phenomena that will render
them almost behaviouristic in nature.
Let us see how this plays out in Doidge’s analytic case. Doidge describes
Mr L’s emotional life and his actions as consequences of (a) developmental
deficits that obstructed the formation of important emotional functions and
(b) associations that developed between certain life events and the experi-
ence of a state of threat and anxiety.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_117
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
s that developed between certain life events and the experi-
ence of a state of threat and anxiety. With this view that emphasizes the
direct impact of real life events, the transference that evolves is also viewed
as a realistically positive one, with the analyst actually providing the missing
maternal functions and in this way furthering the developmental process.
Doidge writes:
Past and present were being mixed up together, and a transference was being acti-
vated.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_118
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
ge writes:
Past and present were being mixed up together, and a transference was being acti-
vated. At this point I, as an analyst, did what an attuned mother does, when she
develops the orbitofrontal system, by pointing out emotional ‘basics’ – helping him
name his emotions, their triggers, and how they influenced his mental and bodily
states. Soon, he was able to spot the triggers and emotions himself.
(2007, p.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_119
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
is mental and bodily
states. Soon, he was able to spot the triggers and emotions himself.
(2007, p. 230)
Doidge explains that in the transference the brain recognizes the early
maternal pattern of relationship, a view that fits nicely with simple neurosci-
entific models, but leaves no room for the idea that internal phantasies are
finding expression in the transference. Indeed, no such ideas are discussed
by Doidge – not even in a theoretical context.
The simple, observable approach of neuroscience also finds expression in
Doidge’s view of memory.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_120
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
.
The simple, observable approach of neuroscience also finds expression in
Doidge’s view of memory. Guided by neuroscientific findings according to
which trauma damages the hippocampus and the ability to form explicit
The case against neuroplastic analysis 405
Copyright © 2013 Institute of Psychoanalysis Int J Psychoanal (2013) 94
long-term memories, Doidge suggests that Mr L’s limited explicit memory
from his early years and adolescence is due to a shrinking of the hippocam-
pus following trauma. When Mr.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_121
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
s early years and adolescence is due to a shrinking of the hippocam-
pus following trauma. When Mr. L was in his 20s, Doidge claims, the hip-
pocampus regrew, apparently as a result of improvement in relation to Mr
L’s depression. This, according to Doidge, explains why Mr L has memories
from that age onwards.
The idea that repression may be responsible for Mr L’s limited memory
is not raised as a possibility. Doidge immediately adopts the physical
damage option.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_122
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
imited memory
is not raised as a possibility. Doidge immediately adopts the physical
damage option. It is not presented as a hypothesis, or one possibility
among other more dynamic explanations, but rather is offered as real and
certain. But, of course, whether events were never registered or are being
repressed could hardly be a matter of certainty (see Blass and Carmeli,
2007, pp. 24 –5).
To illustrate the problem: Doidge acknowledges that one of Mr L’s few
memories is seeing his mother at her funeral, but he knows this only from
some associations to a dream.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_123
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
ries is seeing his mother at her funeral, but he knows this only from
some associations to a dream. It seems that, if Mr L had not mentioned
this, Doidge would have concluded (wrongly in his own view) that no mem-
ories of the funeral were registered due to damage to the hippocampus.
Moreover, Doidge’s focus on physical damage also leaves no room for the
question of the meaning of Mr L’s memories. Only the fact of their presence
or absence is of concern to Doidge.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_124
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
the meaning of Mr L’s memories. Only the fact of their presence
or absence is of concern to Doidge. Here, too, Doidge abandons the com-
plexity of analytic thinking and practice.
The choice of simple and physically oriented explanations is particularly
notable in Doidge’s description of the role of the dream in psychoanalytic
thinking. He writes:
Why are dreams so important in analysis, and what is their relationship to plastic
change? Patients are often haunted by recurring dreams of their traumas and awa-
ken in terror.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_125
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
tic
change? Patients are often haunted by recurring dreams of their traumas and awa-
ken in terror. As long as they remain ill, these dreams don’t change their basic
structure. The neural network that represents the trauma … is persistently reacti-
vated … Should these traumatized patients get better, these nightmares gradually
become less frightening …
(p. 238)
In other words, dreams are central to psychoanalysis because of their role
in representing trauma.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_126
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
In other words, dreams are central to psychoanalysis because of their role
in representing trauma. The neglect of the wealth of psychoanalytic thinking
regarding the dream is striking.
Such neglect becomes even more striking in Doidge’s interpretations of
his patient’s dreams. The dreams’ contents are interpreted as direct and self-
evident symbols of early traumatic events, which are only mildly disguised.
For example, Mr L reports regarding one of his dreams: “I am searching
for something, I know not what, an unidentified object, maybe a toy, which

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_127
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
dreams: “I am searching
for something, I know not what, an unidentified object, maybe a toy, which
is beyond familiar territory … I’d like it back again” (p. 217). Reflecting on
this, Doidge states that, although Mr L comments on the fact “that the
dream represented ‘a terrible loss’ … remarkably, he did not link it to the
loss of his mother or family” (p. 217). For Doidge the link is obvious. Mr
L’s failure to take note of it is, therefore, remarkable. More complex asso-
ciative possibilities are not explored.
406 Z. Carmeli and R.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_128
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
efore, remarkable. More complex asso-
ciative possibilities are not explored.
406 Z. Carmeli and R. Blass
Int J Psychoanal (2013) 94 Copyright © 2013 Institute of Psychoanalysis
Another blatant example of Doidge’s constricted perspective on the clini-
cal material may be seen in relation to the final dream brought in the analy-
sis, the one regarding the funeral of Mr L’s mother. Mr L says: “I saw my
mother playing the piano, and then I go to get someone, and when I return,
she is in a coffin” (p. 237).

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_129
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
r playing the piano, and then I go to get someone, and when I return,
she is in a coffin” (p. 237). This dream led Mr L to an association that he
felt to be an actual memory of the situation in which he saw his mother in
her coffin. Consequently, he felt the loss with great intensity: “He let out a
loud wail and, overcome with primitive grieving, his whole body convulsed
for ten minutes” (p.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_130
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
ut a
loud wail and, overcome with primitive grieving, his whole body convulsed
for ten minutes” (p. 237).
At this point, Doidge wonders if the events described were actually
remembered or whether they were fantasized, based on the patient’s wish
that he could remember the event that he experienced at the age of
26 months. Doidge does not reject outright the possibility of fantasy being
involved here, but he is quite certain of it being an actual memory.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_131
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
e possibility of fantasy being
involved here, but he is quite certain of it being an actual memory. In sup-
port, Doidge mentions that a relative confirmed that the patient was present
at the funeral and that the coffin was open and presents research that mem-
ory at that age is possible. Once again, for Doidge the central issue is the
question of the reality of the memory.
In sum, we have seen here how the attempt to integrate neuroscience with
psychoanalysis has a negative impact on the appreciation and utilization of
psychoanalytic thinking and practice.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_132
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
has a negative impact on the appreciation and utilization of
psychoanalytic thinking and practice. Doidge’s understanding of analytic
patients can centre only on deficits, not conflict, since this is what the
neuroscientific models can allow for and encourage (see Deutsch and Deu-
tsch, 2007, p. 351). Freud’s complex thinking on the dream, which encom-
passed ideas on repressed wishes and conflicts and their relationship with
various aspects of the individual’s life and forms of processes, is replaced by
the extremely simple and one-dimensional view of the dream as a method

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_133
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
of processes, is replaced by
the extremely simple and one-dimensional view of the dream as a method
for dealing with trauma. Again, this shift is not based on an in-depth cri-
tique of Freudian theory or practice (which may be legitimate) but simply
on the basis of the adoption of a model of explanation drawn from the
world of neuroscience. It is when such models which, as we have argued,
cannot encompass content or complexity are applied without warrant to the
realm of the understanding of the meanings and motives of human thought,

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_134
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
ied without warrant to the
realm of the understanding of the meanings and motives of human thought,
feeling and action, that analytic thinking and practice becomes deprived of
what is most essential to it.
Although Doidge surprisingly does not mention it, this chapter’s title,
‘Turning Our Ghosts into Ancestors’, is an oft-cited metaphor introduced
by Hans Loewald in his 1960 paper, ‘On the therapeutic action of psycho-
analysis’. There, Loewald described the process of change that takes place
through working with the transference.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_135
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
re, Loewald described the process of change that takes place
through working with the transference. He wrote:
In the daylight of analysis the ghosts of the unconscious are laid and led to rest as
ancestors whose power is taken over and transformed into the newer intensity of
present life, of the secondary process and contemporary objects.
(Loewald, 1960, p. 29)
The transformations Loewald described involve complex psychic processes.
Sadly, in an effort to portray analysis as a neuroplastic treatment supported
The case against neuroplastic analysis 407

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_136
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
o portray analysis as a neuroplastic treatment supported
The case against neuroplastic analysis 407
Copyright © 2013 Institute of Psychoanalysis Int J Psychoanal (2013) 94
by brain research, Doidge’s chapter on psychoanalysis severely constricts
and distorts not only the conceptualization of these processes, but also the
nature of psychoanalysis itself.
Concluding reflections
In this paper, we examined recent claims that evidence regarding the
brain’s neuroplasticity can significantly influence psychological understand-
ing and development and is very relevant for psychoanalysis.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_137
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
ly influence psychological understand-
ing and development and is very relevant for psychoanalysis. Through a
close study of Norman Doidge’s book The Brain that Changes Itself ,w e
showed that these neuroscientific findings are irrelevant to the psychologi-
cal and psychoanalytical processes described. Moreover, we pointed out
how regarding such findings as relevant to psychological and psychoana-
lytic processes poses an obstacle to the development of in-depth under-
standing.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_138
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
al and psychoana-
lytic processes poses an obstacle to the development of in-depth under-
standing. As we have seen, when one thinks in terms of the
neuroscientific correlates of psychological processes, dimensions of mean-
ing and content are ignored as factors determining psychological states.
This is because the neuroscientific data can at best be shown to correlate
with broad formal dimensions, such as the presence of certain kinds of
affective states, or the activation of a certain kind of mental mechanism,
but not with specific ideas.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_139
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
ctive states, or the activation of a certain kind of mental mechanism,
but not with specific ideas. It may indicate the presence of thought pro-
cesses associated with mathematics, but not the numbers of which a per-
son is thinking. And it would never be able to tell us of the infinite range
of associations a person has with those ideas, and the complex ways in
which they interrelate in our minds and actions.
If one holds that psychoanalysis is defined by its concern with meaning
and that its view of pathology and development is intimately tied to self-

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_140
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
its concern with meaning
and that its view of pathology and development is intimately tied to self-
understanding and integration, one must conclude that it stands diametri-
cally opposed to treatments which adopt the formal focus of neuroscience.
For Doidge, there is no such opposition; but accordingly his view of
psychoanalysis is a very limited one. It deals with deficits and with general
and simple events, but not with the complex, multidimensional and ever-
changing world of meaning, phantasy and conflict.
Another negative consequence of wrongly considering neuroscience to be

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_141
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
ning, phantasy and conflict.
Another negative consequence of wrongly considering neuroscience to be
relevant to psychological change is that it supports the illusion that knowl-
edge of the brain and its plasticity could be therapeutic. Thus we are invited
to devote our resources and energy to biological inquiry, while in fact this
cannot help.
Pointing to the irrelevance of the findings on neuroplasticity and their
harm further grounds ideas we put forth in our earlier critique of neuropsy-
choanalysis (Blass and Carmeli, 2007).

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_142
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
unds ideas we put forth in our earlier critique of neuropsy-
choanalysis (Blass and Carmeli, 2007). In that earlier work we addressed
studies which argued that neuroscientific knowledge could be valuable to
psychoanalysis because it provides information regarding dimensions of the
person that are concrete and stable in nature, in contrast to the amorphous
and changing nature of psychological phenomena.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_143
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
and stable in nature, in contrast to the amorphous
and changing nature of psychological phenomena. Here we addressed stud-
ies that value the contribution of neuroscience to psychoanalysis because it
provides information regarding the brain’s unstable nature, its plasticity.
While the plasticity perspective is more attuned to ongoing environmental
408 Z. Carmeli and R. Blass
Int J Psychoanal (2013) 94 Copyright © 2013 Institute of Psychoanalysis
influences on the brain, it fails to recognize that these influences can take
infinite possible forms, the effects of which cannot be foreseen.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_144
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
ze that these influences can take
infinite possible forms, the effects of which cannot be foreseen. It also fails
to recognize that, as a consequence of this complexity, what can be learned
from the study of the brain per se is sharply limited. Thus, what neurosci-
ence primarily adds to psychological understanding is only anecdotal infor-
mation regarding corollaries to psychologically described processes.
In the case of neuroplasticity, this anecdotal level seems especially trivial.
It is a kind of translation to biological language of what is known by com-
monsense.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_145
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
ally trivial.
It is a kind of translation to biological language of what is known by com-
monsense. We all know that people learn. Referring to this process as one
of training the brain adds nothing. People change. To say that they are
expressing neuroplasticity adds nothing to our psychological understanding.
Similarly, it is meaningless to say that because Freud knew that people
change, that understanding and experience modify the way one feels and
acts, he offered ‘neuroplastic therapy’.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_146
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
understanding and experience modify the way one feels and
acts, he offered ‘neuroplastic therapy’. Chris McManus, Professor of Psy-
chology and Medical Education at University College London, emphasizes
this point in the sole strikingly critical review of Doidge’s book (the review
appeared in The Psychologist ). McManus quips: “Should your behaviour
change as a result of reading this review, then perhaps I also [like Freud]
am a ‘neuroplastician’” (2009, p.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_147
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
a result of reading this review, then perhaps I also [like Freud]
am a ‘neuroplastician’” (2009, p. 40).
Given the triviality of translating psychological phenomena into the lan-
guage of plasticity, some explanation of its popularity is in order. In our
earlier work we tied its appeal to the biologistic ethos of our contemporary
culture, the view that what is real is biological (Blass and Carmeli, 2007,
p. 36; see also Brothers, 2002, p. 869).

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_148
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
that what is real is biological (Blass and Carmeli, 2007,
p. 36; see also Brothers, 2002, p. 869). The enthusiastic reception of Doi-
dge’s book in the popular press highlights this cultural trend, as may be
seen in an excerpt from The New York Times review, which appears on the
book’s cover. It reads: “The power of positive thinking finally gains scien-
tific credibility”.
McManus maintains that the kind of brain-based analysis of psychologi-
cal functioning and processes presented in Doidge’s book – “neurobabble”
as he refers to it – should only be of interest to psychologists if they are

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_149
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
s book – “neurobabble”
as he refers to it – should only be of interest to psychologists if they are
“sexing up grant applications, or persuading sceptical university administra-
tors that psychology is actually serious science” (2009, p. 40; Brothers
makes a similar point [2002, p. 869]). It seems, however, that in the course
of the search for recognition and support, many psychologists and psycho-
analysts have actually come to believe that being able to refer to neuroscien-
tific correlates of psychological phenomena is indeed what makes their
profession scientifically respectable.

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_150
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
elates of psychological phenomena is indeed what makes their
profession scientifically respectable. Perhaps others know better, but tolerate
the neuropsychoanalytic discourse so that psychoanalysis may benefit from
the appreciation that neuropsychoanalysis’s purported scientific status sup-
posedly endows. The consequence has been that, up until now, there has
been no serious criticism of Doidge’s book in the psychoanalytic literature.
As we have made clear in the course of this paper, such tolerance and
support of the approach that Doidge’s book presents are problematic, par-

chunks.id: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf_151
chunks.source: The case against neuroplastic analysis  A further illustration of the irrelevance of neuroscience to psychoanalysis through a critique of Doidge s The.pdf
chunks.text:
paper, such tolerance and
support of the approach that Doidge’s book presents are problematic, par-
ticularly in light of its negative implications for how psychoanalysis is
understood and practised.

The feeling brain: Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis
by Mark Solms
Karnac Books, London, 2015; 240 pp; £23.04
One hundred and twenty years ago, Freud commenced his transition from
neurologist to psychoanalyst and furnished us with his ‘Project for a scien-
tific psychology’ of the mind. So began a necessary divergence from the
dominant biological doctrine of the day.

chunks.id: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_5
chunks.source: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
ogy’ of the mind. So began a necessary divergence from the
dominant biological doctrine of the day. The feeling brain attempts to
provide us with an accessible bridge back, between these two pursuits and
between brain and mind, through an exploration of the various facets of the
emerging discipline of neuropsychoanalysis. Solms and colleagues seek, in
doing so, not to “prove Freud right or wrong but rather to finish the job he
started; namely of introducing the psyche to the field of neuropsychology”.
The collected papers presented together raise to our awareness the poten-

chunks.id: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_6
chunks.source: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
ield of neuropsychology”.
The collected papers presented together raise to our awareness the poten-
tial for that process to become more fully realized, with the trajectory of
discussion focused first on neurological and then psychiatric conditions
before the implications for the understanding of normal mental functioning
are considered. Through this broad arc, detractors and naysayers are antici-
pated and at points, countered.

chunks.id: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_7
chunks.source: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
dered. Through this broad arc, detractors and naysayers are antici-
pated and at points, countered. The fact that their identities move between
neuroscientist, behaviorist and even psychoanalyst, relates no doubt to the
discipline of neuropsychoanalysis itself, as not wholly represented within
any of the other fields. In considering the place for psychoanalytic
understanding, Solms limits himself almost exclusively to those findings of
Freud, drawing upon a similar capacity to integrate these different fields
into something new.

chunks.id: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_8
chunks.source: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
s of
Freud, drawing upon a similar capacity to integrate these different fields
into something new. That he writes, as a result, in a manner that
556 Book and Journal Reviews
Int J Psychoanal (2017) 98 Copyright © 2016 Institute of Psychoanalysis

approaches the style of Freud might offer some comfort through this, at
times, foreign landscape.
As a starting point, the mind is considered as both subject and object.
Neuropsychoanalysis places itself as a link to the findings of the ‘science of
the mind as an object with those of the mind as a subject’.

chunks.id: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_9
chunks.source: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
link to the findings of the ‘science of
the mind as an object with those of the mind as a subject’. Initial discussions
are given over to the historical, philosophical and scientific foundations to
neuropsychoanalysis, together offered as argument against a reductionist
solution to the mind-body problem. Psychoanalysis does not, we might agree,
simply study the emergent properties of the brain as epiphenomena of a bio-
logical ‘reality’.

chunks.id: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_10
chunks.source: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
ree,
simply study the emergent properties of the brain as epiphenomena of a bio-
logical ‘reality’. The difference between psychoanalysis and neuroscience
instead, Solms holds, rests upon the perceptual surface that we use, with the
former directing observations internally and the latter to the external. In this,
his theory of ‘dual-aspect monism’, both disciplines merit an important posi-
tion, with neuropsychoanalysis offering the potential for correlation between
the two; a view stated at the outset and emphasized at regular intervals.

chunks.id: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_11
chunks.source: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
l for correlation between
the two; a view stated at the outset and emphasized at regular intervals.
Solms hopes through this endeavor to redress a perceived imbalance; specifi-
cally that neuroscientific research has not historically recognized as important
the nature of the subjective experience. He notes the emergence of a new plat-
form from which this work can fruitfully take place, citing advances through
the last century in affective and social neuroscience, neuropsychology and
attachment theory as central in the relating of mind to brain.

chunks.id: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_12
chunks.source: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
al neuroscience, neuropsychology and
attachment theory as central in the relating of mind to brain.
Accounts of discrete neurological conditions provide a fascinating and
grounded account of therapeutic work within the developing interface
between psychoanalysis and cognitive neuroscience. Firstly, in his discussion
of patients with right hemispheric brain injury, Solms explores resultant loss
of bodily functioning as a profound narcissistic wound, with associated feel-
ings stemming from dependency upon the affected body part, perceived as a
lost object.

chunks.id: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_13
chunks.source: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
ciated feel-
ings stemming from dependency upon the affected body part, perceived as a
lost object. Despite suffering broadly similar insults to their brain that are
considered as breaching the integrity of the body ego in this way, however,
he discovers radically different emotional symptoms and groups of defensive
reactions. Their origins are traced to unique, earlier psychological traumata
that may only be understood psychologically.

chunks.id: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_14
chunks.source: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
s are traced to unique, earlier psychological traumata
that may only be understood psychologically. Again, then, the argument is
underlined that mental functions can never be found inside neuroanatomical
structures, but may instead be said to exist between them such that one can-
not be reduced to the other. In short, the mind is recognized as being no
less real than the brain.
Secondly, a case of Korsakoff’s syndrome highlights how some of the
meta-psychological abstractions derived from Freud’s works might begin to
find their correlates in anatomical structures.

chunks.id: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_15
chunks.source: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
tractions derived from Freud’s works might begin to
find their correlates in anatomical structures. The amnesia and tendency to
confabulation is well known in Korsakoff’s syndrome to be linked to dam-
age to an area of the brain just in front of the third ventricle. What is newly
expounded, however, is the dynamic interplay resulting when the reality-
monitoring part of the mind is weakened in this manner, leaving something
to fill the gap in memory deficit.

chunks.id: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_16
chunks.source: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
g part of the mind is weakened in this manner, leaving something
to fill the gap in memory deficit. The resultant confabulation is not mean-
ingless at all, we find, but symbolically connected and conforming to all the
principal characteristics of the unconscious. The hope is proffered that in
studying further neurological syndromes that also display a release of
aspects of primary process functioning, we might not only make further

Book and Journal Reviews 557
Int J Psychoanal (2017) 98Copyright © 2016 Institute of Psychoanalysis
links between psychoanalytic theory and physical correlates, but also under-
stand more of the composite elements to secondary process functioning.
Thus Solms and colleagues argue, under the umbrella term of neuropsycho-
analysis, in favor of the two disciplines being mutually enriching.
Consideration given to the phenomena of depression and addiction
extends the suggested territory for neuropsychoanalytic enquiry, with the

chunks.id: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_18
chunks.source: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
depression and addiction
extends the suggested territory for neuropsychoanalytic enquiry, with the
link between psychiatric conditions and physiological correlates also being
highlighted. Extrapolating from the findings of animal-based studies of
emotional brain development within affective neuroscience, the prevailing
current psychiatric understanding about the aetiology of these disorders is
challenged.

chunks.id: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_19
chunks.source: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
prevailing
current psychiatric understanding about the aetiology of these disorders is
challenged. Depression, viewed as the pathological state of mourning first
set down by Freud, is contextualized in relation to the now known physio-
logical processes of separation distress encountered during the absence of
an attachment figure. A premature shutting down of seeking behaviour
aimed at recapturing the lost object accounts for depressive symptoms both
physiologically and psychoanalytically.

chunks.id: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_20
chunks.source: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
uring the lost object accounts for depressive symptoms both
physiologically and psychoanalytically. Under such examination, serotonin
depletion is relegated from causative to a correlate of depression.
Correlation is found in studying addiction by this same method. Addic-
tion is discussed as a failure to transition from auto-erotic self-soothing to
mastery of the real world and attainment of a secure love object. Viewed as
an object-less state akin to masturbation, the parallel voiced first by Freud
is again invoked.

chunks.id: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_21
chunks.source: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
as
an object-less state akin to masturbation, the parallel voiced first by Freud
is again invoked. Affective neuroscience additionally now highlights that the
physiological processes involved in seeking the lost object may become
blunted. Individuals then come to learn, erroneously, that substances gener-
ating a physiological reward may enable them to gain access to further plea-
surable experiences and lost attachment figures.

chunks.id: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_22
chunks.source: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
rd may enable them to gain access to further plea-
surable experiences and lost attachment figures. Substituting addiction for
the lost objects of sexual and social interaction offers up again a focus to
successful treatment and so we glean, through Solms’ discussion of the dis-
orders of depression and addiction, the potential fruits of a marriage
between psychoanalytic and physiological understandings.

chunks.id: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_23
chunks.source: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
iction, the potential fruits of a marriage
between psychoanalytic and physiological understandings. Together, direct-
ing investigation into the core basis of each disorder offers more effective
integrated interventions to be realized.
In turning finally to dreams and to the subject of consciousness, we are
offered examples of how neuropsychoanalysis may be usefully applied to
normal mental life. Solms flies the flag for the place of psychoanalysis as
equal partner to contemporary neuroscience. Some interesting findings
emerge.

chunks.id: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_24
chunks.source: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
of psychoanalysis as
equal partner to contemporary neuroscience. Some interesting findings
emerge. Freud’s inferences, derived of course through the ‘subjective’
method of analysis, about the causes and functioning of dreams appear
compatible with and supported by the latest objective neuroscientific
research. For instance, the close link outlined between those brain structures
responsible for dreaming and those responsible for emotions and motivation
is consistent with the notion that dreams are triggered by an arousing stim-
ulus, giving expression to instinctual drives.

chunks.id: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_25
chunks.source: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
otion that dreams are triggered by an arousing stim-
ulus, giving expression to instinctual drives. In keeping with Freud’s concept
of regression within the psychic apparatus during dreaming there does also
appear to be a neuropsychological correlate in the now known movement
of activity from motor system (dorsolateral frontal cortex) to perceptual
system (occipito-temporo-parietal area) of the brain.

chunks.id: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_26
chunks.source: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
m (dorsolateral frontal cortex) to perceptual
system (occipito-temporo-parietal area) of the brain. These recent neurosci-
entific findings arise on the back of Freud’s dream theory having been con-
558 Book and Journal Reviews
Int J Psychoanal (2017) 98 Copyright © 2016 Institute of Psychoanalysis
sidered previously debunked. This not only speaks to Freud’s own genius in
being ahead of his time (and in this area until recently, of our time too),
but also to the historically acrimonious relationship between cognitive
science and psychoanalysis that now has the potential to begin a useful

chunks.id: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_27
chunks.source: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
ationship between cognitive
science and psychoanalysis that now has the potential to begin a useful
working through.
In dealing with the subject of consciousness, the role of neuropsychoanal-
ysis in testing Freud’s theories against the evidence base of neuroscience is
brought into sharp focus. This is not to assume a biased function that
serves to vindicate psychoanalytic theory, however, but instead to extrapo-
late from and in some cases overturn previous understandings.

chunks.id: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_28
chunks.source: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
ory, however, but instead to extrapo-
late from and in some cases overturn previous understandings. Freud’s
famous maxim that the ego is first and foremost a bodily ego gains new
ground through, most notably, the link to affective neuroscience. Here
higher cortical external and phylogenetically older internal body representa-
tional systems are discussed, with the former corresponding to the ego and
the latter to the id. Of special interest is the proposition then arising for an
affective consciousness, generated by the id and forming a background state
of being.

chunks.id: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_29
chunks.source: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
rising for an
affective consciousness, generated by the id and forming a background state
of being. The id is considered conscious. Moreover, the ego is itself consid-
ered unconscious, transforming this ‘affective consciousness’ into mental
solids, or object representations, to establish (master) predictions about
external reality and reduce the experience of surprise and uncertainty about
reality.

chunks.id: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_30
chunks.source: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
ictions about
external reality and reduce the experience of surprise and uncertainty about
reality. These predictions can then be rendered unconscious.
Solms considers cognitive neuroscience as ‘neurotic’ in having failed to
recognize and give space to the importance of the affective dimension of the
mind. To do otherwise, it must allow itself to be surprised by reality and
generate a more suited ‘mental solid’. I add to this the need to establish a
priori the capacity to endure not knowing, to inhabit a state of ‘negative
capability’.

chunks.id: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf_31
chunks.source: The feeling brain  Selected papers on neuropsychoanalysis.pdf
chunks.text:
establish a
priori the capacity to endure not knowing, to inhabit a state of ‘negative
capability’. This book is also extending the same invitation to psychoanaly-
sis, in the hope of a more creative engagement with the reality of both brain
and mind. As Solms concludes, what could be more fascinating than that?

Abstract: It is commonly believed that consciousn ess is a higher brain function. Here we 
consider the likelihood, based on abundant ne uroevolutionary data that lower brain 
affective phenomenal experiences provide the “energy” for the developmental construction 
of higher forms of cognitive consciousness. Th is view is concordant with many of the 
theoretical formulations of Sigmund Freud. In this reconceptualization, all of consciousness 
may be dependent on the original evolution of affective phenomenal experiences that 
coded survival values.

chunks.id: The id knows more than the ego admits .pdf_3
chunks.source: The id knows more than the ego admits .pdf
chunks.text:
ependent on the original evolution of affective phenomenal experiences that 
coded survival values. These subcortical ener gies provided a foundation that could be used 
for the epigenetic construction of perceptual  and other higher forms of consciousness.  
From this perspective, perceptual experiences were initially affective at the primary-process 
brainstem level, but capable of being ela borated by secondary learning and memory 
processes into tertiary-cognitiv e forms of consciousness.

chunks.id: The id knows more than the ego admits .pdf_4
chunks.source: The id knows more than the ego admits .pdf
chunks.text:
orated by secondary learning and memory 
processes into tertiary-cognitiv e forms of consciousness. With in this view, although all 
individual neural activities are unconscious, perhaps along with secondary-process learning 
and memory mechanisms, the primal sub-neoc ortical networks of emotions and other 
primal affects may have served as the sentient  scaffolding for the construction of resolved 
perceptual and higher mental activities with in the neocortex.

chunks.id: The id knows more than the ego admits .pdf_5

chunks.text:
ng for the construction of resolved 
perceptual and higher mental activities with in the neocortex. The data supporting this 
neuro-psycho-evolutionary vision of the emerge nce of mind is discussed in relation to 
classical psychoanalytical models.

1. Introduction 
Our aim here is to introduce a novel way of integr ating affective and cognitive aspects of conscious

3. Freud’s Notion of Unconscious Mental Processes 
The notion that the brain knows more than it conscious ly admits can be traced  back historically to 
the clinical and conceptual wo rk of Sigmund Freud. He based this notion, which was considered 
radical at the time, upon observations he made of  post-hypnotic suggestion an d clinical states of 
dissociation, where behaviors were demonstrably caused by motivations of which the subject was not

explicitly aware, some of which could subseque ntly be brought to awareness during psychological 
treatment. Since a scientific acc ount of mental life cannot exclude unconscious cognitions with such 
demonstrable causal effects, Freud concluded that the objects of psychology must include unconscious 
processes, notwithstanding the conventional equation of “mind” with consciousness [5]. Thus, Freud 
devoted the remainder of his scientific life to studying the unconscious mental processes.

6. The Exteroceptive Fallacy  
The close parallelism between the brain mechanisms  for the external and in ternal aspects of body 
representation, on the one hand, and the functional prope rties of the ego and id on the other, reveal a 
stark contradiction between current affective neuroscience concepts of mind and those of Freud.

chunks.id: The id knows more than the ego admits .pdf_98
chunks.source: The id knows more than the ego admits .pdf
chunks.text:
a 
stark contradiction between current affective neuroscience concepts of mind and those of Freud. In this 
respect Freud inaugurated the conflation of unc onscious processes with cognitive unawareness of 
instinctual consciousness, thereby prematurely rele gating unmonitored affective processes into the 
“unconscious” category (see [29], and the accompanying commentaries). As we will see, this practice 
oversimplifies the varieties of conscious and unconscious processes that actually exist.

chunks.id: The id knows more than the ego admits .pdf_99

chunks.text:
practice 
oversimplifies the varieties of conscious and unconscious processes that actually exist. 
To begin to expose this problem, we need to po int out that Freud never questioned the classical 
assumption that consciousness was a cortical function: 
“What consciousness yields consists essentiall y of perceptions of excitations coming from 
the external world and of feelings of pl easure and unpleasure which can only arise from 
within the mental apparatus; it is therefore possible to assign to the system Pcpt.-Cs. a 
position in space.

lodged on the surface of the brain instead of be ing safely housed somewhere in its inmost

The “state” of consciousness as a whole is generated in the upper brainstem. We have known this 
for many years. A mere decade after the death of Freud, Moruzzi and Magoun [42] first demonstrated 
that global consciousness, in the sense measured by EEG activation, is generated not by exteroceptive

above) “a unique opportunity to stu dy the neuronal substratum of consciousness” ([43], p. 480).

11. If the Id Is Conscious… 
The realization that Freud’s id is intrinsi cally conscious has massive implications for 
psychoanalysis, biological psychiatry, and our understanding of the nature of mind. This turn of events 
could be profound, not least because when Freud famous ly proclaimed “where id was, there shall ego 
be” ([57], p. 80) as the therapeutic goal of his “tal king cure”, he assumed that  the ego enlightened the 
id.

. 80) as the therapeutic goal of his “tal king cure”, he assumed that  the ego enlightened the 
id. It now appears more likely that the opposite happens; reflexive “talking” is apt to dampen and 
constrain core consciousness. How is  this fact to be reconciled with  the stated aim of psychoanalytic 
therapy, namely the undoing of re pressions? And what are the implic ations for other approaches to 
psychotherapy and psychiatry?  
To just begin to answer this question, it seems r easonable to suggest that repression must involve 
withdrawal of declarative awareness ( autonoetic

variety of feelings in addition to actual surprise—tha t requires the affective presence of the id (of the

of reflexive awareness, automatization of a mental-b ehavioral algorithm before it actually fits the bill.

The irony of the foregoing historical -scientific review is that Fre ud might appear to have done a 
disservice to psychology by denying consciousness its pride of place. But this is not really the case.

anyone speaks of consciousness we know immediately and from our most personal

13. In Conclusion 
Our goal here was to re-establish a primary-pr ocess affective foundation of mind to the higher 
mental apparatus that is receiving the lion’s share of attention in cognitive science and cognitive 
neuroscience, as well as consciousness and psychoanalytic studies. We chose to frame our argument in 
classical Freudian psychoanalytic theory, since during the 20th century, perhaps he came closest to the 
vision we have shared.

vision we have shared. Although he, in the modern vein, situated consciousness on top of the brain, the 
weight of evidence now indicates that raw affects arise from the “basement” of the brain. Our argument 
has been largely restricted to the basement, a nd we recognize that when it is interfaced with 
unconscious secondary learning-memory and the re sulting affectively energized cognitive thought 
processes, there will be vast additional complexiti es to be faced, along with  the possibility of many

Even though emotions are central in many counselling modalities, how
best to work with emotions has not often been clearly articulated or
practically presented for counsellors.

Defining our terms: emotion regulation
The concept of emotion regulation emerges as one of the most far-ranging and influential processes
at the interface of emotion and cognition (Koole,
2009, p. 4). It involves the “ability to respond to the
ongoing demands of experience with a range of emotions in a manner that is socially tolerable and
sufficiently flexible to permit spontaneous reactions as well as the ability to delay spontaneous reac-
tions as needed ” (Cole, Michel, & Teti,

eactions as well as the ability to delay spontaneous reac-

1994, p. 73). A lack of healthy emotion regulation has been
implicated in many forms of psychopathology (Neacsiu, Bohus, & Linehan, 2013), in social difficulties
(Lopes, Salovey, Côté, & Beers, 2005) and even physical illness (Sapolsky, 2007). Contemporary
research on emotion regulation has its roots in the study of psychological defences, psychological
stress and coping (Lazarus, as cited in Gross & Thompson,

Discussions of clinical intuition have remained in the academic shadows for several reasons.

Discussions of clinical intuition have remained in the academic shadows for several reasons.
Intuitive insights are often seen as idiosyncratic and ineﬀable, being intimately related to implicit
meanings and emotional salience rather than to observable cognitions and behavior, which
renders them diﬃ cult to quantify. While evidence-based research tends to consider subjective
experience to be “soft science” (McWilliams, 2013), psychoanalytic writings often assign it
a privileged status that shapes external reality i tself (Coburn, 2009).

Abstract: 
 
Recent advances in the cognitive, affective and social neurosciences have enabled these fields to study 
aspects o f the mind that are central to psychoanalysis. These developments raise a number of 
possibilities for psychoanalysis.

some have voiced concerns about their potentially deleterious effects on psychoanalytic the ory and 
practice.

1. Introduction 
 
Psychoanalysis and neuroscience have either ignored each other or were in a state of mutual hostility 
through most of the twentieth century. The few notable exceptions (e.g. Pribram and Gill, 1976) have 
steadily increased over the last twenty years ( for a review see Fotopoulou, 2012b), as proponents of 
these divergent approaches to the human mind gradually realized that they might have something to 
gain from an interdisciplinary dialogue (Kandel, 1998; 1999).

ed that they might have something to 
gain from an interdisciplinary dialogue (Kandel, 1998; 1999). Th is evolving dialogue, despite (or 
perhaps because of) its inherent complexities , has aroused considerable interest. It was generally 
welcomed in both fields as a source of new insights and fresh perspectives (Crick and Koch, 2000; 
Fonagy, 2004; Kernberg, 2004; Mayes, 2003; Michels and Roose, 2005; Nagera, 2001; Northoff and 
Boeker, 2006; Panksepp, 1998; Ramachandran, 1994; Semenza, 2001; Shevrin, 2002; Shulman and 
Reiser, 2004; Watt, 2000).

pp, 1998; Ramachandran, 1994; Semenza, 2001; Shevrin, 2002; Shulman and 
Reiser, 2004; Watt, 2000). However, the rapprochement between psychoanalysis and the 
neurosciences also aroused deep concerns on both sides ( Brothers, 2002; Hobson, 2004, 2005; 
Mechelli, 2010; Pulver, 2003).  
 
In this paper, we initially sketch the development of neuropsychoanalysis and its impact and reception 
in both fields. We then focus on the concerns expressed in psychoanalysis regarding the theoretical 
foundations and scope of neuropsychoanalysis .

pressed in psychoanalysis regarding the theoretical 
foundations and scope of neuropsychoanalysis . In address ing these concerns we  place special 
emphasis on the historical and philosophical (ontological and epistemological) issues at the heart of 
the relation between psychoanalysis and the neurosciences. To the best of our knowledge, Blass and 
Carmeli (2007) have put forward the most extensive critiq ue of neuropsychoanalysis in the 
psychoanalytic literature to date. They have repeated many of their arguments in an expanded, more 
recent book review (Carmeli and Blass, 2013).

repeatedly throughout this paper. While a  full discussion of the clinical applications of 
neuropsychoanalysis is beyond the scope of this paper , we offer and discuss a brief case illustration 
in order to demonstrate our view that neuroscientific findings can – and should – be used to inform 
and enrich the ways in which analysts work with their patients.

Justifying psychoanalysis
I coined the term neuropsychoanalysis in 1999 not to give
psychoanalysis ‘a fashionable prefix’ but to describe the efforts
of a group of scientists attempting to integrate our findings on
the same part of nature, derived from different viewpoints. We
believed integration was necessary because the capacity of the
brain to feel subjective states has significant implications for
how it works; feelings have causal effects and mean something.
Freud was not the only scientist to explore this perspective, but
he did so more systematically than anyone before him.

ly scientist to explore this perspective, but
he did so more systematically than anyone before him. The
resulting body of hypotheses is called psychoanalysis. The advent
of neuropsychoanalysis coincided with the emergence of new
methods capable of correlating hypotheses derived from the
objective and subjective perspectives, and thereby correcting
viewpoint-dependent errors. Ramus

Conclusions
The aim of this review was to bridge an existent gap
between neurobiological and clinical models of emotion
regulation and psychotherapy by reviewing the evidence
for the involvement of the neural substrates of executive

and of semantic processes, and by formulating possible
mechanisms through which modifications of semantic
processes may bring about change that is not only adap-
tive but is also associated with better regulation.

their importance in internal accounts of what psychother-
apy is about, semantic processes have been neglected in
current neurobiological models of the mechanism of psy-
chotherapy. Drawing on the dual-process framework,
these models posit increased activation of prefrontal areas
and decreased activation in limbic areas when participants
are exposed to emotional stimu li, representing successful
recruitment of control processes in the context of emotion
regulation.

l on the Research Topic
The Interface between Psychoanalysis and Neuroscience: the State of the Art
The Research Topic “The Interface Between Psychoanalysis and Neuroscience: The State of the
Art” was cross-linked in two Frontiers journals: Frontiers in Human Neuroscience and Frontiers
in Psychology and the contributing authors could choose to submit their ar ticle to the journal
that best suited the research content. Among the 11 contribu tions ﬁnally accepted, 7 have been
published in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience and the other 4 in Frontiers in Psychology.

chunks.id: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf_4
chunks.source: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf
chunks.text:
have been
published in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience and the other 4 in Frontiers in Psychology. This
balanced distribution between the two journals is in line wi th the wide range of topics dealt with
by the various authors, from the theoretical reviews aiming at converging psychoanalytic concepts
with discoveries in neuroscience, to the neuroscientiﬁc in vestigation of the mechanisms involved
in psychodynamic psychotherapy.
The Research Topic includes articles presented in the form of Rev iew, Hypothesis and Theory,
Perspective Article, and Original Research Article.

chunks.id: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf_5
chunks.source: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf
chunks.text:
in the form of Rev iew, Hypothesis and Theory,
Perspective Article, and Original Research Article.
The implicit question posed to the contributors was to oﬀer thei r point of view on the
usefulness of combining a theoretical psychoanalytic approach with an empirical-experimental one
derived from neuroscientiﬁc studies. The idea was to encour age an overall theoretical expansion
capable of promoting a more complex vision of the mental and psychi c functioning underlying
scientiﬁc research.

chunks.id: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf_6
chunks.source: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf
chunks.text:
omoting a more complex vision of the mental and psychi c functioning underlying
scientiﬁc research. A validation of psychoanalytic theorie s has not been deliberately indicated
as the purpose of the Research Topic, in favor of a possible and bidi rectional conjugation of
the same theories with empirical evidence, with the belief th at a conceptual enlargement of
psychic and cerebral functioning could be an indispensable ne cessity both for psychoanalysis
and for neuroscience. As expected, the authors answered the q uestion starting from diﬀerent
perspectives.

chunks.id: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf_7
chunks.source: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf
chunks.text:
neuroscience. As expected, the authors answered the q uestion starting from diﬀerent
perspectives. In papers of a more theoretical nature, some autho rs have placed psychoanalytic
concepts at the basis of neuroscientiﬁc reﬂection, whereas o thers applied a psychodynamic theory
of mind to beneﬁt the interpretation of empirical neuroscient iﬁc evidence. Still other authors have
designed experimental studies aimed at investigating psychi c mechanisms that were not explicitly
conceived according to a psychoanalytic theoretical framew ork, but that paved the way for a re-

chunks.id: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf_8
chunks.source: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf
chunks.text:
ly
conceived according to a psychoanalytic theoretical framew ork, but that paved the way for a re-
evaluation and reconceptualization of psychoanalytic conce pts themselves. Finally, for some, these
mixed aspects represented the starting point for implementing t herapeutic approaches in speciﬁc
mental disorders.
In particular, several authors have used a framework of the discoveries that derive from Aﬀective
Neuroscience: one paper investigated the instinctive compone nt of the imagination, combining
cardinal concepts of psychoanalytic theory (dynamic mental s tructures such as Unconscious

chunks.id: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf_9
chunks.source: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf
chunks.text:
ombining
cardinal concepts of psychoanalytic theory (dynamic mental s tructures such as Unconscious
di Giannantonio et al. Editorial: Neuroscience-Psychoanalysis Interface
Fantasies) with the function of the basic emotional-motiva tional
systems, especially the SEEKING SYSTEM, in a neuro-
ethological context, possibly leading to perspective changes in
psychology and psychotherapy (
Alcaro and Carta ); another
article highlighted diﬀerent components of aggression,
especially the Dominance motivational/emotional system,
at the basis of competitive behaviors in human relationships,

chunks.id: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf_10
chunks.source: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf
chunks.text:
inance motivational/emotional system,
at the basis of competitive behaviors in human relationships,
often compromised in diﬀerent mental disorders (
Giacolini
and Sabatello).
Another neuroscientiﬁc model, based on the centrality of th e
Default Mode Network and Cortical Midline Structures in the
expression of Self, was used in relation to a psychodynamic
perspective, with consequent, important clinical and
therapeutic implications.

chunks.id: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf_11
chunks.source: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf
chunks.text:
n to a psychodynamic
perspective, with consequent, important clinical and
therapeutic implications. Some authors conceived multiple
levels of the Self (relational alignment, self-constituti on, self-
manifestation, self-expansion), corresponding to diﬀerent
levels of personality organization, theorizing for the ﬁrst time
an integrated neurobiological and clinical personality mod el
in which spontaneous brain activity plays a fundamental
role (
Scalabrini et al. ).

chunks.id: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf_12
chunks.source: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf
chunks.text:
sonality mod el
in which spontaneous brain activity plays a fundamental
role (
Scalabrini et al. ). According to other authors, a similar
neuropsychodynamic perspective could be useful to conceive an
imbalance between the Default Mode Network and the Executive
Network as a core feature in depressive disorders, hypothesiz ing
therapeutic interventions aimed at contrasting this imbala nce
by acting on speciﬁc mechanisms of compensation and defense
(
Boeker and Kraehenmann).
Focusing on unresolved trauma in mothers, a neuroscientiﬁc

chunks.id: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf_13
chunks.source: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf
chunks.text:
n and defense
(
Boeker and Kraehenmann).
Focusing on unresolved trauma in mothers, a neuroscientiﬁc
perspective of the Attachment Theory (in particular, the Dynamic
Maturational Model of Attachment and Adaptation—DMM) is
used to investigate the reorganization of their attachment style
and the neurobiological correlates underlying the behavio ral
response of adaptation to motherhood (
Iyengar et al.).
The experience of pleasure, starting from classic
psychoanalytic concepts of instinct and aﬀect, is conceptually
enriched in the light of studies on primary-process emotional

chunks.id: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf_14
chunks.source: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf
chunks.text:
f instinct and aﬀect, is conceptually
enriched in the light of studies on primary-process emotional
feelings with a consequent reﬂection on libido-independent
intrinsic motivations and their role in structuring self-r elated
processes (
Moccia et al.).
Among the authors who promote the importance of
the link between psychoanalytic theories and neuroscientiﬁ c
investigations for therapeutic approaches for speciﬁc psychic
disorders, the proposal of emotional regulation as a central ability
favoring a balanced defensive structure in healthy psycholo gical
functioning stands out (

chunks.id: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf_15
chunks.source: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf
chunks.text:
ability
favoring a balanced defensive structure in healthy psycholo gical
functioning stands out (
Frederickson et al.).
Also the interrelation between a theoretical approach based on
Embodied Cognition studies and classical psychoanalytic th eory
frames the therapeutic proposal of authors who suggest the
importance of psychoanalytic psychodrama for the treatment
of internet addiction disorder and eating disorders, which is
proposed to stimulate a recovery of the Embodied Self with
respect to the excessive Narrative Self (
Scorolli et al.).
Moreover, a reﬂection on improving the speciﬁcity

chunks.id: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf_16
chunks.source: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf
chunks.text:
the excessive Narrative Self (
Scorolli et al.).
Moreover, a reﬂection on improving the speciﬁcity
of therapeutic approaches is presented in the context
of pharmacotherapy and its psychic meaning within a
psychoanalytical treatment (
Iannitelli et al.).
Finally, with a focus on unconscious processes, two Original
Research Articles propose interesting results both on the
unconscious inﬂuence of phonological ambiguity detection i n
response to subliminal stimuli, correlated with the defensiv e
personality structure of the subject (
Bazan et al.

chunks.id: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf_17
chunks.source: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf
chunks.text:
liminal stimuli, correlated with the defensiv e
personality structure of the subject (
Bazan et al. ) and on
the eﬀects of 3-Hz binaural beat stimulation on sleep stages
(
Jirakittayakorn and Wongsawat).
In addition to the satisfactory number of published articles ,
our Research Topic has garnered considerable interest among
readers. In our opinion, this represents the signal of a growin g
interest in the area of dialogue between psychoanalysis and
neuroscience, the response to the need of both disciplines to
broaden their horizons in the direction of the complexity of

chunks.id: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf_18
chunks.source: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf
chunks.text:
nse to the need of both disciplines to
broaden their horizons in the direction of the complexity of
the human being, in which a separation between psychic and
neurobiological functioning can no longer be hypothesized.
Psychoanalysis represents a most complex theoretical model
of the human mind and could be a useful stimulus for
neuroscientiﬁc research oriented toward the subjectivity and the
relational nature of human experience, and the importance of
unconscious processes.

chunks.id: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf_19
chunks.source: the interface between psychoanalysis i neurosciences.pdf
chunks.text:
ctivity and the
relational nature of human experience, and the importance of
unconscious processes. On the other hand, while remaining two
distinct areas, adequately designed neuroscientiﬁc resea rch can
contribute to an expansion of the metapsychological perspectives
of psychoanalysis itself.
Much work certainly remains to be done and the present
Research Topic is not representative of all the areas of interes t
currently investigated in neuropsychoanalysis; yet, in our opinion
it represents a fruitful stimulus to move forward in a deﬁnite ly
constructive direction.

to bridge neuroscience and psychoanalysis.

europsychoanalysis is a new school of thought attempting
to bridge neuroscience and psychoanalysis. Yet few
neuroscientists and psychiatrists would have heard of it
if it had not recently received public support from notable
neuroscientists. The present paper discusses whether such
support is warranted.

I have no doubt that the respected neuroscientists mentioned
above condemn all these abuses and show indefectible commitment
to evidence-based psychology and psychiatry. But they should think
twice before making any statement that may be interpreted as a
rehabilitation of psychoanalysis (unless they have stunning new
data to reveal, of course). They should be aware of all the
consequences of unduly preserving the popularity of psycho-
analysis.

If psychoanalysis is to be rehabilitated, this will have to be on
the basis of its own merits. It is not enough for empirical research
to tackle the influence of early life experiences, the neural
correlates of unconscious processing, or the decoding of dream
content using neuroimaging, to support psychoanalysis as such,
even if Freud happened to use the same words.
